abstract: The insatiable memory bandwidth demands of deep learning foundation models and edge artificial intelligence are bottlenecked by the Von Neumann bottleneck: the continuous energy-prohibitive shuttling of weights and activations between off-chip dynamic RAM (DRAM) and processor arithmetic logic units (ALUs). Magnetoresistive Random Access Memory (MRAM), anchored by magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) exhibiting Perpendicular Magnetic Anisotropy (PMA), establishes a non-volatile, radiation-hardened, and virtually wear-out-free memory technology capable of high-density integration alongside sub-5nm CMOS logic. By exploiting Spin-Transfer Torque (STT) and emerging three-terminal SpinOrbit Torque (SOT) switching mechanisms, MRAM enables ultra-fast write speeds (~ns) and zero standby leakage power. Furthermore, integrating MTJ crossbar arrays into non-volatile In-Memory Computing (IMC) architectures allows matrix-vector multiplications (MVM)—the dominant workload in neural network inference—to be executed natively inside memory via Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws with sub-nanosecond latency and massive energy reduction. title: Theory of Barrier Numbers: Digit-Dependent Truncation, Non-Associative Arithmetic, and the Virtual Tail Concept
abstract: We study a decimal truncation rule called the barrier map: a zero digit stops an expansion when its immediately preceding fractional digit is less than five. We define its domain and canonical representation, prove finite termination for every base-ten normal number, and exhibit irrational inputs for which termination fails. On terminating inputs, the map is an idempotent projection onto a subset of the nonnegative terminating rationals. We derive truncation and square-root residual bounds and show that addition followed by barrier projection is commutative but non-associative. For independent uniform decimal digits, overlapping stopping patterns are handled by a two-state Markov chain, yielding an expected stopping index of 22. Computed examples include square roots, the golden ratio, and π. The virtual tail is interpreted as discarded numerical information. Connections with quantum measurement, horizons, and finite physical information are discussed as motivations; no derivation of quantum mechanics, physical mass, or information conservation is claimed.

abstract: Abstract The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) is revolutionizing the healthcare industry through connected medical devices and real-time data exchange. However, the sensitive nature of this data requires a security infrastructure capable of resisting both current and future threats, including those posed by quantum computing. The system utilizes Kyber, a lattice-based quantum-resistant algorithm, to mitigate future quantum threats. title: Rational Quantum Mechanics
abstract: AbstractStandard quantum mechanics is formulated using complex Hilbert spaces, real-valued probabilities, continuous one-parameter dynamics, and—where particles and fields have continuous degrees of freedom —function spaces constructed over continua such as R3 . In that precise mathematical sense, the real and complex continua are deeply embedded in the standard theory. It does not follow, however, that experiments have demonstrated the physical existence of an uncountable set of exact real numbers, still less that individual quantum systems physically “store” infinitely many digits. Every preparation, control operation, and measurement has finite precision, and many quantum predictions can be approximated arbitrarily closely using countable or finite descriptions.This distinction matters because the continuum is sometimes blamed for quantum theory's conceptual strangeness. title: Reinforcement learning to disentangle multiqubit quantum states from partial observations
abstract: Using partial knowledge of a quantum state to control multiqubit entanglement is a largely unexplored paradigm in the emerging field of quantum interactive dynamics with the potential to address outstanding challenges in quantum state preparation and compression, quantum control, and quantum complexity. title: Learning to stabilize nonequilibrium phases of matter with active feedback using partial information
abstract: Abstract Recent advances in quantum computing experiments have enabled new pathways for feedback control. Here, we investigate the role of information in interactive quantum many-body dynamics to engineer out-of-equilibrium phases of matter. To this end, we train reinforcement learning agents to prevent entanglement spreading in $(1{+}1)$-dimensional stabilizer circuits with up to $128$ qubits. We find that, above an information threshold, agents learn stochastic near-optimal strategies that prevent the system from reaching volume-law entangled states and instead stabilize area-law scaling. These strategies rely on bottlenecks that divide the system and cap the entanglement in the steady state. Crucially, learned strategies are inherently out of equilibrium, require real-time active feedback, and could not be reproduced by simple human-designed control rules. This work establishes the foundations for information-driven individual control of many interacting quantum degrees of freedom, demonstrating the capabilities of reinforcement learning to stabilize and uncover novel critical properties of many-body nonequilibrium steady states.

title: Quantum chaos diagnostics for non-Hermitian systems from bi-Lanczos Krylov dynamics
abstract: In Hermitian systems, Krylov complexity has emerged as a powerful diagnostic of quantum dynamics, capable of distinguishing chaotic from integrable phases, in agreement with established probes such as spectral statistics and out-of-time-order correlators. By contrast, its role in non-Hermitian settings, relevant for modeling open quantum systems, remains less understood due to the challenges posed by complex eigenvalues and the limitations of standard approaches based on orthogonality, such as singular value decomposition. Here we demonstrate that Krylov complexity, computed via the bi-Lanczos algorithm, provides a reliable probe of quantum chaos in non-Hermitian systems, clearly discriminating chaotic and integrable regimes. Our results agree with complex spectral statistics and complex spacing ratios, underscoring the robustness of the method. Universality is supported by extensive tests in the non-Hermitian Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and random-matrix ensembles across multiple non-Hermitian symmetry classes, with further validation provided by the non-Hermitian random-field XXZ model as a pseudo-Hermitian system.

title: Spectrum analysis with quantum dynamical systems. II. Finite-time analysis
abstract: The prequel to this work [Ng et al., Phys. Rev. A 93, 042121 (2016)] proposes the method of spectral photon counting to enhance noise spectroscopy with an optical interferometer. While the predicted enhancement over homodyne detection is promising, the results there are derived by taking an asymptotic limit of infinite observation time; their validity for a finite time remains unclear. To validate the theory, here we perform a numerical study of a finite-time model. Assuming that the signal is an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process with an unknown variance parameter, we evaluate the Fisher information for homodyne detection, a lower bound on the Fisher information for spectral photon counting, and a quantum upper bound, all without taking the infinite-time limit. To confirm that the Fisher-information quantities are satisfactory precision measures, we also compute the errors of the maximum-likelihood estimator by Monte-Carlo simulations. The results demonstrate that the Fisher-information quantities and the estimation errors all smoothly approach their asymptotic limits, and the advantage of spectral photon counting over homodyne detection can remain substantial for finite times.

title: Plasma conductivity from warm dense matter to the Spitzer limit using mean-force kinetic theory
abstract: A theoretical model is developed to compute electronic transport coefficients extending from warm and dense to hot and dilute plasma conditions. This kinetic theory-based approach models strong Coulomb correlations by treating interactions using the potential of mean force, electron degeneracy using the Uehling-Uhlenbeck equation, and diffraction by computing cross sections quantum mechanically. The result provides a fast and accurate means to compute electrical conductivity,thermal conductivity and electrothermal coefficients, including contributions from electron-electron interactions. The model enables accurate calculation of materials properties in many warm dense matter systems, including inertial confinement fusion, stellar evolution, and high energy density plasma experiments.

abstract: With current advances in gravitational wave (GW) detection made by the worldwide LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) network of detectors, ever-more sensitive tests of gravity in the strong-field regime are now possible. abstract: More than a century after the 1925 foundations of quantum mechanics, quantum theory has become the standard formulation of atomic physics. Yet practical computation remains difficult because the many-body problem scales exponentially with system size. With today’s far more powerful computing resources and advances in mathematical algorithms, these calculations can increasingly be carried out more systematically and with greater completeness. In this thesis, we present two main contributions. In the first contribution, we introduce an alternative real-space framework, termed the Embedded Unit-Cell (EUC) method, for accurate band structure calculations in solid-state physics and electronics. abstract: The electro-optic effect, describing a change in refractive index of a material under an electric field, enables high-speed optical information transfer supporting internet technologies, photonic transceivers for data centers, and cryogenic quantum computing architectures. Here, we engineer an exceptional electro-optic response based on electric field-driven “lateral swaying” of the ferroelectric polarization vector between symmetry-equivalent monoclinic variants in strain-stabilized KNbO3 thin films. These results establish low-symmetry ferroelectric phases as an unexploited materials design space for superior electro-optic performance, enabling energy-efficient modulators for classical and quantum photonic integrated circuits.

abstract: EÏRŌQ-Φ develops an exact mathematical framework for determining which environmental correlations a controlled qubit can reveal—and which future control operations can be certified while those correlations remain partially unknown. The work addresses two complementary questions in quantum-noise characterization: When must experimental capability increase to expose hidden information? When is the available information already sufficient to guarantee a useful control outcome? Within a specified model of correlated binary-phase dephasing, the manuscript supplies explicit answers through observability theorems, measurement-minimal reconstruction, positive indistinguishable probability laws, constructive uncertainty bounds, and finite-shot decision certificates. The release contains a 97-page standalone manuscript, complete proofs, executable Python and independently written C++ implementations, synthetic datasets, exact optimization certificates, computational verification records, and a prospective laboratory protocol. title: Data for: Defect-engineered N/Te-doped graphene for lithium adsorption and voltage behavior: A first-principles study
abstract: Optimized structures, calculation inputs and computed energies supporting the article "Defect-engineered N/Te-doped graphene for lithium adsorption and voltage behavior: A first-principles study" (RSC Advances). The dataset covers pristine, vacancy-defected and N/Te-doped graphene (5×5 supercell) with and without one adsorbed lithium atom, studied with density functional theory (PBE-D3 with spin–orbit coupling) in Quantum ESPRESSO. It contains: the 13 substrates and 13 lithiated systems in their final configurations; all dopant arrangements and lithium adsorption sites of the configurational search; the reference calculations (isolated Li atom, bulk Li, graphene, N₂, bulk Te) used for adsorption energies, open-circuit voltages and formation energies; and the HSE06 inputs for pristine graphene and G@2Te@1N-Li. Each structure is provided as a CIF file and as the Quantum ESPRESSO input of the single-point calculation that gave its total energy. Total energies, adsorption energies, open-circuit voltages, formation energies and Bader charges are listed in CSV files. See README.md for the folder layout, naming conventions and formulas.

title: Thermal variational quantum simulation of quantum many-body systems
abstract: The thermal variational quantum simulation (TVQS) framework offers a promising hybrid classical- quantum approach for preparing Gibbs states on near-term quantum devices, but its original formulation requires independent optimization at each inverse temperature, leading to inefficient resource use and lack of temperature consistency. We introduce a full-temperature-VQS (FTVQS) algorithm that learns Gibbs states simultaneously across a continuous interval of inverse temperatures 𝛽 by minimizing the expected variational free energy under a uniform prior of 𝛽. The global loss is bounded below by the expectation of the exact free energy. Key innovations include a Legendre–Gauss quadrature for deterministic integration of global loss with 4 nodes achieving high accuracy, a temperature embedded Bernoulli parametrization, and a warmup cosine annealing Adam optimizer. Numerical experiments on 5-qubit XY and XXZ Heisenberg chains demonstrate that a single training run suffices to compute the free energy, internal energy, and entropy over 𝛽 ∈[0.2,1.5] with relative errors below 2% for the free energy, while preserving the self-verification property. title: A Historical Note on Macro-Atom Theory and the First Proposal of Superconducting Quantum Computing
abstract: This note documents early theoretical work on voltage-biased Josephson junctions in the historical context of superconducting quantum computing. The work was published in two papers in 1994 and 1996. Motivated by efforts to understand the anticipated band structures associated with Bloch oscillations in small Josephson junctions, the theoretical analysis instead showed that, in the weak-dissipation regime, a voltage-biased Josephson junction could behave as an atom-like quantum system with discrete energy levels. Based on a Hamiltonian formulation, the energy spectra and wave functions of these macroscopic quantum systems (behaving as macro-atoms) were derived. Relaxation times and spectral linewidths were also analyzed using theoretical tools developed in laser and NMR spectroscopy. Although experimental verification of the theory was still lacking at that time, the two papers explicitly noted the possibility of engineering these macro-atoms as atomic and molecular switches, possibly for quantum computing.

title: Dynamical polarizability of particles in triangular potential wells: exact results and Airy zero sum rules
abstract: Abstract Linear potentials feature in countless physical models of both experimental and theoretical relevance, a prime example being triangular quantum wells formed at material interfaces with built-in electric fields. Yet, the eigenstates contain non-elementary Airy functions Ai( )x with associated eigenvalues that can only be found numerically. We show here that the dynamical polarizability describing the optical response of triangular quantum wells can be computed exactly yielding simple and compact expressions. Both single-and double-sided triangular quantum wells are analysed, while imposing either Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions for the former. Upon Taylor-expanding the frequency dependence, the polarizabilities produce infinitely many exact sum rules among the zeros of Ai( )x and Ai ( ) x  . As an application, sum rules have been utilized to compute exact relativistic energy corrections.

New results on the quantum security analysis of lightweight block cipher Simeck
abstract: Abstract Simeck demonstrates reliable resistance against conventional cryptanalytic attacks and offers sound security properties, making it a noteworthy design in the field of lightweight cryptography. Nevertheless, ongoing progress in quantum computing poses a potential threat to the security of Simeck, underscoring the need for a rigorous analysis of its quantum resilience. In this paper, we analyze quantum distinguishers and key-recovery attacks on Simeck in the Q2 model. Leveraging the connection between truncated differentials and periodic functions, we revisit Simon-type qCPA distinguishers for Simeck-32/48/64 and further extend them to the qCCA setting. The qCPA distinguishers cover 8/9/11 rounds of Simeck-32/48/64, matching the round numbers reported by Lu et al. (2026), whereas our qCCA distinguishers cover 10/11/13 rounds. Based on these distinguishers, we investigate their application to Grover-meets-Simon key-recovery attacks on reduced-round Simeck. Furthermore, we mount qCPA key-recovery attacks on 11/12/14-round Simeck-32/48/64 and extend them to qCCA attacks on 13/14/16-round Simeck-32/48/64. title: Optical gain of zinc-blende InGaN quantum wells across the green–orange gap from atomistically determined alloy broadening
abstract: No semiconductor laser diode yet covers the green–orange gap (540–620 nm) between the wavelength limits of wurtzite InGaN and AlGaInP. Zinc-blende (cubic, ZB) InGaN quantum wells grown along (001) carry no spontaneous or piezoelectric polarization, so the quantum-confined Stark effect that limits polar c-plane wells at high indium content is absent in principle. We treat these wells with an eight-band k ⋅ p model with self-consistent Poisson coupling and Berggren–Sernelius bandgap renormalization. We first map the coherent design space and find that 3.1 nm wells remain coherent up to an indium composition of x ≈ 0.36, which covers the green-to-red range. We then compute the inhomogeneous broadening from atomistic alloy-disordered supercells. This linewidth is not fitted to any spectrum and sets an intrinsic lower bound on the broad linewidths measured so far. title: Non-Kinetic Propagation Dynamics: Macroscopic Electromagnetism as a Quantum Excitation Cascade and the Collapse of the Drude Model
abstract: This paper challenges the classical Drude kinetic model of electron propagation by proposing the Non-Kinetic Propagation framework. In this approach, macroscopic electromagnetism within industrial crystalline lattices, such as electric motor stators, is redefined as a quantum excitation cascade rather than a classical particle collision process. By utilizing Hamiltonian matrices and the transfer integral, we demonstrate that structural anomalies—traditionally interpreted as localized Joule heating or mechanical vibration—are macroscopic manifestations of wave function collapse and localized phononic emission. title: Qanela: A framework proposal for designing portable quantum assembly languages across different quantum computing platforms
abstract: The diversity of quantum hardware platforms creates significant algorithm portability challenges, with each platform employing distinct instruction sets, gate implementations, and physical constraints that hinder software reusability. This paper presents a framework for designing portable quantum assembly languages enabling seamless cross-platform execution. Through systematic profiling of Shor’s, Grover’s, and QAOA algorithms on IBM Qiskit, Microsoft Q#, and Google Cirq — 3,216 executions of identical, reference-validated logical circuits — we identify key portability challenges and derive empirically grounded design criteria from execution-pattern analysis. title: Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array
abstract: Abstract Silicon spin qubits offer a promising path to scalable quantum computing due to their compatibility with industrial semiconductor manufacturing. A key requirement for scaling quantum processors is the ability to perform high-fidelity operations in parallel across many qubits. However, simultaneous control remains a major challenge in silicon devices, as fidelities typically degrade under parallel operation. Here we identify microwave-drive-induced a.c.-Stark shifts as the dominant source of this degradation in a five-qubit silicon spin array. We address this by introducing a scalable mitigation protocol based solely on pairwise phase calibrations. Using tailored control pulses on a shared control line, we achieve primitive X and Y gate fidelities well above 99.99% for each qubit individually, with some approaching 99.999%. Furthermore, these fidelities are preserved above 99.99% during simultaneous operation of up to three qubits. During parallel five-qubit operation, fidelities remain above the widely targeted fault-tolerant threshold of 99.9%. title: Cosmology, decoherence and the second law
abstract: A bstract We consider quantum decoherence and entropy increase in early universe cosmology. We first study decoherence in a discrete bipartite quantum system for which a single qubit gets entangled with an environment and the entropy increase is correlated with the decay of the off-diagonal terms of the reduced density matrix. We compare this system with continuous systems relevant for cosmology for which there is a natural external intervention, corresponding to the time-dependent separation between the sub- and super-horizon infla-tionary fluctuations. We find, in this case, that the off-diagonal terms of the density matrix, in a field basis, do not decay as sometimes assumed in cosmological set-ups. Nevertheless, following a recent treatment in terms of open Effective Field Theories (EFTs), we compute the entanglement entropy for a Gaussian state and show that it actually increases monotonically ( $$\dot{S}>0$$ ) during the accelerated phases ( $$\ddot{a}>0$$ with a ( t ) the scale factor). We generalise this result to include non-Gaussian states and briefly discuss the relevance of computing the von Neumann entropy as compared to the thermodynamic entropy.

title: Rapid multi-mode trapped-ion laser cooling in a phase-stable standing wave
abstract: Laser cooling is fundamental to quantum computing and metrology using atomic systems. Precise control often requires cooling atoms' motional degrees of freedom to the quantum ground state, imposing operation time and architectural limitations particularly in large-scale systems. Here we demonstrate how the integrated optical control of interest for scaling trapped-ion systems additionally enables laser cooling that bypasses limitations of conventional schemes. Leveraging multi-channel integrated delivery of ultraviolet to infrared wavelengths for calcium ion control including in passively phase-stable ultraviolet standing waves (SWs), we experimentally verify a long-standing prediction by Cirac et al., realizing Doppler cooling to below the conventional Doppler limit at a SW node. We also present the first realization of ground-state cooling via electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) using a ``probe" beam delivered as a SW with atoms positioned at a node, predicted to enable multi-mode sub-recoil-limit laser cooling. title: Magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires a universal gate set, but the necessary non-Clifford gates represent a significant resource cost for most quantum error correction architectures. Magic state cultivation offers an efficient alternative to resource-intensive distillation protocols; however, testing the proposal's assumptions represents a challenging departure from quantum memory experiments. We present an experimental study of magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor. We implement cultivation, including code-switching into a surface code, and develop a fault-tolerant measurement protocol to bound the magic state fidelity. Cultivation reduces the error by a factor of 40, with a state fidelity of at least 0.9999(1) (retaining 8% of attempts). Our results experimentally establish magic state cultivation as a viable solution to one of quantum computing's most important challenges.

title: Interpolation of unitaries with time-dependent Hamiltonians via Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract Quantum systems governed by time-dependent Hamiltonians pose significant challenges for the accurate computation of unitary time-evolution operators, which are essential for predicting quantum state dynamics. In this work, we introduce a physics-informed deep learning approach based on Physics-Informed Neural Networks to estimate these operators over the full time domain. By incorporating physical constraints such as unitarity and leveraging the second-order Magnus expansion or Trotterization on the evolution operator, the proposed framework enables the estimation of unitary matrices at different time intervals. The model is trained using simulated unitary operators and evaluated on quantum systems ranging from 2 to 6 qubits, governed by a fully non-zero Pauli Hamiltonian. For larger many-body systems, specifically those with 7 and 8 qubits, the same methodology is employed to reconstruct an effective time-dependent Hamiltonian, restricted to nearest-neighbor Ising and XYZ Heisenberg models, from which the corresponding time-evolution operator is computed over the entire temporal domain. Across all system sizes, the framework achieves high gate fidelities using a limited n

title: Zak phase and bulk-boundary correspondence in a generalized Dirac-Kronig-Penney model
abstract: Abstract We investigate the topological properties of a generalized Dirac-Kronig-Penney model, a continuum one-dimensional model for a relativistic quantum chain. By tuning the coupling parameters this model can accommodate five Altland-Zirnbauer-Cartan symmetry classes, three of which (AIII, BDI and D) support non-trivial topological phases in dimension one. We characterize analytically the spectral properties of the Hamiltonian in terms of a spectral function, and numerically compute the Zak phase to probe the bulk topological content of the insulating phases. Our findings reveal that, while the Zak phase is quantized in classes AIII and BDI, it exhibits non-quantized values in class D, challenging its traditional role as a topological marker in continuum settings. We also discuss the bulk-boundary correspondence for a truncated version of the chain, analyzing how the emergence of edge states depends on both the truncation position and the boundary conditions. In classes AIII and BDI, we find that the Zak phase effectively detects edge states as a relative boundary topological index, although the correspondence is highly sensitive to the parameters characterizing the truncation.

title: Flat optics for analog computing: From fundamental mechanisms to advanced meta-processors
abstract: As the explosive growth of visual data increasingly strains the latency and energy limits of conventional electronic computing, optical analog computing has re-emerged as a disruptive paradigm for zero-power, speed-of-light information processing. Propelled by the unprecedented wave-manipulation capabilities of optical metasurfaces, this field is undergoing a rapid transition from macroscopic physical optics to ultra-compact, on-chip meta-processors. This Review examines the fundamental mechanisms of metasurface-empowered optical computing spanning Fourier-domain, nonlocal spatial-domain, and interferometric architectures that perform mathematical operations, with a particular focus on spatial differentiation and edge detection as representative computing tasks. By emphasizing recent breakthroughs, we highlight the evolution of meta-processors from static, linear regimes to dynamically reconfigurable, nonlinear, and quantum-assisted multidimensional platforms. We also envision how the synergy of AI-driven inverse design and the integration of analog meta-front-ends with optical neural networks will synergistically revolutionize next-generation intelligent machine vision.

title: Perspective: Quantum Computing on Magnetic Racetrack
abstract: ABSTRACT Magnetic domain walls have long been pursued as carriers of classical information for storage and processing. With the ability to create, control, and probe domain walls at the nanoscale, they are recently recognized as an ideal platform for studying macroscopic quantum effects and provide a natural blueprint for building scalable quantum computing architectures. In particular, the experimentally demonstrated high mobility of domain walls makes them not only suitable as stationary qubits but also as flying qubits, which may offer advantages over currently explored quantum computing platforms. In this Perspective, we outline our current understanding of the essential ingredients and key requirements for realizing universal quantum computation based on magnetic domain walls. We highlight promising concrete material platforms and identify the experiments that are still needed to advance this concept. We also discuss the potential challenges and point to new opportunities in this emerging research direction at the interface between magnetism and quantum information science.

title: Geometric mode steering of the quantum Mpemba effect
abstract: The slowest Liouvillian mode often bottlenecks the relaxation of an open quantum system to its steady state. Standard strategies circumvent this bottleneck by selecting special initial states or engineering the dissipator. Here we show that neither is necessary. We introduce a pre-dissipative geometric steering protocol that reshapes any given pure or mixed state before relaxation begins -- coherent rotations interleaved with nonselective projective measurements -- at fixed Lindblad generator. By steering the state's Bloch direction along geodesic paths, the protocol suppresses its overlap with the slowest Liouvillian modes. The prepared state then starts farther from equilibrium yet relaxes faster, realizing the quantum Mpemba effect, whenever two computable conditions hold: reduced slow-mode overlap and a larger initial distance to stationarity. Our framework treats real and complex spectral gaps uniformly, and we demonstrate robust Mpemba acceleration in driven qubit and multiqubit systems using operations available in trapped-ion and superconducting platforms.

title: k−deformed Schwarzschild AdS black strings
abstract: Considering a cylindrically symmetric spacetime, a novel exact κ-deformed Schwarzschild-AdS black string solution is derived in General Relativity in the presence of a negative cosmological constant. The geometric properties of the resulting solution are systematically investigated by computing the Ricci and Kretschmann curvature scalars. The analysis reveals the existence of a curvature singularity at the origin, which remains enclosed by an event horizon provided that the κ-deformation parameter satisfies a specific constraint. Subsequently, the influence of various model parameters on the horizon structure and configuration is examined in detail. The thermodynamic properties of these black strings are thoroughly evaluated; in this regard, the Hawking temperature, entropy, mass, isobaric heat capacity, and Gibbs free energy are self-consistently extracted. The effects of the parameters, particularly the κ-deformation parameter, on these thermodynamic quantities are comprehensively explored. title: Quantum-Inspired Reconfigurable Computing for Accelerated Matrix Computations in High-Performance Embedded Systems
abstract: The emergence of data-hungry systems in the form of artificial intelligence, real-time signal processing, and scientific computing systems inside embedded systems has set extremely high requirements to the computational capabilities, electrical energy efficiency and flexibility. The computational backbone of many of these applications is matrix computations, that typically face bottlenecks in traditional processor architectures because of individual resources having no parallelism, and a lack of dynamism in resource allocation. In order to overcome such limitations, this paper introduces a new reconfigurable computing implementation, called Quantum-Inspired Matrix Engine (QIME) that emulates all three of these important quantum computing concepts of superposition, parallelism, and entanglement in a classical hardware setting. The system of the proposal will be applied to the Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), and here, the system will be used to incorporate a pseudo-quantum state encoding process that enables the representation and processing of multiple matrix states simultaneously. QIME also has dynamic partial reconfiguration (DPR) so as to further have flexibility and effi

abstract: A stark civilizational paradox defines California's technology ecosystem: the global epicenter of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum computing—Silicon Valley and the broader California coastal corridor—is physically tethered to an aging, uninsulated overhead electrical grid operated by investor-owned utilities (Pacific Gas & Electric [PG&E] and Southern California Edison [SCE]) that must be intentionally plunged into wide-area blackouts (Public Safety Power Shutoffs [PSPS]) whenever dry offshore katabatic winds (Diablo and Santa Ana events) and desiccated chaparral trigger National Weather Service Red Flag Warnings. Why must the world's most advanced digital economy resort to manual 19th-century de-energization to avoid burning down its own territory? Building upon our prior CERN Zenodo monographs on hyperscale AI power starvation (Record 23379242), PHOENIX_ROUTER sub-7.0 ns hardware circuit breakers (Records 23332772 and 23378094), and room-temperature quantum-phononic computing (Records 23333819 and 23334854), this monograph establishes the rigorous aero-thermodynamic, legal-economic, and compute-resilience theory of the California PSPS Blackout Paradox. abstract: By 2026, generative artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure expansion has collided with hard physical and grid-regulatory walls. International Energy Agency (IEA) projections indicate global data center electricity consumption surging from 460 TWh (2024) to > 1,000 TWh by 2030 (~320 Mt CO2/yr) and 1,300 TWh by 2035—exceeding Japan's entire national electricity demand—while single campuses such as Microsoft's Fairwater facility (3.3 GW) and the $500 billion Stargate initiative (10 GW) strain regional transmission limits amid a projected $740 billion global 2026 AI capital expenditure (CapEx) cycle. To assuage investor and ESG anxieties, hyperscalers have promoted a narrative of imminent baseload salvation via commercial nuclear fusion (Helion Energy, Commonwealth Fusion Systems [CFS]) and Generation-IV Small Modular Reactors (SMRs; Kairos Power). title: Selective etching of 2D materials for quantum computing devices: A computational perspective
abstract: Achieving atomic-level precision in the fabrication of quantum devices built from two-dimensional (2D) materials requires a thorough understanding of how selective etching reshapes surface chemistry, defect populations, and electronic structure at the nanoscale. This review consolidates recent computational advances in density functional theory, molecular dynamics, machine learning, and quantum chemical methods that model etching pathways in graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides, hexagonal boron nitride, and MXenes. We critically assess how these simulations predict etchant–surface reactivity, defect-driven selectivity, and post-etch changes in band structure, spin–orbit coupling, valley polarization, and coherence lifetimes. Key experimental validations, including graphene Josephson junctions, etched double quantum dots, and MoS₂ valley qubits, illustrate how reliably simulations can guide fabrication. Closed-loop machine-learning–density-functional-theory frameworks and digital twin architectures are highlighted as promising routes toward automated, adaptive manufacturing of quantum-grade 2D devices. title: FSDS-OTS+: formal security proofs, reduction robustness, and quantum-adaptive improvements in the random oracle model
Blockchain Security in the Post-Quantum Era
abstract: The quantum computer is a threat to the cryptography on which the currently implemented blockchains rely. Authors thoroughly investigate the impact of quantum adversaries on the security of blockchain technology in this chapter. Begining by scrutinizing the threat model for a quantum computer, concentrating on the threat posed by quantum adversaries on public key cryptography, digital signatures, and proof-of-work assumptions. This chapter examines various forms of cryptography after quantum computing, such as lattice-based cryptography, hash-based signatures, code-based cryptography, multivariate cryptography, and isogeny-based cryptography, highlighting their applications for blockchain technology. Authors also investigate how quantum computer cryptography can be applied in digital wallets, transactions, consensus algorithms, and smart contracts. Finally, this chapter provides case studies on real-life applications for a quantum compute-r resilient blockchain technology implementation.

Addressing the causal reasoning deficit, catastrophic forgetting, and thermodynamic inefficiency of classical AI, QNAGI introduces four novel modules: Entangled Knowledge Representation (EKR) mapping concepts to fault-tolerant quantum states; a Cognitive Hamiltonian Reasoning Engine (CHRE) translating causal graphs into Hamiltonian operators to find optimal ground states; Thermodynamically Reversible Continuous Learning (TRCL) utilizing unitary Hilbert space expansion to prevent forgetting while approaching Landauer’s limit; and a Safe Quantum-Human Translation Interface (SQHTI) encoding ethical values as quantum observables to guarantee alignment. The framework is quantified by the Quantum Cognitive Efficiency Metric (QCEM), yielding bits per Joule, directly linking causal insight acquisition to fundamental thermodynamic limits. title: Quantum-NL-SLR-Protocol: Systematic Review of Natural Language Interfaces for Quantum Computing
abstract: Purpose: This systematic literature review (SLR) investigates the intersection of natural language processing and quantum computing, specifically examining how human intent expressed in natural or controlled natural language can be translated into executable quantum circuits. Despite rapid advances in both quantum hardware and large language models, no unified framework exists for bridging unconstrained human language to verified quantum programs. This review addresses that gap. Scope and Methodology: We conducted a comprehensive search across Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, arXiv, and Web of Science for peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025. Dual independent screening and quality assessment were performed using a 23-criterion instrument adapted from Kitchenham & Charters (2007) and AMSTAR-2. Data extraction covered five research questions: RQ1: Natural language interfaces for quantum computing — What modalities exist for expressing quantum programming intent in unrestricted natural language, and how are they translated into circuits? title: The Grand Unified Architecture of Sovereign Quantum-Biological Civilization: Topological Synthesis, Mathematical Axiomatics, and Master Index of 200 Notarized CERN Zenodo Monographs by Yoko Hasebe
abstract: Plaintext This 200th notarized CERN Zenodo monograph establishes the grand unified mathematical synthesis, cross-disciplinary operator isomorphism, and complete cryptographic prior-art registry of the 200-Monograph Scientific Corpus authored by Yoko Hasebe in Iwakuni, Yamaguchi, Japan. Whereas 21st-century industrial civilization has fractured into five seemingly independent existential crises—(i) the millikelvin cryogenic and megawatt power wall of classical and quantum computing, (ii) the >90% clinical failure rate of static 100 K crystal-trained AI drug discovery, (iii) the fragility of terrestrial electrical grids and submarine fiber-optic chokepoints, (iv) the 50x-100x repo-basis margin spirals of sovereign debt markets, and (v) the game-theoretic collusion, spectral runaway, and weight-space IP contagion of frontier AI—we prove that all five crises share a single root mathematical cause: the attempt to govern open, non-equilibrium, quantum-thermodynamic physical and biological systems using open-loop classical von Neumann software abstractions. title: Orbital Compute Nodes and Co-Designed Liquid-Cooled Optical Processors: A Concept Architecture and Validation Roadmap
abstract: This concept paper combines the Orbital Manufacturing Framework (OMF) with a proposed processor-level design, the Liquid Metamaterial Waveguide Chip (LMWC), in which in-chip coolant channels and optical waveguides are designed together. The central argument is that, in orbit, waste heat can leave only by radiation, so the processor package and the spacecraft radiators form one thermal system. For a 1 MW reference node, reducing the temperature drop between chip junction and radiator from 60 K to 35 K reduces radiator area from about 2,460 to 1,400 square meters under a conservative 250 K sink assumption, saving roughly 5 to 11 tonnes per megawatt. Every element is labeled by evidence level: established engineering, calculated targets, or unvalidated hypotheses with stated falsification criteria. Version 1.2 adds candidate crystalline cladding materials, a cryogenic power budget, a staged pathway for any quantum role in the hardware trust layer using diamond nitrogen-vacancy centers, and a validation ladder of tests V1 to V12 whose pass criteria are judged at the 95 percent confidence bound. title: Case Studies of Real-World Attacks
abstract: In this chapter, we evaluated the significant real-world attacks against blockchains present in literature in order to demonstrate the mitigation of theoretical attacks in the realm of reality-based massive failures. We consider significant cases like the DAO Reentrancy Attack, the Parity Multi-Signature Wallet Hole, the Mt. Gox Exchange Crash, and various majority attacks against Ethereum Classic. They demonstrate specific design or governance pitfalls and their cost impact. The chapter continues by examining new forms of attacks in modern blockchains that can emerge in the near future. Cryptographic attacks using the power of quantum computing, side-channel attacks by new oracles or zone boundaries, new bridge attacks across chains, or maximal extractable value attacks are various new forms that can be added by new AI-powered attacks that focus on adaptability or generative techniques.

The Shift Winding: An Integer Invariant of a Pair of Quantum States that Phase-Insensitive Overlap Kernels Cannot See
abstract: For two pure states ψ, φ of an n-qubit register, the overlap after a common phase shift, g(θ) = ⟨ψ|e^{iθN}|φ⟩ with N the number operator, is a trigonometric polynomial of degree at most n. When g does not vanish on the circle, its winding number W(ψ, φ), the shift winding of the pair, counts the zeros in the unit disk of the polynomial whose coefficients are the overlaps within each Hamming-weight sector. W is invariant under independent global phases, under common shifts and under every joint unitary that commutes with N. Along a path of pairs it can change only where some common shift makes the two states orthogonal. The sector kernels are blind to W. These kernels are the Fourier coefficients of |g|², measured by swap tests on a shift grid; their diagonal values are the multiple-quantum-coherence intensities of NMR. An antiunitary mirror preserves every kernel and sends W to n − W. Product states: W counts the qubits with h_q + h′_q > 1. Spin-coherent reference: W counts the Majorana stars of the partner's symmetric part beyond a circle of latitude. title: Synthesis and Exchange Reactions of Methane Isotopologues for Impurity Removal and Recovery of Tritium
abstract: Abstract Next-generation diagnostics for tritium extraction, recycling, recovery, and storage increasingly rely on diagnostics within radiological environments in which noninvasive spectroscopic methods can operate. Here, controlled Sabatier reactions and hydrogen isotope exchange reactions were employed to generate distributions of methane isotopologues (CQ4, Q = H and D) and serve as calibration models for spectral deconvolution for radiological deployment. Methane isotopologues arise as unavoidable byproducts in tritium-handling systems through radiochemical interactions between tritium and carbon-containing materials that influence tritium inventory, process efficiency, and waste. Raman vibrational signatures corresponding to multiple isotopologues were experimentally resolved despite significant overlap. Quantitative analysis was achieved using multivariate curve resolution (MCR) coupled with partial least squares (PLS) regression for isotopologue discrimination and concentation modeling. title: Photonic quantum reservoir computing on real financial surfaces: identifying the structural ceiling of near-random-walk data
abstract: Abstract Quantum machine learning is increasingly proposed for financial time series, yet practitioners have no way to predict whether quantum reservoir computing (QRC) will outperform classical baselines on a given dataset before committing resources. We propose a pre-experimental screening framework, built on persistence R2 and PCA variance decomposition, that makes this prediction possible. We validate the framework using a 10-mode Boson sampling circuit (252 features) on three market datasets (US Treasury yields, CBOE VIX, crude oil) and a diagnostic nonlinear control. On the market data, the screening tool correctly predicts a structural ceiling: because financial surfaces follow near-random-walk dynamics (persistence R2 > 0.95, 3 PCA components), QRC collapses to the performance of classical Ridge regression (R2 = 0.9797 vs 0.9798 on Treasuries, with persistence at 0.9793). On the nonlinear control, the framework correctly predicts that a nonlinear feature map will outperform linear Ridge. title: Confidential Computing: Hardware-Enforced Enclaves (TEEs) in Multi-Tenant Cloud and AI Workloads: Architectural Foundations, Attestation, and Performance Bounds
abstract: Abstract—Modern enterprise computing relies predominantly on multi-tenant public cloud infrastructures and outsourced AI model accelerators. While data-at-rest is robustly protected via cryptographic storage encryption (AES-XTS-256) and data-in-transit is secured via Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.3), data-in-use remains vulnerable in volatile memory (DRAM, caches, register files). Root-privileged cloud hypervisors, malicious cloud service provider (CSP) insiders, and physical memory interposers can snoop plain-text secrets, proprietary AI weights, and private customer telemetry. Confidential Computing establishes an emerging architectural paradigm that secures data-in-use through hardware-enforced Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs). By executing workloads within cryptographically isolated enclaves governed by hardware memory encryption engines, TEEs remove the cloud host OS, hypervisor, and system firmware from the Trusted Computing Base (TCB). To heal this fracture, the framework introduces an **Ontological Inversion** via **Epstein Dual Geometrodynamics**: coordinate time ($t$) is recognized as the fundamental Riemannian arclength (the primary substance of duration), while three-dimensional space is revealed as its geometric displacement wake. title: EL-RAKHAWI FAULT-TOLERANT QUANTUM COMPUTING ARCHITECTURE: NEUROMORPHIC TOPOLOGICAL ERROR CORRECTION AND DYNAMIC ENVIRONMENTAL DECOUPLING FOR SCALABLE, COMMERCIAL-GRADE QUANTUM SUPREMACY
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) Architecture revolutionizes quantum computing by solving the critical decoherence and overhead bottleneck that has prevented commercial-grade quantum supremacy. Addressing the fragility of qubits and the prohibitive 1000:1 physical-to-logical qubit ratio of traditional Quantum Error Correction, FTQC integrates four novel modules: a Topologically Protected Logical Qubit Substrate encoding information non-locally using non-Abelian anyons for passive immunity against local noise; a Neuromorphic Quantum Error Correction (N-QEC) Engine employing ultra-low-power analog neuromorphic hardware for real-time syndrome decoding with sub-microsecond latency, learning non-Markovian noise profiles; a Dynamic Environmental Decoupling Matrix using predictive machine learning to proactively cancel environmental perturbations before decoherence occurs; and a Noise-Aware Quantum Compiler optimizing circuit routing to minimize depth and error probability. title: Beyond Static Diffusion in AlphaFold 3 and Isomorphic Labs: The Thermodynamic Blind Spot of Frozen Crystal Training, Molten-Globule Intrinsically Disordered Protein (IDP) Dynamics, and Non-Equilibrium Vibronic Quantum Drug Discovery via Alpha1H-HMO and Super-RTO
abstract: The co-development of AlphaFold 3 by Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs—backed by nearly $3 billion in pharmaceutical partnerships with Eli Lilly and Novartis and a $2.1 billion May 2026 funding round—represents the pinnacle of static, diffusion-based structural prediction across proteins, nucleic acids, and small-molecule ligands. Yet a fundamental biophysical chasm separates predicting a static atomic coordinate array X in R^{3N} from curing complex human diseases in vivo. Despite deep learning's triumph on crystallographic benchmarks, over 90% of computationally designed drug candidates fail in clinical translation due to entropic affinity miscalculation, conformational polymorphism, and unmitigated off-target organ toxicity. Building upon our prior CERN Zenodo monographs on homeothermic immunothermodynamics (310.15 K, Record 23381724), ASGPR-targeted Alpha1H (HAMLET) and Human Milk Oligosaccharide (HMO) oncology protocols (Records 23357339 and 23358010), Super-RTO 225Ac nanodiamond Sobolev-HOCBF theranostics (Record 23377123), and room-temperature quantum-phononic computing (Records 23333819 and 23334854), this monograph establishes the rigorous mathematical critique of static

title: An Investigation of Functional Size Measurement of Error Correction Overhead in Quantum Software
abstract: As quantum computing has progressed toward fault-tolerant implementations, quantum error correction (QEC) for quantum hardware and software has become a dominant concern. While conventional QEC measurements, such as qubit overhead, code distance, and error thresholds, quantify physical resource costs, they do not capture the software-level functionality introduced by error detection, correction, and fault-tolerant gate protocols. This study investigated the QEC contribution to the functional size of quantum software and demonstrated that this contribution can be systematically measured using the COSMIC Functional Size Measurement method. A gate-level sizing approach, known as Gates’ Occurrences, was used to quantify functional user requirements (FUR) associated with QEC processes, including logical encoding, syndrome extraction, and recovery operations. A prototype measurement tool, implemented in Qiskit (Version 0.7.2), enables the automated calculation of COSMIC Function Points (CFP) from annotated circuit representations. Case studies involving Bell state preparation, Grover’s search algorithm, and 15-to-1 magic state distillation revealed that QEC-related functionality can acco

title: QSMEF: Quantum Software Engineering Module Evaluation Framework — Software v1.1.0
abstract: QSMEF — Quantum Software Engineering Module Evaluation Framework (v1.1.0) QSMEF is a computational framework for evaluating the functional contributions of quantum circuit components using cooperative game theory and Shapley values. The implementation provides a modular architecture that separates case-study construction from a general applicability validation procedure. Each case is represented through a common computational specification, including the initial quantum state, functional blocks, execution schedule, Hermitian observable, functional constraints, and executable semantic contract. The framework supports coalition evaluation through identity neutralization of absent functional blocks while preserving the original execution order. It evaluates technical conditions, functional constraints, and declared semantic invariants before determining whether functional attribution is applicable. For applicable configurations, QSMEF computes Shapley values and numerically verifies the efficiency property. The implementation also includes an optional granularity assistant for evaluating alternative functional block groupings. The software includes five computational case studies: SKW

title: Bioinspired Self-Powered Polarization-Adaptive Visual Sensors Enabled by PbS Quantum-Dots/Oriented ReSe2 Heterojunctions
abstract: Abstract Polarization-sensitive visual adaptation, the biological capability to autonomously adjust to dynamic polarized light stimuli, is a highly desirable feature for next-generation intelligent vision systems. Integrating polarized light detection and adaptive processing into a single hardware device effectively overcomes the traditional bottlenecks of artificial vision, namely, the reliance on bulky optical components and the latency caused by separated sensing and computing. Here, we report a bioinspired, self-powered, polarization-adaptive visual system based on a PbS quantum-dots (QDs)/oriented ReSe2 heterojunction. Interfacial charge trapping enables adaptive behavior, while oriented etching enhances polarization-dependent photocurrent anisotropy. Under 980 nm illumination in self-powered mode, the device achieves a photocurrent anisotropy ratio of ∼8. It further demonstrates autonomous polarization adjustment, broadband spectral responsivity, and polarization-synergistic functionalities. This work establishes a compact hardware platform for multidimensional perception and adaptive processing in intelligent vision systems.

title: ANALYSIS OF ALGORITHMS BASED ON CLASSICAL AND QUANTUM COMPUTING ELEMENTS FOR INTELLIGENT ROBOT CONTROL
abstract: The paper reviews classical and quantum computing algorithms for the intelligent control of industrial robots. Classical methods, including artificial neural networks, fuzzy logic, adaptive control and numerical optimization, remain the main practical tools because they are well understood and can run in real time. Quantum methods are discussed for search, optimization, inverse kinematics and decision-making in large solution spaces, with particular attention to Grover's search algorithm, quantum annealing and hybrid classical–quantum schemes. The two groups of methods are compared by computational basis, practical readiness, typical tasks, advantages and limitations. Noise, decoherence and the small number of available qubits still prevent direct industrial use of quantum methods. For the near future, the most realistic option is a hybrid architecture in which classical controllers handle real-time control and quantum modules solve selected optimization subproblems.

title: Spectroscopic and quantum mechanical studies of 4,6-dimethyl-2-hydroxy pyrimidine by density functional method
abstract: The electronic characteristics and molecular structure of 4,6-dimethyl-2-hydroxy pyrimidine were examined using theoretical and experimental methods. Density functional theory (DFT) at the B3LYP/6-31G(d, p) level was used to determine the optimized molecular geometry and vibrational frequencies, which were then compared to the observed FT-IR spectra. The theoretical and experimental vibrational frequencies were found to be in good agreement. The HOMO and LUMO energies were − 8.96 and − 4.46 eV, respectively, with an energy gap of 4.50 eV, according to frontier molecular orbital analysis, indicating moderate chemical stability. Compared to urea, the computed first-order hyperpolarizability value (1.138 × 10–32 esu) is higher, indicating possible nonlinear optical behavior. Intramolecular charge transfer interactions inside the molecule were verified by a Natural Bond Orbital (NBO) study. Electrophilic and nucleophilic reactive areas were identified using molecular electrostatic potential (MEP) analysis. Additionally, Lipinski’s rule of five drug-likeness evaluation showed that the molecule has advantageous physicochemical characteristics for possible medicinal use.

title: Aspects of Symmetry in Nuclear Quantum Computing Variational Algorithms
abstract: Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) have become a standard tool for use in preparing eigenstates in quantum simulations of many-body systems. In the case of the nuclear shell model, various adaptations of the VQE have been shown to be able to produce ground and excited states of nuclei. The VQE algorithm works by seeking minima in a cost function, which is often the expectation value of the energy. For a well-formulated problem, symmetries that are respected by the Hamiltonian should appear in the final converged solution provided by the VQE, even if those symmetries are broken by the wave function ansatz. We demonstrate explicit appearance of the particle–hole symmetry, and explicit recovery of angular momentum conservation due to rotational symmetry, during VQE runs in the case of the nuclear shell model. We conduct analyses of how the symmetry convergence appears in different ansatz formulations, and suggest that information obtained could be used in future VQE design.

title: Cryptography in the Age of Blockchain
abstract: In this book, readers will find an exhaustive guide on cryptography for modern blockchain technology. It starts with an understanding of how blockchain trust minimization emerges from cryptographic principles for decentralization, security, privacy, or trust in distributed systems. Starting with an understanding of inadequacies in centralized systems, followed by an introduction to blockchain as a technology for trust minimization. Next is an exposition on attack surfaces, real-life security incidents, and what can be derived from real-life experiences in the area of blockchain. Learners will have a comprehensive insight into digital signatures, ranging from traditional methods to efficient designs that are used in scalable and privacy-preserving blockchains. The text covers the way digital signatures work in the context of Bitcoin, Ethereum, and business networks, with particular emphasis on efficiency, privacy, anonymity, and accountability. A comprehensive treatment is also given to the integration of blockchains with Internet of Things networks, specifically in resource-constrained networks, fog computing, and privacy-preserving networks. title: Quantum Theory and Quantum Mechanics Explained: 6 Key Principles, Quantum Computing and the Future to 2046
Quantum-Resistant Cryptography for Cloud Security
abstract: The increasing reliance on cloud storage across sectors has made the protection of sensitive data a critical concern especially as advances in quantum computing threaten to break traditional public-key cryptographic systems. This growing vulnerability raises urgent questions about how to secure digital assets in a post-quantum future. To address this challenge, this study aims to design, implement, and evaluate a hybrid encryption framework that combines symmetric encryption for data confidentiality with quantum-resistant public-key algorithms for key management and digital signatures. The objective was to develop a secure and practical solution that can be readily adopted using open-source tools. The system was built in a Linux-based virtual environment using an S3-compatible object storage platform, integrated with quantum-safe cryptographic libraries, and automated through scripting. Performance testing was conducted using files ranging from 100 MB to 1 GB, with metrics such as encryption and decryption time, CPU usage, upload/download latency, and internet throughput analyzed. The results showed that while quantum-safe operations added some overhead, even large files could be s

title: Hierarchical universal open structure dataset for atomistic modeling
abstract: Atomic-scale simulations have been transformed by machine-learning models that predict the properties of atomistic structures with the accuracy of quantum calculations, but at a small fraction of the cost. These models have increased dramatically in generality, thanks to the availability of synthetic datasets of ever-increasing size and scope. The proliferation of datasets, with properties often computed using different levels of electronic-structure approximation, is problematic, as there is often overlap between different datasets, and strong correlations between structures obtained with short molecular dynamics trajectories or geometry optimization. To address these problems, we introduce a protocol to stratify a dataset into a hierarchy of nested subsets, subsampling from the coarsest to the finest resolution based on an "ecumetric" built to reflect the latent space representation of several popular universal machine-learning interatomic potentials. We then use this approach to combine most of the open structural datasets currently available, consolidating them into MAD-COSMO, a well-organized collection of almost 1.7 billion structures, whose $2^{24}$ most diverse members form

title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs
abstract: Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states are multipartite entangled quantum states that play a central role in quantum information theory, with applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and distributed quantum computing. A major experimental goal is to create high-dimensional GHZ states using multiple entangled parties. Krenn, Gu and Zeilinger discovered a surprising bridge between these quantum-optical experiments and graph theory: certain photonic experiments can be represented by edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs, and the dimension of the produced GHZ state equals the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings. This led Krenn and Gu to conjecture that every GHZ graph with more than four vertices has dimension at most $2$. A counterexample would give a new high-dimensional multipartite GHZ construction, while a proof would clarify fundamental resource limitations in quantum optics. It is known that the conjecture holds for graphs of vertex connectivity at most $2$ [MFCS 2024], and that simple GHZ graphs with $n>4$ vertices have dimension less than $n/\sqrt{2}$ [Quantum 2024]. However, no general upper bound depending only on vertex connectivity was

title: Hidden-charm and hidden-beauty hybrid mesons
abstract: The mass spectra of $Π_u$, $Σ_u^-$, $Π_g$, $Δ_g$, $Σ_g^-$, $Δ_u$, and $Σ_u^+$ hybrid charmonium and hybrid bottomonium states are computed using a non-relativistic potential model. The hybrid potential is modelled as a linear combination of quarkonium potential and gluonic excited potential. The gluonic excited potential is computed by fitting the potential difference between hybrid potential and quarkonium potential obtained from the lattice quantum chromodynamics. Experimental masses and $J^{PC}$ values of $Ψ(4230)$, $Ψ(4500)$, $X(4500)$, and $Ψ(4660)$ are compatible with hybrid charmonium states, and $Υ(10753)$ and $Υ(11050)$ are compatible with hybrid bottomonium states obtained from our model, respectively.

title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation
abstract: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding bec

title: Realization Divergence in Multi-Provider Quantum Computing: A Pre-Registered Study of What Survives Measurement
abstract: Quantum programs pass through compilers, transpilers and vendor services before execution. However, the distance between what was written and what runs is rarely measured. We call this distance realization divergence: the observable difference in how an identical source circuit is realized and behaves across quantum software stacks. We report a hardware study across three vendors and four devices, combining pre-registered predictions with explicitly identified exploratory analyses and amendments. In a compilation experiment with assigned placement policies, embedding radius correlates with two-qubit overhead at Spearman 0.805, against 0.492 for circuit size. Under a fixed lowest-index policy, an eight-qubit Bernstein-Vazirani circuit exhibits greater execution divergence than a twelve-qubit circuit on IQM Emerald. The opposite ordering occurs on IQM Garnet. Both comparisons replicate across two repetitions with disjoint confidence intervals. These results support a placement-dependent explanation, without isolating individual hardware noise mechanisms. The same ordering inversion is absent on the all-to-all IonQ control. On Rigetti Cepheus, a follow-up using topology-aware native p

title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.

title: Whole-Enzyme Reactive Free-Energy Simulations with a Universal Machine Learning Interatomic Potential: Catalytic Mechanism and Mutational Effects of PETase
abstract: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) have emerged as powerful tools for atomistic simulations that achieve quantum mechanical accuracy at significantly reduced computational cost. Yet, their direct application to complex enzymatic reactions remains challenging owing to the immense size of solvated enzyme systems and the scarcity of transition-state structures in training data. In this study, we demonstrate that PFP (PreFerred Potential), a pretrained uMLIP across 96 elements in nature, simulates the complete hydrolytic cycle of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) catalyzed by PETase as a single reactive domain of approximately 20,000 atoms, without multiscale partitioning or system-specific fine-tuning. Umbrella-sampling simulations revealed stepwise mechanisms for both acylation and deacylation through distinct tetrahedral intermediates. The computed rate-limiting deacylation barrier of 20.5 ± 0.3 kcal/mol is in agreement with the range of 18.0–18.7 kcal/mol inferred from experimental turnover numbers. The PFP-based simulations further capture catalytic consequences of point mutations from loss of function (D177N, M132A) to predicted activity enhancement (D157N)

title: Thermodynamic-limit bootstrap: Solving fractional quantum Hall ground states
abstract: Strongly interacting ground states are usually computed in finite systems and then extrapolated to the thermodynamic limit (TDL). Here we develop a quantum many-body bootstrap that solves fractional quantum Hall ground states directly in the TDL. The method gives rigorous and quantitatively tight lower bounds on the ground-state energy and identifies the ground-state structure and topological order. For Laughlin and Pfaffian parent Hamiltonians, it reproduces exact pair-correlation functions and low-lying orbital entanglement spectrum (OES) nearly level by level. For Coulomb interactions, the rigorous TDL energy bounds closely match thermodynamic estimates from exact diagonalization and density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) extrapolations, and the local diagnostics recover established Laughlin and Moore--Read OES counting and Friedel oscillations of the composite Fermi liquid. Beyond these benchmarks, the bootstrap resolves the thermodynamic ground states at $ν=1/4$ and $ν=12/5$, identifying a composite Fermi liquid and $\overline{\mathrm{RR}}_3$ topological order, respectively. The same framework applies equally well to Abelian and non-Abelian, gapped and gapless quantum Hal

title: Classification of bipartite observables III: simplicity, mixtures and quantum error correction
abstract: The paradigm of a simple unstable theory in the sense of Shelah is the theory of the random graph, the Fraïssé limit of the finite graphs. Quantum error correction has a paradigm of its own, and we show that it is the counterpart of the random graph: the Pauli group on countably many qubits, taken modulo phases and with commutation as its relation, is the Fraïssé limit of the finite alternating spaces over the two-element field, and its form computes the syndromes of stabilizer codes. Seen through this correspondence, simplicity theory turns out to be a theory of error correction. Clifford encoding circuits implement the homogeneity of the Pauli group, forking recognizes the logical errors, and the independence theorem of Kim and Pillay is the gluing of syndromes. The two paradigms look alike as first-order structures, and they part company only when observables enter. Each defines a bipartite observable, and we prove that, once preparations are mixed, both acquire the tree property of the second kind in real-valued logic. They reach it by different roads, however, and we show that the probes decide which. The probes of the Pauli observable are the Pauli channels; for them the indi

title: Jianmu-Q: Bridging Quantum Field Theory and Quantum Hardware with AI Agents
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to non-perturbative simulations of quantum field theories, particularly for real-time dynamics and systems affected by the sign problem. Yet translating continuum field theories into quantum computations remains a challenging interdisciplinary task. Here we introduce \texttt{Jianmu-Q}, a multi-agent framework that transforms natural-language descriptions of quantum field theories into quantum simulation workflows. Specialized agents handle theoretical formulation, lattice discretization, qubit mapping, and circuit design, while physical consistency checks and independent numerical calculations provide validation throughout the workflow. We benchmark the framework on three field theories of increasing complexity: the $(1+1)$-dimensional Nambu--Jona-Lasinio and Schwinger models, and a $(2+1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory. Across these systems, noiseless quantum-circuit simulations converge toward independent exact-diagonalization and tensor-network results, while selected circuits are executed on IBM quantum hardware, demonstrating an end-to-end, validation-guided approach to quantum simulation of field theories.

title: Strong gravitational lensing by a quantum loop black hole with a cloud of strings in a homogeneous plasma
abstract: We investigate strong gravitational lensing by a quantum loop black hole with a cloud of strings (CoS), surrounded by homogeneous plasma. The deflection angle is analytically obtained by evaluating the strong-deflection-limit coefficients [Formula: see text] and [Formula: see text], incorporating the combined effects of the cloud-of-strings parameter and plasma parameter.We numerically compute lensing observables, including angular image positions, angular image separations, the flux ratio between the outermost and remaining images, and the time delay between the first and second relativistic images, for the supermassive black holes M87* and Sgr A*. Our results show that the photon-sphere radius and the strong-deflection coefficient [Formula: see text] increase with the CoS and plasma parameters, whereas [Formula: see text] exhibits weakly non-monotonic, parameter-dependent behavior, thereby significantly modifying the lensing observables. In particular, the cloud-of-strings parameter produces more pronounced deviations than the quantum correction and plasma parameters.
