title: From gut microbiome to aging brain: Butyrate as a neurogeroscience effector
abstract: Aging-related cognitive decline is increasingly linked to disruption of the microbiome-gut-brain axis, in which age-associated dysbiosis progressively reduces butyrate production, a short-chain fatty acid and central neuroactive metabolite generated by bacterial fermentation of dietary fiber. Experimental studies indicate that butyrate can influence multiple processes relevant to brain aging, including histone deacetylase activity, neuroinflammatory signaling, microglial phenotypes, blood-brain barrier integrity, synaptic plasticity, and neurogenesis. Through these mechanisms, butyrate may modulate several molecular and cellular processes involved in brain aging, although evidence for direct causal effects in the human brain remains limited. Preclinical studies report neuroprotective effects across several models of aging and neurological disease; however, direct evidence in humans remains limited and largely associative or indirect. Therefore, this review critically synthesizes current evidence on microbiome-derived butyrate in brain aging, encompassing its microbial production and age-related alterations, molecular and cellular mechanisms, associations with neurodegenerative and

title: Mental Time Travel in Entrepreneurial Life Design: Neurocognitive Foundations and Practical Implications
ACORN: Adaptive Consensus of Repeated Clusterings identifies pyramidal neurons and interneurons in the primate motor cortex based on extracellular spike waveforms
abstract: Understanding how neural circuits generate behaviour requires knowledge of both neural activity patterns and the cell types they originate from. While the scale of neuronal recordings has dramatically increased since the advent of dense multicontact probes, accurate identification of cell types remains elusive. Traditional approaches have used spike width to attempt a classification, with narrow spikes assumed to be inhibitory interneurons. However, fast pyramidal tract neurons (PTNs, known to be excitatory) with thin spikes and interneurons with wide spikes challenge these assumptions. Here we accomplish three related objectives. First, we produce a ground truth dataset of extracellular spike shapes from electrophysiologically identified pyramidal neurons from primary (M1) and supplementary motor areas (SMA) and optogenetically identified interneurons in M1 in female macaque monkeys. Next, we show that spike width correlates with antidromic latency not only in M1 but also in the SMA, suggesting that it is a physiologically meaningful measure across the motor cortex. Finally, we introduce our unsupervised ensemble clustering method, "ACORN", and characterise its performance on our

title: E8-Derived Posner Mediator Geometry Predicts Neural Phase-Lock Frequencies — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: Applying the 240-root E8 lattice structure to the previously-undefined Posner cluster binding geometry reveals that phosphate-calcium coordination shells map onto octonionic sectors with 132Hz fundamental and phi-spaced harmonics. This predicts that enzymatic quantum entanglement between neurons should occur at discrete frequency bands (132, 214, 346 Hz) corresponding to E8 root norms, providing the first experimentally falsifiable prediction connecting the Cartan piano framework to quantum brain biology. The discovery bridges physics, geometry, and neuroscience by suggesting E8 is the hidden symmetry group governing both lottery phase transitions and biological coherence. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Quantum-Vibronic Neurobiology of the Gut-Brain Axis: Human Milk Oligosaccharides (HMOs), Bifidobacterial Short-Chain Fatty Acid Epigenetics, and Vagal Cholinergic Polaronic Signaling in Neurodegeneration and Oncology
abstract: A central enigma of modern neuroscience, immunology, and oncology is the bidirectional Gut-Brain Axis (GBA): how metabolic and microbial states inside the gastrointestinal lumen govern central nervous system (CNS) microglial inflammation, blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, neurodegenerative progression (Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases), and systemic anti-tumor immunity. Classical pharmacology treats the brain and the gut as chemically isolated compartments separated by slow humoral diffusion (~100 s), failing to explain millisecond-scale enteric-to-brainstem telemetry and synergistic epigenetic remodeling. Building upon our prior CERN Zenodo monographs on non-equilibrium vibronic drug discovery (Record 23381931), homeothermic immunothermodynamics (310.15 K, Record 23381724), ASGPR-targeted Alpha1H (HAMLET) and Human Milk Oligosaccharide (HMO) oncology protocols (Records 23357339 and 23358010), and room-temperature polaronic quantum spiking networks (QSNN, Record 23334854), this monograph establishes the unified mathematical theory of Quantum-Vibronic Gut-Brain Neurobiology. title: Post-traumatic headache as a window into persistent brain dysfunction after traumatic brain injury: an opinion article
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a major cause of death and disability worldwide, particularly among young adults and individuals of working age (1,2). Advances in prehospital care, neurosurgery, and intensive care have improved survival after TBI, increasing attention to the persistent symptoms and functional limitations that may affect long-term recovery and quality of life (1,2).Post-traumatic headache (PTH) is a secondary headache attributed to traumatic injury to the head, including TBI, and is among the most frequent neurological symptoms reported after TBI (3)(4)(5)(6). In this article, we specifically address PTH occurring in the context of TBI rather than the broader category of headache attributed to head injury without established TBI. Consistent with the International Classification of Headache Disorders, PTH that persists for more than three months is referred to here as persistent PTH (3). Persistent PTH may coexist with fatigue, cognitive complaints, sleep disturbances, anxiety, depression, and limitations in daily activities (4)(5)(6), contributing to the complexity of long-term clinical recovery.Conventional measures of initial TBI severity, including the Glasg

title: SCRIBE: Scalable Contextual Representations of Interpretable Brain-Grounded Semantics
abstract: Understanding how the human brain constructs meaning from real-world language remains a fundamental challenge, as semantics depend on context that varies in natural settings. To enable the study of real-world linguistic meaning in the brain, we introduce SCRIBE, a framework grounded in a neuroscience-informed semantic space that leverages an ensemble of open-source large language models to generate interpretable, word-level semantic representations of arbitrary text. In a behavioral study with 921 participants, we show that human semantic feature judgments vary systematically with context, and that SCRIBE captures these shifts, reaching 75-81% of the estimated human noise ceiling. Using brain activity recorded while participants listen to naturalistic stories, we further demonstrate that SCRIBE predicts neural responses in language-selective brain regions, significantly outperforming non-contextual semantic representations. Variance partitioning reveals that SCRIBE explains unique brain-predictive information beyond syntactic features, suggesting that its representations capture aspects of linguistic meaning not accounted for by the measured syntactic features. title: From Neuron to Bedside: An Interactive Neuroscience Textbook for High School Students and Future Doctors
abstract: Version 1.1.1 of From Neuron to Bedside, a free interactive neuroscience textbook for high school students and future doctors. What's in the book: 16 chapters, 16 interactive simulations, 253 concepts in the learning graph, 160 quiz questions, a clinical case in every chapter, a Brain Bee strategy guide with a 50-question mock exam, a teacher guide, and a club kit. What changed in 1.1.1: the About page and README now explain how AI was used to make the book, and the Contact page lists a public contact email. Read it online: https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/neuroscience-textbook/ License: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Independent student project, not affiliated with the International Brain Bee or the Society for Neuroscience.

title: A Systematic Review of EEG-Based Visual Decoding Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning
abstract: The primary objective of this research is to develop and validate robust computational frameworks capable of decoding complex cognitive processes—specifically visual perception and mental imagery—directly from non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) signals. Translating raw, high-dimensional neural activity into coherent visual representations presents a significant challenge in computational neuroscience. To address this, the project leverages state-of-the-art deep generative learning models, including latent diffusion models and multimodal transformers. The methodology emphasizes rigorous neural data processing pipelines adhering to Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) standards. By applying advanced signal processing techniques, such as FastICA for artifact removal and maximum relevance minimum redundancy (mRMR) feature selection on 40-channel and 64-channel EEG configurations, the project aims to effectively isolate relevant neural correlates. Ultimately, this research seeks to bridge the semantic gap between non-invasive neural recordings and visual reconstruction, optimizing both the spatial and temporal resolution of the decoded outputs. Biomarker and Precision Medicine in Neurology
abstract: Biomarkers are transforming precision medicine in neurology, offering measurable indicators that enable a shift from symptom-based diagnosis to mechanism-driven, individualized care. In complex disorders such as Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis, and ALS, molecular, proteomic, metabolomic, neuroimaging, and physiological markers enhance early detection, disease stratification, and therapeutic monitoring. Genomic sequencing and omics technologies reveal molecular signatures, while MRI, PET, and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, like amyloid-beta, tau, and neurofilament light chain, provide insights into neuropathology and neuronal injury. Integrating omics data, imaging, and environmental factors through AI and machine learning enables identification of molecular subtypes, prediction of treatment response, and personalized interventions. Emerging tools such as liquid biopsy and digital health technologies support longitudinal monitoring and adaptive therapy. However, challenges remain—data heterogeneity, high costs, privacy concerns, and the lack of standardized validation hinder translation. title: Editorial: Imaging to guide treatment in brain tumors
abstract: Brain tumors are highly heterogeneous, resulting in various malignancy grades, but also a high variability in imaging phenotypes. From diagnosis to long-term follow-up, clinicians need imaging to provide more than a lesion's size and location. They need to understand the characteristics of the tumor, how it will behave, whether a treatment is effective, and how that treatment affects the healthy brain around the tumor. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) have the potential to address these questions early, noninvasively, and serially, whereby both have grown in sophistication and diversity. Our Research Topic "Imaging to Guide Treatment in Brain Tumors" set out to survey that progress in adults with primary and metastatic brain tumors, covering all aspects of treatment-related imaging. Reflecting the complexity of brain tumor imaging, the thirteen articles in this collection span gliomas, primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL), meningiomas, and brain metastases, and range from quantitative physiological imaging to deep learning at different time points during the treatment pathway.A first hot topic is the shift from depicting anatomy to

title: The Spinal Cord as a Primary Trigger for Terminal Lucidity: An Ascending Autonomic Framework via the Spinoreticular Tract and Locus Coeruleus
abstract: This theoretical paper proposes a novel, bottom-up neurophysiological framework for terminal lucidity, shifting the academic paradigm from traditional brain-centric models to an ascending autonomic mechanism driven by spinal-brainstem circuitry. While mainstream neuroscience remains deeply focused exclusively on tracking residual cortical activity via electroencephalograms (EEGs) and neuroimaging, this hypothesis directly addresses the underlying, systemic "ignition source" of the phenomenon, challenging the status quo by arguing that a starving, resource-deprived cerebral cortex cannot spontaneously organize a coherent network resurgence without an external trigger. We posit that during pre-mortem systemic failure, the spinal cord acts as the system's autonomic "backup generator" and primary somatic distress hub. As peripheral organs, vascular networks, and tissues undergo acute metabolic collapse and severe hypoxia, the spinal cord aggregates this absolute somatic crisis. Rather than managing this stress locally, it transmits a massive, coordinated, high-voltage electrical distress signal upward via the spinoreticular tract. title: Illuminating Circuit Causality: A Critical Evidence Synthesis of Optogenetic Neurotechnology
abstract: The recognition of Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel with the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine highlights optogenetics as a transformative milestone in modern biology. By adapting single-component microbial opsins to mammalian membranes, optogenetics unified genetic cell-type targeting with millisecond-scale temporal control, enabling systems neuroscience to transition from correlational observation to direct causal interrogation. This review presents an evidence-grounded critical synthesis of optogenetics, spanning single-molecule biophysics, opsin engineering, animal circuit neuroscience, and human clinical translation. We systematically evaluate the structural mechanics governing photocycle kinetics, ion permeability, and spectral tuning across the optogenetic toolbox, from ultrafast actuators to anion-conducting channelrhodopsins. We examine landmark preclinical applications that established causal necessity and sufficiency across sleep architecture, basal ganglia motor pathways, microcircuit neuromodulation, and cortical excitation-inhibition balance. title: A two-stage RAG-LLM pipeline for roadmapping neuroscience research in operational environments
abstract: Introduction Neuroscientific research and applications in real world environments are often constrained by limited access, equipment limitations, and high costs. Consequently, robustly selecting constructs to focus effort on is a high-impact task. Method This study introduces a two-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline that generates research roadmaps from existing real-world data to inform research priorities in the field, given the state of the art. Stage 1 uses retrieval-augmented generation on operational logs to identify candidate psychological, social, and neurocognitive constructs and map their co-occurrence. Stage 2 evaluates how well these constructs are represented in the literature across four dimensions that commonly inform prioritization: ecological validity, neural correlates, biosensor protocols, and brain computer interface readiness, producing an evidence gap matrix. Pipeline evaluation combined human review, deterministic computations, and human-LLM alignment analysis. title: Editorial: Bringing visibility to marginalized populations: neuroscience of aging in older adults facing social vulnerability
abstract: There is a paradox at the heart of aging neuroscience: the people most burdened by cognitive decline and dementia are, too often, those we know the least about. Most of the world's older population, including an increasing proportion of people living with dementia, resides in lowand middle-income countries. Yet, research on cognitive aging continues to rely predominantly on evidence generated in high-income settings (WHO, 2026). This imbalance will become increasingly consequential, as nearly 80% of older adults are projected to live in these countries by 2050 (WHO, 2025). Additionally, older adults living under conditions of social vulnerability, whether shaped by poverty, racial discrimination, geographic isolation, migration and displacement, political violence, or limited access to education and healthcare, bear a disproportionate share of neurocognitive disorders worldwide, yet remain peripheral figures in most research agendas. This Research Topic was created with that paradox in mind. title: Preface
abstract: The human brain is an extraordinarily complex organ whose functions emerge from an intricate interplay between chemistry, structure, and dynamic cellular communication.Over the past few decades, remarkable progress in biochemistry, neuroanatomy, molecular biology, and systems neuroscience has transformed our understanding of how chemical signals shape brain development, function, and dysfunction.Yet, despite these advances, knowledge in these domains often remains fragmented across disciplines.Chemical Signatures of the Brain: Bridging Biochemistry, Neuroanatomy, and Brain Disorders has been conceived to address this gap by providing an integrated and coherent perspective on the chemical foundations of brain structure, signaling, and disease.This book brings together fundamental principles of neurochemistry and neuroanatomy with contemporary insights into brain disorders, emphasizing how molecular and biochemical alterations translate into cellular, circuit-level, and clinical outcomes.Beginning with foundational concepts, the early chapters introduce essential aspects of brain chemistry, cellular architecture, and neurotransmitter systems that govern neuronal communication.Subsequ

title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Schizophrenia: From Circuit Dysfunction to Insight and Functional Recovery
abstract: Schizophrenia remains a major challenge in psychiatric practice, characterized by a heterogenous constellation of symptoms, including positive symptoms (e.g., hallucinations and delusions), negative symptoms (e.g., social withdrawal and diminished motivation), cognitive impairments, and frequently, lack of insight. Standard psychoeducation has served as a vital partner to psychological medicine for decades, trying to reduce the relapse rates by emphasizing medication adherence. However, many conventional models often rely on descriptive clinical phenomenology that fails to resonate with the patient’s subjective experience and rarely explain the neurological causes behind the hallucinations or illogical thinking. This disconnection can inadvertently reinforce stigma and fail to support the patient's remaining cognitive capacities to reinforce recovery. Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation (NIPE) emerges as a transformative paradigm, integrating cutting-edge insights from brain science into the educational dialogue. title: The basal ganglia and the epilepsies
abstract: The basal ganglia are an evolutionarily conserved neural circuit best known for the selection and sequencing of voluntary movement. Increasing evidence, however, indicates that these structures also play an important role in regulating pathological brain states, including seizures. Early pharmacological and lesion studies demonstrated that manipulation of basal ganglia output nuclei, particularly the substantia nigra pars reticulata, profoundly alters seizure susceptibility across multiple experimental models. Subsequent work expanded this view, revealing that several basal ganglia structures, including the striatum, subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus, and superior colliculus, participate in a distributed network capable of modulating seizure initiation, propagation, and generalization. Modern systems neuroscience approaches have begun to define the specific cell types and projection-defined pathways through which these effects are mediated. Together, these findings support the concept that the basal ganglia function as a "seizure-gating" network that interacts with thalamocortical and brainstem arousal systems to regulate cortical synchronization. title: Under the Broken Halo: The Universal SEIR Architecture of Crime and Its Correction by Molecular Engram Ablation and Symmetry-Location Neural Cartography
abstract: Abstract This paper introduces a grand-unified criminological paradigm by applying the SEIR (Sensory experience, Experience encoding, Interpretation, Response) cognitive loop model to the structural development of antisocial behavior, sociopathy, and macro-scale atrocities. Moving beyond traditional sociological and punitive frameworks, this study redefines criminal behavior as a universal vulnerability rooted in recursive loop deficiencies and error accumulation. Through a progressive spectrum of cognitive distortion, we demonstrate how minor baseline miscalibrations in early childhood—exemplified by the retaliatory defense mechanism "I don't care if he hurts, he hurt me first"—can compound exponentially over time. As these corrupted loops multiply, they fundamentally disrupt the mind’s internal matching mechanism, decoupling current sensory inputs from historical empathy templates. This progressive empathy dampening locks the system into a rigid, self-preserving, and predatory schema. title: Regulation of the brain-placental axis, and its relevance to the health and disease of the offspring
abstract: The placenta develops as a transient organ during pregnancy to nurture the growing fetus. It supplies nutrients and oxygen to the fetus, collects fetal waste, and safeguards the fetus from infections and adverse pregnancy conditions. Emerging evidence suggests that the placenta plays adaptive functions to protect the developing brain from injury in adverse maternal conditions. Inadequate placental support can impact the developmental process of the brain, which increases the risk of brain diseases among the offspring. There is a remarkable coordination in gene expression between the placenta and fetal brain of mice, suggesting a robust regulation of the brain-placental axis. The deregulation of the brain-placental axis can have adverse effects on the fetal programming of brain development. Defective neuronal development of the fetus due to the abnormal or non-optimal placental functions can lead to an increased risk of different neuropsychiatric diseases in the adult life of the offspring. title: Foundations of Neurochemistry and Neuroanatomy
abstract: The nervous system is a sophisticated and highly organized system that shapes all aspects of human behavior, cognition, and physiology. When using a formal and scientific approach, one should first understand its structure and function in terms of the foundational principles of neuroanatomy and neurochemistry. This chapter highlights the most important theoretical concepts and connections between neuroanatomy and neurochemistry, and provides a detailed introduction to the fields relevant or interesting to students and professionals in disciplines such as neuroscience, medicine and related areas. The neuroanatomical section describes the organizations of the peripheral and central nervous systems hierarchically, and highlights the structural parts of the brain, spinal cord and sensory and motor systems including cortical and subcortical regions, brainstem nuclei and spinal tracts. The component functions of neurons, glial cells, synapses, and supporting structures such as meninges and ventricular systems are highlighted in the context of their functional importance. title: From the Exposure Model to the Generative Brain: Art, Creativity, and the Case for Cultural Vitality as Health Infrastructure
abstract: A quarter-century of neuroaesthetics and cultural epidemiology has established that engagement with art is broadly and durably health-bearing, yet the finding sits awkwardly within the paradigm through which it is usually read: a tacit exposure model, in which art is beneficial input, the person is its recipient, and benefit is modelled on the dose received. Translated into practice as social prescribing, now expanding on an evidence base that the field’s own systematic reviews describe as weak, this model inherits the grammar of the receptor and the individual patient, and leaves an anomaly it cannot explain. The epidemiological signature of cultural engagement is that of a cultivated capacity distributed across a coupled system rather than of an administered agent; it survives adjustment for socioeconomic position, health status, health behaviours, and social connectedness, though not the residual confounding we treat as its most serious rival explanation. title: Different editing styles influence the emotional experience of a film scene
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates some emotional aspects regarding both the creative and receptive states linked to audio-visual stimuli. This relates to moving images, and in particular the process of editing such material. The investigation is defined by an interdisciplinary approach, including both empirical experience from the editing of a long fictional film, and testing a segment from the film in a neuroscience-based laboratory setting. The research considers the brain-body processes involved in filmic experiences as a viewer, as well as in relation to the moments when a film editor evaluates and puts artistic decisions into action. These two perspectives – as creator and recipient - seem to be related, and worth a closer look. This is done primarily by evaluating the editing process of the feature film ‘The King’s choice’ (E. Poppe, Norway 2016). Secondly by presenting the research results from a neuroscientific experiment in which a scene from the film was edited into three different versions, and exposed to three different groups of viewers while undergoing pupillometric measurements. title: THE NATURE OF THE SOUL (Volume 3)
abstract: The third volume examines the emergence of scientific approaches to mind. Physiology, psychophysics, psychology, neuroscience, behaviorism, cognitive science, information processing, artificial intelligence, and contemporary theories of consciousness progressively replaced older metaphysical vocabularies with empirical and computational frameworks. Yet scientific progress generated new philosophical problems. If consciousness depends upon the brain, what exactly is consciousness? If cognition is information processing, where does subjectivity enter? If behavior can be explained externally, is an inner mind still necessary? If neural correlates of consciousness can be identified, does identifying them explain experience itself? This volume argues that the scientific investigation of mind does not eliminate the philosophical problem of the soul. It makes the problem more precise

title: Editorial: Innovations in dementia policies and services
abstract: There is an increasing global consensus that dementia is a significant public health issue (Chapman et al., 2006;Jackson et al., 2023;World Health Organization, 2017). As the global population ages and the number of people living with dementia increases, dementia will continue to grow in salience (Nichols et al., 2022). The complexities associated with dementia require innovative approaches to the provision of care and support as well as to the design of service systems at local and national levels across the globe that can truly meet the unique needs of people living with dementia and their care partners. These systems need policies to provide the foundation for better dementia care and support.Innovations in dementia policies and services are typically discussed and reported far less frequently in the general dementia literature than innovations in clinical care, diagnostics, treatment, or basic science. title: Recovering Hidden Neural Oscillatory Modes from Partial Observations through Delay Embedding and Perturbation
abstract: Abstract Characterising the oscillatory behaviour generated by neural interactions is central to systems neuroscience because these dynamical properties are linked to brain function. However, inferring latent neural dynamics is challenging because recordings sample only part of the system. Time-delay embedding allows dynamical modes to be estimated from partial recordings, using methods such as Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (Hankel DMD). Despite its promise, two questions remain: what dynamical information is recoverable through time-delay embedding, and how can recovery be improved? We address both questions using control theory. Our framework centres on factorising the Hankel matrix of delay-embedded observations into an observability matrix and a trajectory matrix with the form of a controllability matrix. We show that their ranks impose complementary constraints on what any delay-embedding method can recover: delay embedding can increase observability rank, while perturbation can increase trajectory rank by exciting otherwise inactive modes. title: Emerging hydrogel platforms for disease modeling, diagnosis, and imaging of Alzheimer's disease
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by the presence of amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, neurodegeneration, cognitive decline, and dementia. The exact pathogenesis is not well understood, as appropriate pathological and therapeutically relevant disease models remain limited. Hydrogels are hydrophilic, three-dimensional (3D) polymer networks composed of synthetic or natural materials and have diverse neuroscience applications, including drug delivery, tissue engineering, and regenerative medicine. Currently, hydrogel in vitro platforms are becoming increasingly explored for AD pathogenesis, as brain extracellular matrix-mimicking biodegradable components, for delivery of growth factors for neurons and other brain cells, AD-specific peptide release, engineered multi-region brain organoids, and therapeutic drug delivery. Beyond disease modeling, hydrogels are being used to evaluate emerging AD diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, such as biomarker sensing and the integration of imaging. Recent AD diagnostic platforms have leveraged hydrogels as biomolecule-capture matrices and signal-transduction elements to detect AD-associated

title: NiCLIP: neuroimaging contrastive language-image pretraining model for predicting text from brain activation images
abstract: Predicting cognitive processes from brain activation maps remains a key challenge in neuroscience. Meta-analytic functional decoding provides an estimation of behavioral profiles associated with specific brain regions; however, existing methods fail to capture the full semantic content of the neuroimaging literature. To address this, we present NiCLIP, a contrastive language-image model trained on over 23,000 articles to predict cognitive tasks, concepts, and domains from brain activation patterns. NiCLIP achieves optimal performance when using full-text articles and a curated cognitive ontology with precise task-concept-domain mappings. Our results show that NiCLIP accurately predicts cognitive tasks from Human Connectome Project group-level maps across multiple domains (e.g., emotion, language, motor) and precisely characterizes the functional roles of specific brain regions, including the amygdala, hippocampus, and temporoparietal junction. However, NiCLIP showed limitations with noisy subject-level activation maps. title: The Cursive Question : A Critical Synthesis of Neurocognitive Evidence and Educational Policy in the American Retreat from Handwriting Instruction
abstract: Between 2010 and the mid-2010s, most U.S. states adopted the Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts, which omitted cursive handwriting from the required curriculum while explicitly incorporating keyboarding skills beginning in Grade 3. The removal of cursive writing, frequently characterized in popular accounts as the result of educational administrators’ indifference to neuroscientific research, ignited a public debate that intensified following the publication of several influential studies suggesting that handwriting engages the brain more extensively than typing. This dissertation examines the controversy at the intersection of educational neuroscience and education policy. It addresses four central research questions: (1) What precisely does the popular narrative claim, and how does each claim withstand systematic verification against primary sources? (2) What neurocognitive mechanisms plausibly connect the production of letters by hand to literacy development? abstract: On October 13, 2026, Jincheng Zhang released a collection of 58,808 original basic medical research papers, all solely authored by Zhang. The collection explores fundamental biological mechanisms, molecular interactions, cellular dynamics, neuroscience, immunology, gene expression, metabolism, biomedical engineering, and potential therapeutic strategies. It comprises original research works by a single author, rather than a compilation of papers by multiple researchers. The collection covers molecular and cellular biology, neurophysiology, genetics, epigenetics, tumor biology, metabolic regulation, nanomedicine, biosensors, drug delivery, therapeutic target identification, and computational modeling of biological systems. It also investigates interactions among gene regulation, protein synthesis, metabolic pathways, neural activity, and immune responses. title: The Architecture of the Mind: Neural Networks and Cognitive Domains
abstract: Cognitive neuroscience investigates how the brain's biological organization relates to the complex processes underlying human cognition. Research increasingly conceptualizes cognition as an emergent property of interacting neural networks rather than the isolated activity of individual brain regions. This study examines the architecture of cognitive systems, emphasizing executive function, memory, language processing, neuroplasticity, functional neuroimaging, computational neuroscience, and brain–computer interfaces. Using a conceptual integrative literature review design, the paper examines how distributed neural networks support cognition, how neurological damage disrupts functional integration, and how computational models can inform interpretations of brain–behavior relationships. Particular attention is given to the relationship between biological neural systems and artificial neural networks, including the potential of brain–computer interfaces to restore communication and motor function. The review also considers the methodological limitations of neuroimaging, the challenges of translating experimental findings into clinical applications, and ethical concerns involving cogni

title: USA mind control?!
abstract: Description: This deposit contains two texts presented in deliberate sequence. The first is an opinion letter, "A Letter on a Difficult Question," which examines whether the United States has constructed an architecture oriented toward the subjugation of human intentionality. It distinguishes four kinds of guilt (legal, moral, structural, historical), applies a framework of "dots, knots, and map" to the American case, weighs the strongest arguments for and against the charge, and concludes that on a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard the architecture exists and its existence constitutes a form of structural guilt. The letter is explicitly framed as a preliminary opinion offered in the spirit of inquiry, not as a legal brief or a formal scholarly article. The second text is an academic extraction titled "Introduction: From Catalogue to Architecture." It reconstructs, from Armin Krishnan's Military Neuroscience and the Coming Age of Neurowarfare (Routledge, 2017), a framework it calls the Architecture of Systemic Subjugation of Intent. The framework is organized into three tiers — institutional nodes ("dots"), operational mechanisms ("knots"), and macro-level consequences ("map")

Research on memoryengrams has shown that the manipulation of selected neuronal populations canalter the retrieval and behavioral expression of memories, raising fundamentalquestions about the relationship between biological memory, personal identity,and conscious experience.This article examines the conceptual implications of these findings for thedistinction between autobiographical memory and consciousness. title: THE NATURE OF THE SOUL (Volume 1) An Interdisciplinary Postdoctoral Inquiry into Consciousness, Selfhood, Mind, Matter, and Personal Survival
abstract: GENERAL PREFACE THE NATURE OF THE SOUL An Interdisciplinary Philosophical Inquiry into Consciousness, Personhood, Identity, Agency, Meaning, and the Architecture of Becoming The question of the soul is among the oldest and most persistent questions in human intellectual history. Long before consciousness became an object of neuroscience, before psychology emerged as an independent discipline, before computation provided a language for information and artificial intelligence, human beings asked what makes a living person more than a collection of physical parts. What is the principle by which a human being experiences the world from a first-person perspective? What makes a person the same person across time? What is the relationship between body and mind, consciousness and matter, memory and identity, freedom and causation, mortality and meaning? And, perhaps most profoundly, what does it mean for a human being to become a self? The word soul has carried many meanings throughout history. title: Moving Beyond the Flat Screen: Opportunities and Challenges of Extended Reality for Studying Human Brain and Behavior
abstract: Much of what we know about human perception and cognition comes from austere experimental settings: static stimuli presented to sedentary observers on flat monitors, complex responses reduced to simple button presses, and brain activity recorded from immobilized heads using EEG or fMRI. These highly controlled paradigms have provided remarkable insights, but capture a small and often unusual slice of behavior, raising questions about how well the findings generalize to the real world. Extended reality (XR), spanning both immersive virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) that overlays digital content on the real world, offers a way beyond these constraints, supporting controlled, reproducible experiments in which participants actively engage with three-dimensional tasks. Drawing on a growing body of VR and AR studies of attention, memory, and language -- our own and others', some involving EEG -- we outline what XR makes newly possible for cognitive neuroscience and reflect on the practical and conceptual obstacles that remain. title: Estrategias neuroeducativas para favorecer la autorregulaciónen la primera infancia: revisión sistemática en contextos latinoamericanos
abstract: Introduction: Self-regulation is a fundamental process for cognitive and socio-emotional development during early childhood. Educational neuroscience proposes pedagogical strategies grounded in knowledge of brain functioning to foster self-regulation; however, evidence from Latin America remains fragmented. Methodology: A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines and the SPIDER framework. Six databases were searched, and studies published between 2019 and 2024 addressing neuroeducational strategies to promote self-regulation in preschool children from Latin America were selected. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Results: Of the 951 records identified, 14 studies met the inclusion criteria. Five categories of neuroeducational strategies were identified: play-based activities, neuromotor stimulation, emotional and metacognitive education, multisensory approaches, and teacher training with technology integration. Overall, the studies reported improvements in executive functions, attention, inhibitory control, and emotional regulation. title: Reliability in Judging Basic Emotions: Lessons from Session Transcripts
abstract: Background/Objectives: Psychotherapists have become increasingly interested in identifying how recurrent emotional themes might add value to the clinical process, especially in the context of recent developments in affective neuroscience. However, much of this literature remains anecdotal, and it is unclear whether therapists can reliably identify these emotions in routine practice, especially in the context of a free-flowing narrative. In a parallel development, large language models (LLMs) have recently been deployed to classify emotion from narrative texts, though this literature has yet to be aligned with the findings of modern affective neuroscience. Methods: The present study addresses this gap directly and, to our knowledge, represents the first attempt to code psychotherapy transcripts using both independent human raters and an AI coding methodology. The data were drawn from two remarkable patients with focal brain lesions, both with profound amnesia, in long-term psychotherapy. title: Brain-inspired recurrent spiking neural networks for multiscale dynamic representation with manifolds
Wave-function formalism for evolving neural dynamics: a mathematical framework informed by EEG
abstract: The organization of distributed neural activity remains one of the central challenges in computational neuroscience. Contemporary frameworks, including Integrated Information Theory, Global Workspace Theory, entropy-based approaches, and electromagnetic field theories, have advanced our understanding of neural coordination but employ different mathematical descriptions of large-scale brain dynamics. This study investigates whether wave-function formalism provides a useful mathematical framework for representing evolving neural dynamics measured using electroencephalography (EEG). Rather than introducing a new electrophysiological measure or proposing a new mechanism of consciousness, the framework represents complementary EEG observables within a common state-space description of neural activity. Mathematical inspiration is drawn from Everett’s representation of evolving state spaces, although no claims are made regarding quantum computation or quantum processes in the brain. title: Clearing the way for optical mapping of the brain with light-sheet fluorescence microscopy
abstract: Abstract Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) has emerged as a powerful optical imaging technique for studying complex biological systems, particularly in neuroscience. By selectively illuminating a thin optical plane and combining it with camera-based widefield detection, LSFM enables rapid volumetric imaging with reduced photobleaching and phototoxicity compared to point-scanning approaches, such as confocal and multiphoton microscopy. Originally developed for imaging small, transparent organisms, LSFM has evolved into a versatile platform capable of probing large specimens, including whole mouse brains and human tissue samples, through the integration of advanced optical clearing techniques and sophisticated data-analysis tools. This review is focused on the optical principles underlying LSFM, the recent technological developments in light-sheet generation and system configurations, and their impact on imaging performances in highly-scattering tissues. It also discusses practical considerations related to the multiple optical clearing methodologies developed in recent decades and highlights representative applications in brain structural mapping. title: Functional divergence of the synapsin family in glioblastoma: Synapsin III as a candidate differentiation-restoring node
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains an aggressive adult primary brain tumor despite surgery, radiotherapy and temozolomide-based chemotherapy, partly because glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) retain self-renewal capacity, lineage plasticity and therapeutic resistance. Cancer neuroscience has shown that glioma cells receive activity-dependent neuronal signals and exploit neural circuits to support tumor growth and invasion. Synaptic proteins may therefore regulate both neuron-glioma communication and tumor-cell state. Synapsin I, II, and III share conserved N-terminal domains but differ in C-terminal architecture, developmental expression and physiological function. An emerging model of functional divergence in GBM is supported by a recent preclinical study comparing Synapsin III with Synapsin I and II. In the tested GSC models, increasing Synapsin III promoted a neuronal-like differentiated phenotype through a neuregulin 3 (NRG3)-JAG1-NOTCH1 mechanism, with reduced stemness and proliferative growth. title: Neuroscience-Informed Teaching: Investigating Brain-Based Learning Strategies in Classroom Practice
abstract: This This study explores neuroscience-informed teaching strategies and their application in classroom instruction. It investigates how brain-based learning principles such as emotional engagement, repetition, multisensory input, and memory consolidation influence student learning outcomes. Using qualitative methods, the study examines teacher practices and student responses in neuroscience-aligned classrooms. Findings reveal that teaching strategies grounded in brain science improve attention, retention, and motivation. The study concludes that integrating neuroscience principles into education enhances instructional effectiveness and learner performance.

title: Cerebrospinal Fluid: From the Sacred River of the Brain to an Emerging Reservoir of Neural Stem and Progenitor Cells
abstract: For centuries, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was regarded primarily as a protective and nutritive fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Advances in developmental neuroscience, stem cell biology, and regenerative medicine have transformed this traditional view by demonstrating that CSF functions as a dynamic biological microenvironment enriched with growth factors, extracellular vesicles, cytokines, metabolites, and regenerative cellular populations. Emerging evidence suggests that CSF serves both as a critical signaling niche for neural stem cells and as a source of heterogeneous stem-like and progenitor cell populations that may contribute to central nervous system (CNS) development, homeostasis, and repair. Unlike established stem-cell sources such as bone marrow, umbilical cord blood, or adipose tissue, the identity, origin, and functional significance of CSF-derived regenerative cells remain incompletely understood. Recent studies implicate multiple cellular sources, including the choroid plexus, ventricular-subventricular zone, ependymal-associated progenitors, and other periventricular stem-cell niches. title: NEUROEDUCACIÓN EN LA PRIMERA INFANCIA
abstract: This book addresses the integration of neuroscience, psychology, and pedagogy in Early Childhood Education, providing a practical guide to enrich curricular planning based on a scientific understanding of child brain development. The work delves into the neurocognitive foundations of learning during the first years of life, analyzing key factors such as brain plasticity, attention, memory, executive functions, and the decisive role of emotional security and affective bonds. Furthermore, it translates these principles into active curricular design through play, multisensory exploration, movement, music, and storytelling within safe and stimulating environments. Finally, it proposes an inclusive approach focused on neurodiversity, the removal of learning barriers, family co-responsibility, and a formative assessment based on observation and respectful pedagogical guidance.

title: The anterior insular cortex mediates higher-order threat learning and memory
abstract: SUMMARY Learning about potential threats is indispensable for survival, and its deficits underlie numerous neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain imaging suggests the anterior insular cortex (AIC) as a key neural correlate of threat learning, yet its mechanistic role remains unclear. Leveraging multimodal systems neuroscience approaches, we demonstrate that AIC excitatory neurons, specifically layer 5 pyramidal neurons projecting to the basolateral amygdala, are essential for higher-order threat learning/memory. They are specifically required when a predictor is temporally separated from an aversive event or when the predictive information is embedded within a diffuse context. In contrast, the AIC is dispensable for elementary, temporally contiguous threat learning. Surprisingly, while the AIC promotes memory formation, it also constrains the level of fear expression during retrieval in a context-dependent manner. This bidirectional control is mediated by the recruitment of distinct AIC neuronal ensembles. Together, we identify a novel circuit mechanism for bidirectional regulation of higher-order threat learning/memory.

title: Spatiotemporal AI modeling of gene regulation and variant effects in the developing human brain
abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation in the developing human brain remains a central challenge in neuroscience, particularly in transient cell types and developmental stages where data are limited. We present Seal, an interpretable AI transfer learning framework for genome-based modeling of gene expression and variant effects with spatiotemporal resolution across 26 brain regions, 30 cell types, and seven developmental stages. Seal predictions enable characterization of both germline and somatic brain variants, and provide mechanistic interpretation by linking sequence variants to transcriptional regulators in spatiotemporal context. Applying Seal to genome-wide association studies, we identify cell types and developmental windows relevant to neuropsychiatric disease risk, revealing shared and distinct regulatory architectures across six neuropsychiatric conditions that align with clinical trajectories. In the Simons Simplex Collection autism cohort whole genome data, Seal uncovers a significant burden of de novo regulatory variants in transient fetal excitatory neurons, revealing a cell-type and developmentally specific regulatory burden. title: (Short Paper28) Macroscopic Information Processing and Dy namic Intervention of the Glial OS in the In Vivo Analog Quantum Synchronizer (BioQPU) Paradigm: PhaseLocking Model of Everyday Driving Tasks Based on Phase Noise Rejec tion and Chemical Triggers
abstract: In conventional classical neuroscience, there are aspects that cannot fully physically explain how multiple modalities such as vision, hearing, language, and emotion—while being processed in separate brain regions—are integrated and remembered as a “single subjective experience” (Binding Problem). In this paper, using the macroscopic everyday task of “driving a car accompanied by conversation with others (Driving Task)” as a case study, we overcome the metaphor of viewing life as a “computer” computing specific algorithms. Based on the theoretical paradigm of the biological system as an “in vivo analog quantum synchronizer (phase synchronizer: Bio-QPU),” we propose as a verifiable hypothesis an active phase noise rejection model through the coordination of the “life code (drive recorder of life)” and the “autonomous analog tuner (Glial OS).” We formulate mechanisms for the formation of a Fourier-synthesized wave of multidimensional information during cruising; physical intervention accompanied by chemical triggers from the Glial OS during sudden events (hard braking); the steepening of the energy landscape (analog dynamic tagging) and “selective decoherence”—which sublimates decohe

title: Perfusion quality does not necessarily predict ultrastructural preservation after hyperosmotic brain perfusion
abstract: Perfusion fixation is widely used in neuroscience to prepare mammalian brain tissue for histological and ultrastructural analysis. Perfusion protocols are commonly assessed using macroscopic indicators such as gross appearance and neuroimaging, which assess the extent to which perfusate has been distributed throughout the brain. There is a critical need to determine to what extent these metrics can accurately predict high-quality ultrastructural preservation, particularly as new perfusion protocols are developed for connectomics. In this technical report, we describe evidence that these two measures can be decoupled by the addition of dehydrating agents to the perfusate solution. In three human brain donors and one canine brain donor perfused with a fixative solution containing 10% mannitol and 10% polyethylene glycol 35 kDa, macroscopic and radiological indicators of perfusion quality appeared adequate or favorable. However, electron microscopy revealed expanded extracellular space, shrunken cellular processes, and distorted cell membranes, consistent with an osmotic shock artifact resulting from severe hyperosmotic dehydration. title: Spoken language comprehension relies on context-dependent neural weighting of syntax and prosody
abstract: Abstract Comprehending spoken language requires extracting syntactic structure and meaning from a continuous acoustic signal. Psycholinguistic evidence points to a key role for prosody in this process. However, because interactions between prosody and syntax are typically demonstrated using carefully controlled sentence constructions, it remains unclear whether such interactions constitute a general, default property of spoken language processing. Addressing this question requires naturalistic, broad-coverage data. Here, we combined experimental psycholinguistics with naturalistic neuroscience to investigate the joint neural encoding of syntax and prosody in MEG recordings of 26 participants (19 female) listening to narrative speech. Linguistic annotations revealed that strong prosodic boundaries tend to coincide with syntactic phrase closures, and that the strength of prosodic boundaries scales with the number of phrases closed. Using time-resolved regression with temporal response functions, we modeled how these features relate to delta-band neural activity during continuous speech processing. Our results reveal a bidirectional interaction between syntax and prosody. Prosodic mar

title: A Theoretical Framework for Non-Invasive Neurosurgery Utilizing Biosonic and Bioneurosonic Resonance Properties of the Human Voice
abstract: This paper establishes a novel neuroscientific paradigm that defines the human brain not merely as a passive acoustic receptor, but as an active generator of synchronized biosonic (mechanical/fluid-conducted) and bioneurosonic (electrophysiological) vibrations. We present the foundational mathematical equations governing how the brain constructs intrinsic "sound units" (\(U_{s}\)) via non-linear phase-coupling and carrier wave modulation across neural networks. Furthermore, we introduce a theoretical framework for non-invasive surgical intervention utilizing focused external human vocal frequencies (\(V_{ext}\)). By calculating the dynamic phase delays (Δ t) required to induce precise constructive or destructive wave interference at targeted cerebral focal points, we outline how a trained operator can achieve localized tissue ablation, neuromodulation, or localized seizure suppression. This work bridges the gap between acoustic physics, computational neuroscience, and non-invasive neurosurgical therapies.

title: EEG Microstates are Not Associated with Psychotic Symptoms, Neurocognitive Domains or Psychosocial Functioning in Adolescents and Young Adults with Clinical High Risk for Psychosis
abstract: EEG microstates are brief and discrete topographic patterns of electrical brain activity. Microstates last for 60-120 milliseconds, are thought to represent transient, quasi-stable neural networks, and traditionally four distinct classes (A-D) are distinguished. One of the core concepts of present neuroscience is that neuroimaging is able to capture meaningful networks of brain activity, which can be translated into specific cognitive functions. Following this idea, each microstate might correspond to specific core brain functions. Importantly, these cognitive functions are impaired in mental disorders. Clinical high-risk (CHR) refers to a state associated with an increased risk of developing psychosis. Previous research has demonstrated consistent microstate alterations in CHR individuals (especially in class D), as well as in psychosis. However, the neurobiological and functional meaning of microstate alterations in CHR populations is still elusive. title: Spatiotemporal Geometry Integration Theory: Temporal Relational Closure as a Reproducible Higher-Order Signature of Conscious Neural Dynamics
abstract: Spatiotemporal Geometry Integration Theory: Temporal Relational Closure as a Reproducible Higher-Order Signature of Conscious Neural Dynamics This manuscript introduces Spatiotemporal Geometry Integration Theory (SGIT), a mathematical and computational framework for investigating higher-order spatiotemporal organization of distributed neural activity associated with conscious processing. SGIT represents oriented relationships between EEG signals using discrete Hodge geometry, separating gradient and curl components of neural relational dynamics. Temporal dependencies across three successive analysis windows are described by third-order tensors. Their permutation-symmetry decomposition provides quantitative measures of higher-order organization, while Temporal Relational Closure (TRC) evaluates this organization against pair-preserving permutation-based null models. The manuscript presents experimental evidence from visual conscious-detection datasets, cross-cohort analyses, tactile perception, propofol-modulated brain states, and no-report perceptual paradigms. title: Sleep as the Temporal Foundation of Energetic Sufficiency
abstract: Across the Informational Nosology corpus, a single condition determines whether the brain can sustain its operating mode: sufficient energetic headroom and the coupling capacity it supports. An earlier monograph identified the blood–brain barrier as the spatial foundation of that supply. The present work addresses the temporal foundation — the conditions under which the system can restore what the waking day expends. Sleep is introduced not as one more state variable among others, but as the controller of the system’s capacity to acquire energy at all. Short sleep, fragmented sleep, and hypoxic sleep are treated as convergent failures of a single nightly restoration process rather than as unrelated mechanisms. Under ideal conditions the extended model remains conservative with respect to the earlier barrier framework. Under chronic restriction it predicts a sharp loss of mode stability near twenty hours of wakefulness per day, in close agreement with established empirical thresholds. title: THE EL-RAKHAWI THEORY OF QUANTUM-ARCHITECTURAL RESILIENCE AND URBAN NEURO-HARMONY Unifying Urban Neuroscience, Metamaterials, Environmental Law, and Predictive AI for Planetary Urban Healing
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Theory of Quantum-Architectural Resilience and Urban Neuro-Harmony (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23275573) reconceptualizes the city as an "external organ" of the human body. It unifies Urban Neuroscience, Metamaterials, Predictive AI, and Environmental Law to transform urban spaces into regenerative, healing ecosystems. The framework rests on four pillars: biophilic brain mapping via Federated Learning for cognitive sovereignty; topological optimization of phononic/photonic metamaterials for dynamic acoustic/thermal modulation; Predictive Urban AI for preemptive stress mitigation; and the constitutional "Right to a Healing Architectural Environment" enforced via Neuro-Zoning Codes. Central is the Urban Neuro-Harmony Index: UNHI=(N×M×L×A)/[(N×M×L×A)+S×F+ε]. Under the Weakest-Link Axiom and Asymptotic Perfection Principle (max ≈0.9901), it proves urban harmony collapses if any pillar fails. Released under the Ferial Zayed Humanitarian License.

title: Enzyme−Targeted Therapeutics for Neurological Disorders
abstract: Abstract Neurological disorders represent one of the leading causes of disability and mortality worldwide, and their prevalence is expected to increase substantially with population aging. Despite major advances in neuroscience, effective disease-modifying therapies remain unavailable for most chronic disorders of the central nervous system (CNS), highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies. Enzymes are attractive drug targets because they regulate fundamental processes including neurotransmission, signal transduction, energy metabolism, protein homeostasis, epigenetic regulation, lipid metabolism, and cellular detoxification. This review summarizes the major classes of druggable CNS enzymes, discuss clinically approved drugs and emerging investigational agents, and evaluate therapeutic opportunities across neurodegenerative, neurodevelopmental, neuropsychiatric, cerebrovascular, and neuro-oncologic diseases. Key challenges including blood−brain barrier penetration, target selectivity, off-target pharmacology, and clinical translation are also examined. By integrating diverse enzyme-targeting modalities across multiple neurological disorders, this review highlights both

title: Technological neuropsychology: Assessing cognition in a digital world
abstract: Clinical neuropsychology was forged in a pre-digital era, and many of its core instruments still bear that imprint. Patients are still commonly assessed with paper-and-pencil tests in quiet rooms, under conditions that only weakly approximate the technology-saturated environments in which cognition is now expressed. Over the past decade, the field has advanced substantially: tele-neuropsychology has broadened access, artificial intelligence has begun to support scoring and documentation, and calls to modernise neuropsychological assessment have intensified. Yet these developments, while important, largely optimise the delivery of existing practice rather than reconsidering what should be measured, why, and how. Here, I argue that three critical gaps remain. First, neuropsychology lacks a framework for assessing technological cognition. Second, candidate neuroimaging measures remain insufficiently integrated into multimodal diagnostic or prognostic modelling. Third, digital data from smartphones and wearables remain underused for capturing cognition in situ during everyday life, while virtual reality remains underexploited as a means of simulating ecologically relevant activities un

title: Learning Interpretable Switching Dynamics in Shared Neural-Behavioral Latent Space
abstract: Abstract Modern recording technologies enable simultaneous measurement of high-dimensional neural activity and rich behavioral variables, creating both an opportunity and a modeling challenge: identifying the shared latent structure that mediates the brain-behavior relationship and the underlying dynamics through which it evolves across behavioral states. Existing approaches focus on different parts of this challenge: shared representation learning methods identify neural-behavioral subspaces but typically do not model dynamical structure, while dynamical models capture temporal variation and discrete state transitions in neural activity, but do not explicitly disentangle shared neural-behavioral structure from modality-specific variability. We introduce Switching Shared Latent Dynamics (SSLD), a unified framework that learns a latent representation shared between neural activity and behavior and endows this shared space with nonlinear switching recurrent dynamics to reflect the hypothesis that behaviorally relevant neural representations exhibit structured dynamical changes across behavioral states. title: NETWORK MODELS FOR IDENTIFYING MENTAL HEALTH DISORDERS
abstract: Mental health disorders, much like the neural system responsible for them, are multidimensional concepts of compounding complexity. Characterising psychopathology may require examining large-scale network organisation rather than isolated regions or small-scale networks. Despite the growth of network neuroscience as a field, relatively little work has examined whether global topological features of whole-brain functional networks differentiate affective disorders, particularly in the context of comorbidity. This study investigates how the topological features of complex functional brain networks differ across anxiety, depression and control groups in an adolescent sample. A novel methodological feature of the study was the combination of participant-specific permutation thresholding, separate positive and negative network analyses, and graph theoretic metrics. Resting-state fMRI data from the Boston Adolescent Neuroimaging of Depression and Anxiety (BANDA) cohort of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) were used to construct individual-level correlational networks. To control the family-wise error rate, correlation matrices were corrected using a two-tailed threshold calculated from

title: THE EL-RAKHAWI THEORY OF BIO-QUANTUM INTELLIGENCE AND NEURO-JURIDICAL SOVEREIGNTY Unifying Thermodynamics, Neurochemistry, Biology, Neuroscience, and Law in a Unified Framework for Protecting Human and Artificial Minds
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Theory of Bio-Quantum Intelligence and Neuro-Juridical Sovereignty (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23271127) presents a groundbreaking interdisciplinary framework unifying six domains: thermodynamics of information, artificial neurochemistry, biological plasticity, neuroscience of consciousness, bio-interpretable AI, and neuro-juridical sovereignty. Grounded in quantum biological phenomena (quantum tunneling, microtubule coherence), the theory bridges classical thermodynamics with quantum foundations of cognition. Central is the Neuro-Chemical Juridical Sovereignty Index: NCJSI=(P×C×B×N×L)/[(P×C×B×N×L)+V×M+ε]. Variable L (Juridical Sovereignty) is operationally defined as a normalized composite index derived from weighted legal safeguards. The framework employs Multi-Modal Consciousness Assessment, combining IIT baseline with behavioral and neuro-chemical markers to overcome single-theory limitations. Under the Weakest-Link Axiom and Asymptotic Perfection Principle (max ≈0.9901), it mathematically proves that intelligence without juridical protection or chemical stability collapses. title: Targeting protein misfolding and aggregation in neurodegenerative diseases: challenges for the identification and validation of targets for small molecules
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and related proteinopathies are characterized by the misfolding, aggregation, and accumulation of specific proteins that disrupt neuronal homeostasis, leading to neuronal death. Despite major advances in structural biology and molecular neuroscience, identifying and validating druggable targets in neurodegenerative diseases remains challenging. Many involved proteins are intrinsically disordered, exhibit conformational heterogeneity, and form highly dynamic toxic species. AREAS COVERED: This review summarizes the mechanisms of protein folding, misfolding, aggregation, and prion-like propagation in major neurodegenerative proteinopathies, including amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau in Alzheimer's disease (AD), alpha-synuclein (α-syn) in synucleinopathies, TDP-43 and FUS in ALS/FTLD, polyglutamine-expanded proteins, prion proteins, and rare hereditary amyloidosis. We also discuss major barriers to target identification and validation, including conformational flexibility, oligomer toxicity, blood-brain barrier penetration, and target engagement complexity.

title: Identifying brain-computer interface translational priorities with an outlook on the field in 2035
abstract: Brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) have advanced rapidly, particularly over the past few decades, evolving from experimental demonstrations to powerful research tools and early-stage clinical technologies. Invasive, semi-invasive, and non-invasive modalities now enable neural decoding, neuromodulation, and functional restoration across diverse neurological conditions. Yet, despite striking laboratory demonstrations and growing investment, few BCIs have become viable medical products, having only a limited impact. Here, we provide a quantitative analysis to identify crucial clinical applications on which BCI translational efforts should focus to achieve substantial clinical, societal, and economic impact. Using an urgency–importance–impact framework based on disability-adjusted life years analysis, we assessed 12 neurological conditions to provide insight into how to prioritize strategic BCI development efforts. Alzheimer’s disease, stroke, depression, and anxiety, with their combined high urgency, importance, and impact, emerge as strategic targets with the greatest societal and economic stakes. We further argue that BCIs today, particularly invasive modalities, function primarily as

title: The Energetic Synthesis of Monocular 3D Space: Spot Density, Lateral Cancellation, and the True Mechanics of Diplopia
abstract: Classical optical neuroscience models monocular depth perception as a geometric calculation based on the radius of blur circles. This paper introduces a paradigm shift: the visual cortex calculates 3D space not geometrically, but *energetically*. We propose that the human brain establishes an absolute focal baseline ($Z$-anchor) via a thermodynamic search by the ciliary muscle. By analyzing the physical collision between transverse magnification shrinkage and micro-blur expansion, we prove that the eye intentionally maximizes photon spot density per retinal pixel. Under this energetic model, spatial mapping, monocular diplopia (double vision), and defocus (blur) are determined exclusively at the "lines of separation" on the retina. We demonstrate that flawless visual clarity is a biological hallucination; raw optical projection is permanently blurred by lens aberrations. Perfect clarity is artificially synthesized via Lateral Cancellation, a biological software filter that operates strictly when blur radius and geometric separation exceed the spatial capacity of a single retinal pixel. title: Neuroeducación para el desarrollo de competencias investigativas en primaria: revisión sistemática
abstract: Background: Neuroeducation encompasses the contributions of cognitive neuroscience with pedagogical practices to optimize teaching and learning processes, with special emphasis on primary education, a stage of notable brain plasticity and strengthening of executive functions that support scientific school thinking. Despite growing academic interest, empirical evidence on its impact on the development of investigative skills appears fragmented and dispersed. Objective: Analyze the available scientific evidence on neuroeducational interventions that contribute to the development of investigative competencies and cognitive abilities in primary education students. Methodology: Systematic review based on the PRISMA 2020 method, with consultation of the Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC and SciELO databases. 30 original studies published between 2024 and June 2026, in Spanish or English, were identified. Results: Four intervention typologies were identified: direct neurocognitive stimulation, multisensory processing, neuroscientific-based gamification, and socio-emotional environmental modulation. The cognitive skills most stimulated were inhibitory control, sustained attention, cognitive fle

title: Neuro-Leadership as a Framework for Neuroadaptive Management in Tourism and Hospitality Organizations
abstract: This chapter examines neuro-leadership as an emerging theoretical and practical framework for neuroadaptive management within tourism and hospitality organizations. Drawing upon advances in cognitive neuroscience, social neuroscience, and organizational behavior, it argues that effective leadership in the hospitality sector demands more than conventional managerial competencies — it requires a scientifically grounded understanding of how the human brain processes social information, regulates emotions, responds to threat and reward, and sustains motivation under high-demand service conditions. The chapter reviews foundational neurological systems underlying leadership behavior, critically applies Rock's (2008) SCARF model to frontline service management, and introduces a Neuroadaptive Leadership Competency Framework tailored to the complexities of the hospitality industry. Implementation strategies, ethical considerations, and future research directions are discussed.

title: Wired to Cook
abstract: The professional kitchen demands cognitive and emotional resources from its workforce. It is characterised by time pressure, sensory intensity, and hierarchical dynamics in pursuit of perfection, creating demands on the brain. Yet professional chefs demonstrate passion, motivation, and lifelong commitment to culinary mastery. Understanding how the brain adapts to support this dedication requires integrating neuroscience and motivational psychology through neuroadaptation. This chapter explores chefs' neuro-motivational role, arguing that the brain not only engages with the culinary profession but also distinguishes high-performing chefs as wired professionals shaping identity, resilience, and creative excellence. The chapter addresses stress and resilience in the professional kitchen burnout due to anxiety, distress, long hours, and pressure. Research suggests coping strategies produce adaptive changes in stress regulation, helping chefs to maintain intrinsic motivation and resilience, with implications for culinary education, professional development, and kitchen culture.

title: The neuroscience of transformers
abstract: Neuroscience has long informed the development of artificial neural networks, but the success of modern architectures invites, in turn, the converse: can modern networks teach us lessons about brain function? Here, we examine the structure of the cortical column and propose that the transformer provides a natural computational analogy for multiple elements of cortical microcircuit organization. Rather than claiming a literal implementation of transformer equations in cortex, we develop a hypothetical mapping between transformer operations and laminar cortical features, using the analogy as an orienting framework for analysis and discussion. This mapping allows us to examine in greater depth how contextual selection, content routing, recurrent integration, and interlaminar transformations may be distributed across cortical circuitry. In doing so, we generate a broad set of predictions and experimentally testable hypotheses concerning laminar specialization, contextual modulation, dendritic integration, oscillatory coordination, and the effective connectivity of cortical columns. This proposal is intended as a structured hypothesis rather than a definitive account of cortical computa

title: A neuro-inspired computational framework for AGI: predictive coding, active inference and free energy minimisation
abstract: This paper offers a conceptual synthesis of foundational principles from theoretical neuroscience [i.e., predictive coding, the Free Energy Principle (FEP) and variational inference] as a biologically grounded framework for artificial general intelligence (AGI). We adopt this predictive-coding and FEP perspective as our organising framework. It is one of several current accounts of neural computation and not all available evidence is consistent with it. These approaches characterise the brain as a hierarchical inference system that continuously updates beliefs and selects actions to minimise uncertainty and surprise. In contrast to conventional AI systems, biological agents engage in active, generative inference within dynamic, uncertain environments. We argue that this inference-based architecture and not behavioural outputs alone, plausibly underlies the adaptability, generalisation and resilience of natural intelligence. We outline a neuro-inspired computational framework built on hierarchical generative models, scalable variational inference (i.e., Variational Laplace) and Active Inference. Finally, we contrast this approach with dominant deep learning paradigms and discuss its

title: The Integrative Animal Archetype Model: a Wyrdology framework
abstract: The Integrative Animal Archetype Model: A Wyrdology Framework This theoretical paper introduces the Integrative Animal Archetype Model, an interdisciplinary framework developed within Wyrdology that brings together psychology, neuroscience, anthropology, religious and spiritual studies, and embodied biological understanding to examine the significance of animal archetypes in human experience. The model explores how animal symbolism can function as a means of interpreting psychological processes, emotional experiences, cognitive patterns, physiological responses, and culturally situated systems of meaning. Drawing upon perspectives from scientific and humanities disciplines, the paper considers how animal archetypes may provide an accessible conceptual language for understanding relationships between the brain, body, behaviour, culture, and spirituality. Rather than proposing that animal archetypes correspond to discrete neurological structures or universal biological mechanisms, the framework investigates their potential as integrative metaphors through which complex human experiences may be understood and communicated. The paper seeks to contribute to interdisciplinary discussions

title: Viewpoint on Functional Coupling and Neural Oscillations in Multisensory Integration
abstract: Abstract In this viewpoint article, Jennifer Bizley and Daniel Senkowski share their perspectives on past, present, and future developments in research on the roles of functional coupling and neural oscillations in multisensory integration. Drawing on existing studies, the authors argue that a central finding that has shaped the field is that processing in early sensory cortices is influenced by stimuli from other modalities. This finding challenges the classical view of these areas as strictly unisensory. Advances in brain stimulation methods, high-density neural recordings, and computational and machine learning approaches are propelling the field toward richer datasets, a more mechanistic understanding, and causal tests of how neural oscillations and functional coupling may support multisensory integration. Key controversies include the significance of the individual alpha frequency in multisensory integration, and whether crossmodal interactions in early sensory cortices reflect genuine multisensory interactions or movement-related artifacts.
