title: Environmental Performance of Pyrolysis-Based Chemical Recycling: Effects of Feedstock Composition and Pyrolysis Oil Utilization
abstract: The transition towards a sustainable and climate-neutral plastics economy requires the development of recycling technologies capable of recovering valuable resources from mixed plastic waste (MPW) that cannot be effectively processed by conventional mechanical recycling. Pyrolysis-based chemical recycling has emerged as a promising complementary technology by converting heterogeneous plastic waste into secondary chemical feedstocks suitable for the production of new chemicals and plastics. However, the environmental performance of pyrolysis strongly depends on feedstock characteristics, process configuration, and the integration of downstream utilization pathways, while these interdependencies have only been investigated to a limited extent. This thesis therefore evaluates the influence of waste composition on the climate change impact of pyrolysis-based chemical recycling, investigates the effect of pyrolysis oil composition on downstream conversion routes, and assesses its potential to reduce climate change impact relative to waste incineration with energy recovery. The study combines experimental pyrolysis data from the literature, obtained using well-defined model feedstocks an

title: Prospective life cycle sustainability assessment and decision support for solar electricity and industrial heat under uncertainty: a service-specific evaluation of PV, CSP, and CST
abstract: The transition to climate-neutral energy systems requires sustainability assessments that capture future technological, economic, and supply-chain conditions while preserving functional comparability. This study develops an integrated prospective life cycle sustainability assessment (pLCSA) and decision-support framework for utility-scale photovoltaic (PV), concentrating solar power (CSP), and concentrating solar thermal (CST) technologies in high-irradiance Southern Europe. Separate functional units are applied: 1 MWh of net electricity delivered for PV and CSP and 1 MWh of useful heat delivered at the industrial interface for CST. PV and CSP are therefore compared only within the electricity service, whereas CST is evaluated separately as an industrial-heat pathway and is not included in a cross-service ranking. Dynamic inventories represent changes in efficiency, material intensity, recycling, grid carbon intensity, and cost for 2025, 2035, and 2050. title: Congratulatory messages on the publication of this guidance
Patent review on revolutionary electrochemical CaCO 3 conversion for cement manufacturing
abstract: Abstract Sustainable development has become a necessity in conventional cement production to reduce environmental impact. Global demand needs to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The transition to green cement manufacturing plays a key role in achieving net-zero carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions and carbon-neutral concrete by 2050. This patent review highlights the importance and potential of green cement manufacturing through an electrochemical process, converting calcium carbonate (CaCO 3 ) into calcium hydroxide Ca(OH) 2 to produce ordinary Portland cement. This study reveals the entire patent landscape in green cement production and electrochemical green cement production. It highlights and describes the notable patents and their methodology. In addition, this review assesses the innovation of electrochemical technology in cement manufacturing and its potential and feasibility. A roadmap with efficient and effective polices and a framework can enhance the production of green cement. It can be expected that incorporation of electrochemical technology for calcium hydroxide production, when paired with renewable resources, cannot only reduce the overall emission and carbon foo

title: D6.2 Safety and Sustainability Assessment of Supercapacitors
abstract: The report constitutes ARMS deliverable D6.2 SSbD framework report detailing preliminary results and findings for safety and sustainability assessment. The aim of ARMS is to develop safe and environmentally friendly supercapacitors from early-stage material selection to market deployment. This deliverable compares the safety and sustainability performance between a representative commercial product and an ARMS-developed supercapacitor with the SSbD (Safe and Sustainable by Design) framework. The results are publicly accessible, serving as valuable suggestions for diverse stakeholders, including 1. public research institutions, engaged in fundamental and applied research on electrochemical energy storage. 2. Private sector organizations, including battery manufacturers, material suppliers, and technology developers, seeking sustainable innovation pathways. 3. Regulatory bodies and policymakers involved in shaping sustainable energy strategies. The SSbD results elaborated in this report follow a hierarchical approach, in which safety dimension is considered first, followed by environmental (including circularity) assessment. title: Plasma Engineering for Carbon Capture and Greenhouse Gas Reduction
abstract: Plasma engineering has emerged as an advanced and sustainable technology for carbon capture and greenhouse gas reduction in response to increasing global climate change and environmental pollution challenges. While conventional carbon mitigation technologies are energy intensive, expensive catalysts and complex operational systems are used, plasma-based technologies can work as efficient, flexible alternatives under optimized conditions, although energy consumption remains a challenge. Future research in plasma-based technologies for carbon management will continue to advance towards hybrid plasma-catalytic systems, and it is a promising interdisciplinary area with great potential for advancing global efforts to reduce GHGs, optimize carbon neutral energy systems, and participate in solutions for global climate change.

title: Sustainable energy transition options for Russia
abstract: Following the Paris Agreement, one way to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and minimise the consequences of climate change is to pursue the goal of a sustainable energy supply by renewable energy sources. This study explores transition pathways towards sustainable energy system in the regions of Russia. Potential scenarios are presented in the power, heat, transport, and industry sectors. The study leverages an energy-industry system transition model in hourly resolution to investigate various policy scenarios ranging from 100% renewable energy in 2050 to net-zero emissions by 2060 with higher shares of nuclear power, to explore the feasibility and economic implications of the transition to a carbon-neutral energy system. The results show that respective transition pathways are technically feasible and economically viable. The analysis reveals that achieving zero CO 2 emissions by 2050 with very high renewable energy shares composed of wind power (56%), solar photovoltaics (40%), hydropower (3%), and bioenergy (1%) along with the deployment of power-to-X technologies is the lowest cost solution with cumulative CO 2 emissions around 22,000 MtCO 2 until 2060. The study underscores the

title: From Residues to Resources: Sustainable Biomass Pathways for Decarbonising the Economy
abstract: The accelerating climate crisis, geopolitical instability, and continued dependence on fossil fuels have intensified the search for resilient and sustainable decarbonisation pathways. Recent tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz have highlighted the vulnerability of global fossil fuel supply chains and the need for diversified domestic renewable carbon resources capable of strengthening industrial resilience and energy security. Within this context, biomass residues emerge as strategically important renewable feedstocks contributing to climate neutrality, circular bioeconomy development, and industrial competitiveness. This study examines the role of agricultural residues, forestry by-products, and organic waste streams within integrated biomass valorisation systems and evaluates their contribution to decarbonising hard-to-abate sectors including aviation, heavy industry, chemicals manufacturing, and transport. The paper analyses thermochemical, biochemical, and integrated biorefinery pathways while assessing their sustainability, technological maturity, and deployment potential within the European context. Particular attention is given to circular carbon management and carbon-

abstract: Abstract. Peatlands cover only ~3 % of Earth’s land surface yet store ~30 % of global soil carbon (C), making them critical components of the terrestrial C cycle and influential regulators of C-climate feedbacks. However, their responses to climate warming and elevated CO₂ remain highly uncertain, in part because Earth system models represent peatland processes with varying levels of complexity and realism, and because peat C pools turn over on centennial to millennial timescales that challenge model evaluation. Here, we present results from the SPRUCE (Spruce and Peatland Responses Under Changing Environments) Model Intercomparison Project (SPRUCE-MIP), which evaluates 15 terrestrial ecosystem models against observations from a long-term whole-ecosystem warming and CO₂-enrichment experiment at an ombrotrophic bog in northern Minnesota, USA. Models were driven by observed meteorology from in situ warming treatments spanning +0 to +9 °C, at either ambient or elevated CO₂ (+500 ppm). Simulated net ecosystem exchange (NEE), net primary productivity (NPP), heterotrophic respiration (HR), and methane (CH₄) fluxes were benchmarked against multi-year observations. title: Prioritizing decarbonization technologies for climate-neutral railway systems: A qualitative technology assessment of Korea’s rail sector
abstract: Railways are widely recognized as a low-carbon transport mode, but achieving climate-neutral railway systems requires a broader transition beyond modal shift, spanning propulsion technologies, energy supply, infrastructure management, digital operation, and climate resilience. This study develops a document-informed, interpretive technology assessment framework to examine railway decarbonization technologies, using Korea as a case study. Global technology and policy agendas were reviewed and classified into four domains—low-carbon propulsion and electrification, energy optimization and renewable integration, digital and AI-based operation, and climate-resilient infrastructure—and assessed against environmental relevance, technological maturity, operational applicability, policy/regulatory readiness, and R&D urgency. Korea has relatively mature conventional railway technologies, but significant gaps remain in hydrogen and battery-based propulsion, renewable energy–rail integration, standards and certification, and decarbonization-specific demonstration infrastructure. The assessment identifies distinct implementation conditions and R&D priorities across the four domains. Regenerativ

title: Strong growing season soil methane uptake observed in a restored prairie-savanna
abstract: Humid tallgrass prairies in the Upper Midwest have been largely converted to agriculture, creating large regional sources of greenhouse gases through soil oxidation and nutrient enrichment. Although prairie restoration is expanding, greenhouse gas fluxes from restored ecosystems remain poorly quantified. We measured growing season soil carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide fluxes across restored oak woodland, open tallgrass prairie, and wet prairie at Nachusa Grasslands, Illinois, and tested how fluxes were controlled by soil temperature, moisture, cover type, and elevation, and associations with surface soil microbial communities. Across all cover types, soils were consistent carbon dioxide sources (median 2.29 μmol m-2 s-1), methane sinks (median −0.36 nmol m-2 s-1), and neutral for nitrous oxide. Woodland soils were exceptionally strong methane sinks, while open prairie was often near neutral. Notably, net methane emission was absent even in wet prairie. Decision tree models explained 50%–70% of variability in carbon dioxide and methane fluxes, with soil temperature as the dominant control on carbon dioxide and cover type plus soil moisture most important for methane uptake

title: Human-Centric AI-Driven Sustainable and Resilient Design AI for Energy-efficient and Carbon-neutral Buildings
abstract: This chapter examines how Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence is transforming sustainable and resilient design in the built environment. With buildings responsible for nearly 40% of global energy use and 30% of greenhouse gas emissions, the chapter underscores the need for energy-efficient and carbon-neutral architectural solutions. Human-centric AI integrates explainable Artificial Intelligence, human-in-the-loop decision-making, and participatory design to ensure transparency, ethical alignment, and user-driven sustainability. Artificial Intelligence-enabled predictive energy optimization, reinforcement learning heating ventilation air conditioning control, and digital twinbased lifecycle carbon assessment significantly reduce operational and embodied carbon. In parallel, generative design and parametric modeling support climate-adaptive strategiesfrom passive cooling and flood-resilient layouts to low-carbon material selection. The chapter also highlights Artificial Intelligence-driven infrastructure risk modeling, combining hazard prediction, multi-hazard simulation, and scenario-based planning to enhance resilience. title: Hydrogen valleys: Advancing the hydrogen economy through decarbonization, energy flexibility, and sector coupling
abstract: To support the energy-system transition toward climate neutrality, scalable solutions that enable renewable electricity integration, multi-sector coupling, flexibility, and carbon-emission reduction are increasingly required. However, no existing review provides a cross-project assessment of hydrogen valleys as an integrated deployment model. This review addresses this gap by developing an Integrated Hydrogen Valley Systems Framework grounded in Industrial Ecology, Energy Hub theory, and Technological Innovation Systems theory. Using an evidence-based approach, we systematically analyse all 90 hydrogen valley projects listed in the Clean Hydrogen Partnership's H2V database. Peer-reviewed studies, official project databases, technical reports, and policy documents are synthesised to compare renewable-energy integration pathways, electrolyser technologies, hydrogen storage and transport options, sector-coupling strategies, and supporting policy frameworks. The findings indicate that hydrogen valleys can facilitate the integration of wind and solar power, enhance energy-system flexibility, enable long-duration energy storage, and contribute to carbon-emission reductions of up to 30%,

title: Energy security in transition: Multi-Scale risks, metrics, and circular bio-resources from Europe to the Bavarian region of Germany
abstract: ABSTRACT This article reviews how energy security is being reconceptualised and practiced in the context of Europe’s low-carbon transition, with a particular focus on Germany and the state of Bavaria, and on the role of circular bio-resources converted by thermo-chemical-conversion technologies. A targeted review of recent peer-reviewed work was undertaken using major bibliographic databases, complemented by a critical appraisal of widely used indicator frameworks and composite indices, and by a spatially explicit assessment of bio-waste and sewage-sludge conversion potential in Bavaria using Thermo-Catalytic Reforming (TCR®) as an illustrative technology. The synthesis shows that the dominant understanding of energy security has shifted from narrow fuel-supply concerns to broader socio-technical concepts that link security to sustainability, risk, equity and digitalisation. However, prevailing indices remain strongly supply- and price-oriented, rely on overlapping indicators and weakly justified weights, and only partially capture environmental, social and technological dimensions. title: Nitrous oxide emissions from excreta deposited onto tropical pasture in Kenya
abstract: Livestock production systems are dominant greenhouse gas sources in sub-Sahara African (SSA), including emissions of nitrous oxide (N$_2$O) from excreta deposited onto pasture. However, a limited number of studies are available to date. Using the default emission factor (EF) from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) guidelines, which represents a global mean value mainly based on observations in OECD countries, may cause strong uncertainties due to differences in the management practices, climate and soils between OECD countries and countries and livestock systems in SSA. To narrow uncertainties of national greenhouse gas inventories in SSA it is thus needed to develop region-specific N$_2$O emission factors for excreta dropped on tropical pasture which do consider regional characteristics. In my thesis the calculation of N$_2$O emission factors for excreta dropped on tropical pastures was based on a series of field trials in which I varied dung quantity, quality and urine amount. title: Toward Climate Change Resilience and the Carbon‐Neutral Transition in Emerging Economies Through Circular Technologies and Green Energy Transmission Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite growing evidence on the environmental benefits of green innovation, empirical findings for emerging economies remain limited and inconclusive, particularly regarding the joint role of environmental patents and renewable energy in reducing carbon emissions. Given the rapid economic growth of these countries, it is important to understand how environmental patents and climate change mitigation technologies influence sustainable economic growth in emerging markets. Using robust heterogeneous panel estimation methods that account for cross‐sectional dependence, the results consistently show that green innovation, measured by environmental patents, and renewable energy support the carbon‐neutral transition by reducing carbon emissions in emerging economies. The findings demonstrate that while green innovations significantly reduce emissions, the emissions‐reducing impact of renewable energy adoption is quantitatively larger. In contrast, energy consumption remains an important contributor to emissions. Overall, the study highlights that promoting green innovation together with renewable energy adoption is important for supporting long‐term environmental sustainability a

title: Technological neutrality in EU Hydrogen Regulation : An Assessment of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2359
abstract: Hydrogen plays an important role in the European Union’s climate and energy policy, particularly in sectors where direct electrification is difficult. While renewable hydrogen remains in the EU’s long-term priority, low-carbon hydrogen is recognized as a worth considering option. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2359 establishes the methodology for assessing greenhouse gas emissions savings from low-carbon fuels and is therefore central to the legal framework governing low-carbon hydrogen. This thesis applies a doctrinal legal research method. It examines the methodology laid down in Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2359 from the perspective of technological neutrality. The main research question is to what extent is the methodology consistent with the principle of technological neutrality in EU energy law. The thesis examines the regulatory framework within which the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2359 was adopted. The principle of technological neutrality and its application in the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union are analysed, followed by an examination of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2359 and the methodology it

title: Life Cycle Assessment of CCS Scenarios in Biogas-Fueled Combined Cycle Power plants: A Pathway to Low-Carbon Power
abstract: Biogas-fuelled power generation is conventionally treated as carbon-neutral. However, by applying CCS into this biogas-to-electricity chain, net-negative CO₂ emissions can be achieved. This study evaluates the life-cycle environmental performance of such integration for a combined cycle power plant, assuming a baseline 98% CO₂ capture rate. The system boundary encompasses biogas supply, upgrading, power generation, and downstream CO₂ handling. Three configurations were assessed based on a functional unit of 1 kWh of net electricity: conventional amine-based (C-CCS), carbon molecular sieve membrane-based (MB-CCS), and a non-capture reference (C-NoCCS). The implementation of CCS imposes severe parasitic loads. Compared to the C-NoCCS net output of 5771 kW, net electricity generation drops by 33% in C-CCS (3835 kW) due to thermal and solvent demands, and by 45% in MB-CCS (3141 kW) driven by high compression requirements. These energy penalties dictate the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) results. Because of its simpler configuration, C-NoCCS performs best in 11 of 18 non-climate indicators. title: Towards relational timber life-cycle practices
abstract: This thesis examines how contemporary forestry and timber life-cycle practices in Aotearoa (New Zealand) can be critically reinterpreted from an architectural perspective. It situates timber not merely as a construction material, but as a product of land governance, ecological relationships, and cultural responsibility informed by tikanga and mātauranga. While timber is increasingly promoted within architectural and policy discourse as a sustainable and low-carbon material, its upstream conditions of production - forestry systems, governance arrangements, and land relationships - are rarely interrogated as part of architectural responsibility. This research positions forestry as an integral component of architecture’s material culture and ethical domain, where decisions made at the forest edge shape environmental, cultural, and material outcomes across the built environment. Contemporary forestry in Aotearoa primarily operates within institutional structures shaped by colonisation, western scientific management, and market-oriented logics that prioritise efficiency, yield, and short-term economic returns. title: Impacts of Microplastics on Soil Characteristics, Microbial Diversity and Greenhouse Gas Emissions: A Review
abstract: Soil microplastics (MPs) pollution has emerged as a global concern, yet its integrated impacts on soil biogeochemical cycles and greenhouse gas (GHG) fluxes remain incompletely understood. This review synthesizes studies from 2019 to 2026 on MP interactions with soil physicochemical properties, microbial communities, and GHG dynamics, emphasizing carbon and nitrogen cycling. MPs actively modify soil processes rather than acting as inert particles. Fiber and film MPs alter pore architecture, bulk density, and water retention, affecting aeration and microbial habitats. For carbon cycling, MPs modify DOC, MBC, and EOOC pools and trigger polymer-specific priming effects that range from positive to negative depending on polymer composition, with net outcomes varying across studies. For nitrogen cycling, MP-induced shifts in NO3−-N and NH4+-N availability and in nitrification and denitrification pathways yield variable N2O responses; notably, certain biodegradable polymers suppress N2O emissions in a dose-dependent manner, contrasting with the neutral or stimulatory effects of conventional plastics. title: The Impact of Climate Change Through Environmental Degradation and Possible Solutions via Smart, Sustainable Systems
abstract: Environmental degradation has been exacerbated by climate change, resulting in biodiversity loss, resource depletion, and extreme weather events. Rising global temperatures, deforestation, pollution, and water scarcity have reshaped ecosystems, threatening food security and livelihoods. These consequences include desertification, ocean acidification, and increases in greenhouse gas emissions, all of which intensify the climate crisis. Intelligent sustainable systems provide groundbreaking solutions that address and mitigate these impacts. Smart grids, IoT-based environmental monitoring, and advanced technologies such as AI-driven climate modeling improve resource efficiency and resilience. The use of renewable energy, precision agriculture, and circular economy principles supports sustainability. This is complemented by policy frameworks, green infrastructure, and carbon-neutral strategies, which are essential components of both adaptation and mitigation efforts. In this respect, this 340 chapter investigates climate change and its effects on daily life through environmental degradation, as well as the capacity of smart sustainable systems to improve climate resilience. title: Climate Action Strategies and Required Governance Policies for Cold Transitions to Promote and Strengthen Geoeconomics
abstract: Rapid climate changes are gripping the cold regions of the world, with particular consequences for the Arctic and high-altitude zones, giving rise to many challenges to ecosystems, infrastructure, and geopolitical stability. From melting ice caps to shifting trade and resource access, geoeconomic transformations require bold climate action strategies and governance policies. It calls for a more holistic approach to balancing global populations of systems, resources, transmission lines, and industries to provide for sustainable resource management, growth and income equalization, and—ultimately—carbon-neutral ecosystems and economies. Climate-adaptive trade agreements, investments in renewables, and international synergy are key policy interventions that may strike a balance between economic advancement and ecological balance. Moreover, AI-driven climate risk assessments with sustainable financing mechanisms can help build resilience in the long run. This chapter discusses strategic climate 364 actions and governance policies that will both manage cold transitions and buttress geoeconomic stability. This involves promoting adaptive policies and cross-border efforts to prepare for th

title: Voluntary Corporate Climate Targets in a Patchwork Policy Landscape
abstract: Many large, publicly-traded companies adopt voluntary greenhouse gas emission reduction commitments in the presence of a fragmented public policy landscape.To explore the potential emission implications of such commitments, we develop a framework for understanding how firms' voluntary emission targets interact with carbon pricing, regulatory mandates, subsidies, and heterogeneous policies across political jurisdictions.This analysis highlights the difficulty of distinguishing incremental voluntary emission abatement from policy-induced emission reductions.We introduce the Salata Institute Corporate Climate Targets Database, which we produced from public domain reports published by Russell 3000 firms over 2000-2024.The database documents the growth, form, scope, and sectoral distribution of voluntary greenhouse gas emission targets, including net-zero, carbon-neutral, carbon-reduction, energy-related, and qualitative commitments.Comparing this database with CDP, a non-profit organization formerly known as the Carbon Disclosure Project and the most common source of corporate emission targets used in the research literature, reveals substantial omissions in their survey-based data, es

title: Biochar-Compost Co-Application in Climate-Smart Agriculture: A Critical Review of Mechanisms, Interactions, Trade-Offs, and Implementation Pathways
abstract: : Climate-smart agricultural systems require soil-management strategies that improve soil health and crop productivity while reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and enhancing carbon retention. Biochar-compost co-application (BC-COM) has attracted interest because it may integrate complementary functions of carbon storage, nutrient supply, microbial regulation, and organic-waste recycling. This structured critical review synthesizes evidence on the mechanisms, agronomic and environmental responses, interaction behavior, trade-offs, and implementation requirements of BC-COM systems. Field studies report crop-yield responses ranging from negative to positive depending on amendment formulation and application rate, crop species, soil and climatic conditions, and comparator treatment, demonstrating context dependence rather than uniformly beneficial responses. Published quantitative syntheses have reported increases of 74.9% in plant productivity, 37.6% in soil total N, and 98.6% in soil organic matter following biochar-amended compost application; however, these pooled responses do not by themselves demonstrate statistical BC × COM synergy. title: Regulatory stress memory and physiological legacy across temporal scales in long-lived trees
abstract: Forest trees are increasingly exposed to recurrent, sequential, and combined climatic stresses, particularly drought and heatwaves. Because of their long lifespan, responses to environmental extremes are shaped not only by current conditions but also by prior stress exposure and post-stress recovery. History-dependent responses may therefore arise from regulatory stress memory, which modifies responses to subsequent stress, or from physiological legacies of incomplete recovery, residual damage, and resource limitation; these processes may interact, but physiological persistence alone does not demonstrate stress memory. This review integrates molecular, physiological, and ecological evidence to clarify how these processes interact across temporal and biological scales in long-lived trees. Evidence from Populus, Pinus , and other forest taxa highlights roles for transcriptional and epigenetic regulation, hormonal and metabolic reprogramming, hydraulic function, and carbon dynamics, while also revealing substantial gaps linking molecular persistence to long-term field performance. title: Role of Biochar in Soil Fertility Improvement, Soil Remediation and Greenhouse gas Emissions Reduction: A Systematic Review
abstract: Biochar is increasingly recognized for its potential to address interconnected global challenges of soil fertility depletion, soil contamination, and climate change. However, a comprehensive synthesis quantifying biochar's effects on soil properties, remediation, and greenhouse gas emissions with explicit linkages to feedstock, pyrolysis conditions, and application rates has been absent. This systematic review examined 156 studies (2009–2025) addressing these domains. Biochar improved soil physical properties. Bulk density decreased by 0.03 to 0.36 g cm⁻³, porosity increased by 2 to 50%, aggregate stability improved by 1 to 17%, and water-holding capacity increased by 9 to 130%. Chemical properties also improved, with pH changes ranging from a decrease of 0.3 units to an increase of 1.6 units, soil organic carbon increases by 7.5 to 30.5 g kg⁻¹, soil organic matter increases by 0.35 to 3.11%, and cation exchange capacity changes from −1.8 to +5.16 cmol kg⁻¹. Biochar stimulated beneficial microbes (Lactobacillus, Bacillus) and suppressed Fusarium. title: Navigating the land–energy nexus for carbon-neutral power systems in China
Dilemmas and Tripartite Optimization of Banks' Green Credit Development under Dual Carbon Target
abstract: Against the background of China's dual-carbon goals, green credit has expanded rapidly in China, yet problems including green-washing, heterogeneous cost pressure among different banks and potential systemic financial risks remain prominent. Most existing tripartite evolutionary-game studies on green credit only focus on direct interactions among governments, banks and enterprises, ignoring climate-policy uncertainty and supply-chain ESG spillover effects. This paper extends the tripartite evolutionary-game framework by introducing climate-risk shock parameters and supply-chain ESG-collaboration mechanisms. Numerical simulation under three groups of parameter settings identifies multiple equilibrium outcomes: lose-lose equilibrium, gradual win-win equilibrium and rapid win-win equilibrium. Drawing on EU Taxonomy and CSRD as reference, this paper conducts neutral cross-national parameter comparison and interprets how differences in disclosure requirements, penalty intensity and incentive magnitude change game convergence paths. title: PS8-8. Public Perception of Methane Emissions and Climate Change in the Livestock Industry: A Sentiment and Network Analysis of Reddit Discourse (2018–2026).
abstract: Abstract The objective of this study was to analyze public sentiment regarding livestock methane emissions and their perceived impact on climate change through machine learning and network analysis. We sought to quantify prevailing sentiment and identify thematic clusters to understand how the intersection of animal agriculture is perceived by digital communities. The study analyzed a dataset comprising 2,721 Reddit posts collected via the Reddit JSON API, spanning an eight-year period from March 2018 to April 2026. Data collection utilized targeted query strategies focusing on methane, livestock, and greenhouse gas-related keywords. The methodology included a rigorous attrition protocol, involving language filtering and deduplication, and sentiment classification using a multi-model ensemble integrating RoBERTa, ClimateBERT, and VADER. Keyword co-occurrence networks were constructed to identify thematic communities, utilizing the Louvain algorithm for clustering. Temporal analysis was applied across 97 active months to identify trends in discussion volume and sentiment evolution. We found out that overall sentiment is weighted toward the neutral and negative, with 1,306 posts (48.

title: Perspective Chapter: Scaling Pre-Monsoon Dry Sowing for Soil Restoration and Climate-Resilient Agrifood Systems – Evidence from Natural Farming in India
abstract: This case study examines Pre-Monsoon Dry Sowing (PMDS) as a climate-resilient farming practice in restoring soil functions and reviving nutrient cycles. It provides insights into Rani’s transition from chemical-intensive cultivation on barren land to Natural Farming using PMDS, diverse seeds, seed pelletization, bioinoculants, and natural pest management. PMDS enabled early crop establishment before the monsoon, supporting root development, soil moisture utilisation and biological activity. Soil assessments revealed improvements in various indicators. Soil pH declined from 7.32 in the fourth year to 7.02 in the fifth year, indicating a shift towards near-neutral conditions. Soil organic carbon increased from 0.42% to 0.463% in the Natural Farming field, while the chemical field increased from 0.30% to 0.45%, reflecting improved soil structure. The fifth-year Natural Farming field demonstrated increased soil respiration, urease and phosphatase activities, as well as higher bacterial and actinomycete populations and total nitrogen. Improved soil fertility contributed to a gradual increase in yields and farm income. Paddy yield increased from 10 bags per acre in the first year to 40 b

title: Editorial: Dynamics of land use change: ecological conservation, restoration strategies, and carbon balance
abstract: Land use change is a crucial link connecting human activities with Earth system processes and a core entry point for understanding regional responses to global environmental change. Against the backdrop of rapid urbanization, climate change, and carbon reduction targets, the land system is undergoing unprecedented restructuring. How to reveal the ecological and environmental effects of land use change through scientific monitoring, simulation, and optimization, and formulate regionally differentiated management strategies, has become a prominent issue in land science and sustainable development research. This Research Topic, "Dynamics of Land Use Change: Ecological Conservation, Restoration Strategies, and Carbon Balance", gathers eight original studies from diverse geographical and developmental contexts, including China and Italy. Published in Frontiers in Environmental Science, it presents recent studies from three dimensions: carbon emissions and carbon sink processes, landscape ecological risks and ecological security patterns, and land use conflict identification and spatial optimization decisions.Regarding carbon processes and carbon balance, several studies provide empirica
concepts: Land use, land-use change and forestry

title: Indoor Environmental Quality and Occupant Comfort in Educational Buildings in a Tropical Climate: A Critical Review of the Nigerian Evidence
abstract: Educational buildings in tropical, low-resource settings are routinely occupied under conditions of high ambient heat, humidity, natural ventilation and constrained energy supply, yet the indoor environmental quality (IEQ) delivered by these buildings, and its consequences for occupant comfort, health and learning, remains unevenly documented. This narrative review critically synthesises the empirical literature on thermal, indoor air quality (IAQ), visual and acoustic conditions in Nigerian primary, secondary and tertiary educational buildings, situating this evidence within the broader international literature on IEQ in schools. Sources were identified through structured searching of multidisciplinary and subject-specific databases, institutional repositories and citation tracking, with eligibility restricted to empirical or review studies addressing measured or perceived IEQ parameters in occupied educational settings. The review finds consistent evidence that naturally ventilated Nigerian classrooms operate with neutral and acceptable comfort temperatures several degrees above internationally codified thresholds, reflecting genuine adaptive capacity among occupants, although th

title: Carbon black and hydrogen production from upgraded fast pyrolysis bio-oils via high-temperature pyrolysis
abstract: The current manufacturing of carbon black (CB) has a high climate impact and must transition to a carbon-neutral process to meet sustainability goals. In this work, fast pyrolysis bio-oil (FPBO) from biomass and four different upgraded bio-oils (represented by synthetic mixtures made from model compounds) were used to produce renewable CB in an entrained flow reactor (EFR) at different temperatures (1100–1700 °C). The aim of this work was to investigate how the composition of bio-oils produced via the following upgrading technologies, catalytic fast pyrolysis (CFP), catalytic hydropyrolysis (CHP), slurry hydroprocessing (SHP), and slurry hydroprocessing followed by fixed bed hydroprocessing (SHP + FBHP) affects the yield and structural properties of CB. The experimental results demonstrated that CB yield from FPBO were 34–45 wt% on a carbon basis, whereas substantially higher yields (67–93 wt%) were obtained from the upgraded bio-oils depending on the specific upgrading technology and temperature of the EFR. title: Innovative Solutions for Soil Restoration and Prevention of Soil Degradation: collective monograph
abstract: The monograph provides the scientific support for innovative development in the field of soil restoration and the prevention of soil degradation aimed at improving the ecological state of the regions of Ukraine. The authors present modern, innovative solutions for the digitalization of soil use, as well as the modeling and forecasting of spatial and temporal soil changes. Furthermore, the study develops measures to stop and prevent degradation processes and the consequences of military damage to the soil cover, and introduces resource-saving, climate-neutral technologies for managing plant nutrition, soil health, and carbon cycling in agro-ecosystems, as well as harmonizing with European environmental legislation in this field. This publication was prepared with the support of the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine as part of the project «Complex of innovative solutions for soil restoration and prevention of their degradation in order to improve the ecological state of the regions of Ukraine» No. BF A01-2025. It showed that HULIS-a and HULIS-n exhibited the highest emission factors under heating (0.80±0.46 g/kg) and cooking (0.35±0.36 g/kg) scenarios, respectively. HULIS-n exhibited the strongest light absorption compared to the highest OP for HP-WSOM. Total WSOM-C emissions from animal dung combustion on the QTP were 7.5 Gg and 2.0 Gg for heating and non-heating season, with sheep dung for heating contributing the largest (40.6 %). title: The politics of neutrality in climate adjudication: Scientific consensus, judicial legitimacy and equity in rights‐based European climate litigation
abstract: Abstract This article examines two European rights‐based climate litigation cases— Klimaatzaak v Belgium and Milieudefensie v Shell —where courts were asked to set quantified climate mitigation targets. Such determinations inherently involve distributive questions, as they require allocating shares of a finite global carbon budget across actors and over time. I analyse how courts navigate this task while maintaining a posture of neutrality to preserve judicial legitimacy. Courts engage in ‘boundary work’ to distinguish law from policymaking and thereby enable the neutralisation of judicial intervention. I analyse how this imperative operates in these two case studies: Judges rely on the authority of scientific consensus, particularly reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), to delimit the legitimate scope of adjudication. In doing so, courts treat scientific objects, notably climate scenarios and mitigation pathways, as stabilised outputs whose underlying normative assumptions and distributive implications remain largely unexamined. title: Pre-combustion fuel reforming in gas turbines: Hydrocarbon and carbon-neutral fuel pathways
abstract: Gas turbines are a cornerstone of modern power generation, providing reliable and dispatchable electricity across the globe. However, their significant contribution to global CO 2 emissions has become increasingly untenable under international climate agreements such as the Paris Agreement. This creates a critical imperative to develop technologies that can improve the efficiency and sustainability of existing and future gas turbine fleets without compromising their operational flexibility. While the long-term vision is a fully renewable energy system, the intermittent nature of sources like wind and solar necessitates the continued use of thermal power for grid stability in the foreseeable future. Within this context, the transition to low-carbon and carbon-neutral fuels – such as hydrogen, ammonia, and methanol – has emerged as a key decarbonization pathway. However, the direct use of these fuels in conventional gas turbines is hampered by challenges related to combustion stability, flame speed, NO x formation, and, in some cases, fuel infrastructure and storage. title: The Compounding Returns of Early Action Across Development and Climate
abstract: Early action in development and climate policy generates compounding returns because delay is not neutral time. As the report notes, “costs do not simply wait. They accumulate, interact and often become harder to reverse” . Each year of inaction adds physical exposure, locks in carbon‑intensive or fragile infrastructure, and allows human‑capital losses to propagate across generations. A road built without drainage, an inefficient building approved today, or a decade of pollution exposure all create future liabilities that are larger than the initial cost of prevention. Early action therefore functions as an investment in option value, preserving future choices while reducing the stock of damage future societies inherit. The report synthesizes evidence from IPCC, UNEP, IEA, World Bank, OECD, WHO and the Global Commission on Adaptation to show that delay multiplies costs through five channels: accumulated exposure, higher hazard intensity, capital‑stock lock‑in, compressed transition schedules, and foregone learning. title: Conclusion
abstract: This closing chapter reiterates some of the main messages from the volume by dispelling some common myths about climate mitigation. Myth 1. Factors other than greenhouse gas emissions have caused observed warming to date of 1.2°C . No. There is consensus among scientists that the warming to date above preindustrial levels (observed at weather stations and confirmed by satellite data) is from atmospheric accumulations of human-induced, heat-trapping gases, rather than other factors like changes in solar radiation and volcanic activity or urban heat absorption (see Chapter 2 ). Myth 2. Global warming is not a major concern because people can adapt, for example, by adopting air conditioning, drought-resistant crops, and moving to cooler climates . No. Global warming is causing a diverse range of climate risks such as greater frequency and intensity of heat waves, shifting precipitation patterns (which puts at risk water systems, agriculture, and ecosystems), droughts, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes—these risks are escalating because warming causes more energy and water vapor in the atmosphere. Higher atmospheric CO 2 concentrations also eat away at the minerals used by marine life

title: What effect does the projectification of local governance have on the transformative capacity of urban net-zero policies? A French case study
abstract: How does post-democratic urban governance affect the capacity for climate action? What effect does the projectification of local governance have on politics and the political under climate action, and consequently on the transformative capacity of net-zero policies? To address these questions, this article draws on an in-depth case study of a French city that aims to become the first carbon-neutral coastal city. It concludes that projectification has ambivalent effects on climate action. On one hand, because depoliticises climate issues, projectification facilitates both ambitious climate pledges and incremental change. On other hand, like other forms of depoliticisation, projectification doesn’t allow the legitimation of such policies and thus undermines their transformative capacity.

Nutrient density and carbon footprint across food classification systems: evidence from Spain
abstract: Nutrient density (ND) and carbon footprint (CF) have been assessed jointly before, but whether the resulting rankings depend on how foods are grouped remains unexamined. We evaluated the ND and CF of 119 commonly consumed Spanish foods, based on data availability in the national consumption report. Their nutrient-climate profiles were then tested across three classification systems: food origin, conventional food groups, and the WHO Nutrient Profile Model (WHONPM). ND was measured with the Nutrient Rich Foods index (NRF11.3) per 100 g; CF (kg CO₂e/kg, cradle-to-consumer) came from AGRIBALYSE™ 3.1. Both were combined into a Combined Nutrient-Climate Index (CNCI), the ratio of CF to NRF11.3, with negative NRF values floored. Climate was the only environmental dimension assessed; water, land and biodiversity impacts were not. ND and CF were independent (Spearman ρ = −0.040, p = 0.668). Holding both metrics fixed and varying only the classification system altered the discriminatory power of the analysis: the effect of grouping on CF rose from ε² = 0.34 under food origin to ε² = 0.66 under the WHONPM. title: Climate change exposure and firm value in China: evidence consistent with a discount-rate interpretation
abstract: This paper examines the relationship between firm-level climate change exposure and firm value in China. Using A-share listed firms from 2002 to 2020 and a disclosure-based measure of perceived climate change exposure, we find a significant negative association between climate change exposure and firm value. Our measure provides incremental explanatory power beyond conventional proxies, including ESG indicators and climate change news risk measures. Channel tests provide evidence consistent with a discount-rate interpretation. Both transition and physical-risk exposures are negatively associated with firm value. However, for firms in carbon-neutral industries, transition exposure is positively associated with firm value, consistent with transition-related growth opportunities. The negative associations are more pronounced for firms in high-pollution industries and coastal regions. Further results indicate that the negative valuation association is weaker among firms with stronger green innovation and ESG ratings. Overall, our findings highlight the pricing of climate risk and the role of transition opportunities in firm valuation.

title: Forest residue biochars: feedstock, pyrolysis, and properties
abstract: The European Union (EU) is fostering the bioeconomy as a strategy to achieve a climate-neutral and circular economy. In this context, valorization of forest wastes as pine sawdust into biochar is a key opportunity in Galicia (NW Spain), one of the most forested areas of the EU. Moreover, two abundant Galician shrubs, Erica cinerea L. and Ulex europaeus L. have not yet been explored as biochar feedstock, although these shrubs are associated with high biomass accumulation and an increase of forest fires in the region. Therefore, their conversion into biochar offers a sustainable waste management pathway. This study aims to characterize biochar produced from different Galician feedstocks (pine sawdust, Erica cinerea L., and Ulex europaeus L.). The biochar was produced under three pyrolysis temperatures (300, 400 and 500°C) and three pyrolysis times (30, 60 and 120 minutes). The results showed that nitrogen, carbon concentration, and C/N ratio in the biochar were greatly affected by feedstock initial composition and operating conditions during pyrolysis. title: The nuclear-climate nexus for net-zero pathways: Opportunities, challenges, and policy directions: A review
abstract: Rapid decarbonization is now a central sustainability challenge because electricity demand is rising while climate risks are increasingly affecting energy infrastructure. Although solar, wind, storage, efficiency and electrification remain essential for net-zero pathways, many power systems also require firm low-carbon resources, resilient infrastructure and governance arrangements that can sustain reliable energy services under extreme weather, geopolitical disruption and growing industrial demand. This review therefore develops the Nuclear-Climate Nexus as a system-level framework for evaluating nuclear energy not simply as a low-operational-emission technology, but as a conditional contributor to climate mitigation, adaptation, energy security and sustainable development. The review shows that nuclear energy can support net-zero pathways through lifetime extension of safe existing reactors, selective new construction, firm low-carbon electricity, nuclear-renewable integration, industrial heat, reactor hydrogen, desalination, district heating and high-reliability electricity. The Green Investment Paradox in Japan: Growth, Energy, and Financial Realities
abstract: This study examines the concept of "green finance," a cornerstone of sustainable development, in the context of the Japanese economy, exploring its empirical and theoretical dimensions. The relationship between renewable energy consumption (RENE), GDP per capita, and foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows was econometrically tested using data from Japan for the period 1990-2024. ADF unit root tests applied within the econometric analysis framework showed that the variables were not stationary at their level values but became stationary (I(1)) after taking their first differences. The results of the "Bootstrap ARDL Bound Test" applied subsequently confirmed the existence of a long-term cointegration relationship between the variables. Japan has announced its Green Growth Strategy in line with its goal of becoming carbon neutral by 2050, and has become the second-largest green bond issuer in Asia. However, the analysis reveals that there are still significant gaps between goals and practices. title: Solar parks as an opportunity to jointly advance climate-change mitigation and biodiversity conservation
abstract: Anthropogenic climate change is among the most pressing challenges for humanity making carbon-neutral energy production a top priority. Across the globe, solar energy is the single fastest growing energy source with solar parks covering more and more land surface area across many continents. The rise in solar energy production affects terrestrial biodiversity in the areas now occupied by solar parks but our knowledge on the consequences for biodiversity lacks behind the speed of solar-park establishment. This discrepancy likely leads to suboptimal policies regarding solar-park placement, design, and management which, if optimized, could potentially lead to synergies instead of trade-offs between climate-change mitigation and biodiversity conservation. Here, we summarize previous research and remaining knowledge gaps regarding the impacts of solar-park placement, design, and management on biodiversity. If adequately placed, solar parks could increase landscape heterogeneity and habitat connectivity. Solar-park design could enhance microclimate and habitat heterogeneity. title: Short Food Supply Chains as Pathways Towards Carbon-Neutral Rural Development: A Logistics-Adjusted Scenario Analysis for Fresh Produce in Galicia, Spain
abstract: Achieving carbon neutrality requires transformative changes across multiple sectors, including food systems. Short Food Supply Chains (SFSCs) have been increasingly proposed as mechanisms capable of reducing transport-related greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions while promoting more resilient forms of rural development. This study examines the potential contribution of SFSCs to carbon-neutral rural development using Galicia (Spain), with particular attention to the territories of Ferrolterra and As Pontes de García Rodríguez, as a case study. A scenario-based approach was employed to compare Regional Short Food Supply Chains and Conventional Long Supply Chains, assuming average transport distances of 80 km and 800 km, respectively. Transport-related greenhouse gas emissions were estimated using a ton-kilometre methodology based on European freight transport emission factors, while sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate the robustness of the findings under alternative assumptions. Carbon Footprint Assessment and Pathway to Carbon Neutrality in a Higher Educational Institute: A Case Study of the Alpine Institute of Management and Technology, Dehradun, India
abstract: The building sector is a major contributor to global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and higher education institutions, with their diverse operational activities, represent a significant but underexplored subsector for carbon accounting. This study quantifies the carbon footprint of the Alpine Institute of Management and Technology, Dehradun (Uttarakhand, India), over four calendar years (2022-2025) using a bottom-up Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) approach aligned with ISO 14064- 1 and the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard. Emission sources were classified into Scope 1 (static and mobile combustion), Scope 2 (purchased electricity), and Scope 3 (employee commuting, waste disposal, water consumption, and paper/stationery use), with human respiration quantified separately as a supplementary source. Total institutional emissions under Scopes 1-3 were found to be 56,351.77 kg CO2-eq (2022), 60,131.82 kg CO2-eq (2023), 62,168.00 kg CO2-eq (2024) and 59,604.84 kg CO2-eq (2025), with purchased electricity (Scope 2) the dominant contributor at 41-44% of the total in every year studied, followed by Scope 1 combustion sources (38-40%) and Scope 3 activities (18-20%). title: Interaction-based weight optimization framework for adaptive façades: balancing cooling energy, carbon, and comfort
abstract: Adaptive facade performance depends on both window–to–wall ratio and building orientation. Yet most design methods treat WWR as fixed and overlook parameter interactions. This study presents a summer–focused optimization framework for PCM–integrated Venetian blind facades in Tehran’s semi–arid climate. The framework combines EnergyPlus simulation, Sobol sensitivity analysis, XGBoost surrogate modeling, and Bayesian Optimization. An Interaction‑Based Weight Framework derives MCDM weights directly from Sobol higher‑order interaction indices ( S H ), and simultaneously treats WWR as an active variable evaluated independently across four cardinal orientations. The results show that Slat Angle and WWR dominate both individual and interaction effects across all facades. In contrast, PCM Thickness, Slat Depth, and Slat Distance to Glass behave as purely additive parameters with negligible interactions. Optimal WWR varies sharply with orientation, reaching 78.18% for north–facing facades while converging near 20% for south, east, and west. title: A study of CEOs as sustainability leaders
abstract: This doctoral thesis explores non-pecuniary motivations of chief executive officers (CEOs) in driving corporate sustainability and managing carbon transition risks. It investigates three interweaved dimensions: the early-life climate trauma experience, nature-connectedness, and social capital of CEOs and their impact on corporate sustainability outcomes. The three chapters in the thesis are motivated by the previous literature in behavioral characteristics of CEOs in corporate settings (see Malmendier Nagel (2011) for example) and sustainability consideration demanded by investors and society (e.g. Giglio et al. (2021) and Hsu et al. (2023)). Specifically, the field survey by Edmans et al. (2021) reveals that CEOs are more motivated by their non-monetary compensation in their career, compared with conventional monetary compensation. Linking behavioral factors of CEOs (i.e. early- life climate-related disaster experience, nature-connectedness, and social capital) to the literature of sustainability and sustainable investing, this thesis outlines the implicit factors behind firm sustainability. title: From material loops to whole-life value: reframing infrastructure circularity for resilience
abstract: Circular Economy (CE) frameworks for the built environment predominantly address material recovery and prolonged asset use (Akomea-Frimpong et al., 2024). These perspectives are necessary but insufficient for infrastructure. Infrastructure systems deliver essential services over decades through interconnected physical assets, lifecycle information, organizational relationships, and regulatory arrangements. They may therefore achieve high material recovery while still losing functional capacity, institutional knowledge, adaptive capacity, or opportunities for system-wide value creation. Moreover, circularity does not inherently imply resilience: strategies that maximize resource efficiency may reduce the redundancy, diversity, and spare capacity required to withstand disruption, while increasing interdependencies may introduce new vulnerabilities (Kennedy & Linnenluecke, 2022). This tension becomes particularly important when distinguishing static resilience (SR) as the capacity to maintain functionality during disruption (Deloukas and Apostolopoulou, 2017) from dynamic resilience (DR), which concerns recovery, adaptation, learning, and improvement over time (Pant et al., 2014). abstract: The Future of Sustainable Tourism: Balancing Growth, Innovation, and Environmental Responsibility Dattatray Vishwanath Kawade Assistant Professor, Dept. Food and Beverage Service, Sheila Raheja Institute of Hotel Management, Bandra East, Mumbai Abstract The future of environmentally conscious travel lies in achieving a balance between tourism growth, environmental conservation, cultural preservation, and economic development. As international travel continues to expand, concerns related to climate change, carbon emissions, overtourism, and depletion of natural resources have encouraged governments, tourism stakeholders, and travellers to adopt sustainable practices. Sustainable tourism seeks to minimize environmental and social impacts while maximizing benefits for local communities and economies. Technological advancements such as artificial intelligence, renewable energy, smart transportation systems, and data-driven destination management are expected to make tourism more efficient and sustainable. title: Integrating climate-neutrality criteria into sustainable public procurement: A comparative legal study of the United Arab Emirates, European Union and France
abstract: Public procurement increasingly serves as a legal and regulatory instrument through which governments shape markets and pursue sustainability goals. Using doctrinal, comparative and normative legal analysis, this study examines how climate-neutrality criteria can be incorporated into sustainable public procurement in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), drawing on European Union (EU) and French law. The comparison shows that environmental objectives become legally credible when they are translated into transparent specifications, award criteria, life-cycle costing methods, evidentiary rules and performance obligations, rather than left as broad policy aspirations. The UAE federal procurement framework already recognises public value, sustainable development, environmental specifications and products that reduce carbon emissions, but it does not yet provide a fully operational climate-procurement methodology. title: ENERGY SECURITY OF ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES IN UKRAINE UNDER MARTIAL LAW
abstract: Introduction. The large-scale destruction of Ukraine's energy infrastructure caused by the full-scale war has significantly increased risks to the stable provision of environmental services, agricultural production, and waste management. Under these conditions, strengthening energy security has become a strategic priority for maintaining ecosystem resilience, supporting economic recovery, and fulfilling international commitments related to sustainable development and the European Green Deal. The transition from centralized energy supply to decentralized, low-carbon energy systems requires new conceptual approaches that integrate energy, environmental, and economic dimensions. The purpose of the article. The purpose of this study is to assess the current state of energy security of environmental services in Ukraine under martial law, determine the contribution of renewable energy technologies to the resilience of ecosystem services, and substantiate strategic directions for the post-war transformation of environmentally oriented energy systems. abstract: Biochar and hydrochar are increasingly described as fertilizers, nutrient-recovery media, soil-carbon amendments, and climate-mitigation products, although these functions require different evidence. This structured critical narrative review reappraises a 122-source analytic corpus spanning 2019–2026 and applies the Dual-Performance Boundary Framework for Carbonaceous Fertilizers (DPB-CF), which independently tests agronomic fertilizer function and net life-cycle climate benefit. The corpus is strongly recent, with 67 sources (54.9%) published in 2024–2026 and 50 (41.0%) in 2025–2026. Evidence is synthesized from feedstock chemistry through pyrolysis, co-pyrolysis, and hydrothermal carbonization; nutrient partitioning and speciation; nutrient capture; controlled release; soil–plant response; product engineering; safety; techno-economics; life-cycle assessment; regulation; and scale-up. A three-generation author-developed framework is operationalized: amendment char, nutrient-enriched char, and engineered nutrient-recovery fertilizer. title: Innovative energy recovery in wastewater treatment for sustainable environmental and agricultural resilience
abstract: The treatment of wastewater is one of the foundations of environmental protection, which is still energy-consuming and resource-intensive. The realization of carbon-neutral operations relies on sustainable transformations in the application of energy recovery technologies. This chapter addresses advanced systems including bioelectrochemical systems, microbial fuel cells, and hydropower integration at wastewater treatment plant outlets, which support reduced fossil fuel dependence and enhanced energy efficiency. It emphasizes the use of life cycle assessment (LCA) as a tool to evaluate environmental impacts and to determine the most efficient recovery pathways. The conversion of organic carbon into valuable products instead of releasing it as greenhouse gases is highlighted as a key innovation. The importance of system dynamics modelling in estimating the global potential for increased treatment coverage through energy recovery is discussed. The feasibility of nutrient cycling, water reuse, and biogas upgrading strategies is analyzed using European case studies and simulation-based models. title: Consumer understanding of climate targets is low and hard to improve: evidence from three online studies
abstract: Many firms publicize net-zero or carbon neutral targets, yet it is unclear whether consumers understand these targets. Policy proposals-as well as recent court rulings-call on firms to explain what those targets mean. We test whether such explanations enhance consumer understanding in two online studies with nationally representative U.S. samples (N=300; N=1,500) and in a large-scale webcam-based eye-tracking experiment (N=500). Baseline knowledge is low: 95 percent of respondents fail to name even one defining feature of net-zero or carbon neutral targets, yet they are willing to pay a price premium for gift cards from companies with such targets. Concise disclosures raise objective understanding when a single product is shown, but none of the formats alter willingness to pay. In a more realistic setting with multiple products and competing cues, disclosures attract substantial gaze time, yet no longer improve comprehension; the visually salient color-coded format is associated with more misconceptions. title: Impact of bundling and sequencing of measures in retrofit roadmaps with hybrid heat pump systems – A case study for a municipal non-residential building in Germany
abstract: Achieving climate neutrality in the building sector necessitates a well-balanced mix, entailing measures that reduce the space heating demand and measures to decarbonize the heat supply system. In non-residential buildings, the space heating demand can be reduced through both renovation measures targeting the building envelope and heat recovery from the ventilation system. In order to avoid CO 2 emissions, the implementation of the entire set of retrofit measures should be aimed at, but is often not practically feasible due to financial and other constraints. This issue may be addressed with a hybrid heat pump system, wherein the existing, fossil-fueled boiler continues to be operated to cover the residual thermal load until other retrofit measures have reduced the space heating demand to a level that it can only be covered by the heat pump. The proposed approach combines a techno-economic assessment of retrofit measures with a detailed simulation of the hybrid heat pump system across different stages of implemented retrofit measures. title: Reply on RC1
abstract: Abstract. The terrestrial carbon (C) cycle is a key global biogeochemical cycle, linked to climate change and regulation, provisioning and regulating ecosystem services and underpinning human livelihoods. To understand climate risks and to support the development of effective climate mitigation strategies requires rigorous, uncertainty bounded, systemic information on C dynamics and their underpinning ecological processes. Significant effort has been invested into attempting to quantify current C stocks and exchanges of C. These data are often incomplete in space and time, contain poorly characterised errors, and lack internal consistency checks, making the construction of a reliable global C budget a significant challenge. Here, we ask what information on contemporary terrestrial carbon dynamics can an integration of current geospatial data confidently provide? We present a global (0.5 × 0.5 deg), multi-decadal (2003–2024) analysis of the terrestrial C-cycle at a monthly time step. title: Editorial: Advancing the just transition: navigating towards a sustainable future
abstract: By content clustering the contributions, five categories emerge. The first concerns participatory governance and democratic engagement. Keywords such as "participation" and "decision-making" characterize this body of work. Kambo et al. [1] demonstrate how a structured deliberative engagement process can bridge the gap between citizens, policymakers, and industry actors in shaping Australia's future energy and fuel systems. Using the "diamond of participatory decision-making" framework, their analysis reveals that while considerable alignment exists across cohorts on the broad direction of a lowcarbon future, divergences surface around the social and environmental justice dimensions of specific technology choices -including hydrogen and biogas -that require innovative governance mechanisms to navigate. Similarly, Kunlere and Shah [2] challenge the simplistic binaries that often dominate public debates on renewable energy. By introducing the PARO framework, which categorises public responses to energy injustice across a spectrum of positions that conventional "supporter versus opponent" dichotomies cannot capture, the authors provide a more granular analytical perspective for diagnos

title: Emerging Trends and Future Prospects of Bioenergy From Waste Biomass
abstract: This chapter explores the potential of bioenergy derived from waste biomass, addressing global challenges in waste management, energy security, and climate change mitigation. It provides an in depth analysis of emerging technologies such as synthetic biology, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence that are revolutionizing biomass conversion processes. Emphasis is placed on innovations like engineered microbes, nanocatalysts, and AI driven biorefineries that enhance efficiency, scalability, and sustainability. It investigates novel waste utilization techniques, including hybrid conversion systems, plasma gasification, and bioelectrochemical systems, offering pathways to carbon-neutral and carbon-negative fuels. It further discusses decentralized bioenergy systems and integration with circular economy models, highlighting the socioeconomic and environmental benefits. Finally, the chapter identifies key challenges technological, economic, environmental, and policy-related and proposes strategic mitigation measures to support the transition toward a sustainable bioenergy future.

Optical Remote Sensing and Machine Learning Enable Scalable Carbon Mapping in Himalayan Forests Despite Spectral Saturation Challenges
abstract: Accurate aboveground biomass (AGB) estimation is critical for climate change mitigation and carbon accounting in mountain regions, yet spatially explicit mapping remains limited by reliance on conventional field methods and underexplored machine learning approaches in the Himalaya. Bhutan, a carbon-negative nation maintaining 70% forest cover, faces urgent demand to develop robust monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) systems for carbon market participation under the Paris Agreement Article 6. This study developed a random forest (RF) model that integrates Sentinel-2A multispectral imagery, nine vegetation indices, topographic variables, and field-measured AGB from 99 plots across 244.6 hectares in the Kyentshen Community Forest. Using recursive feature elimination, 10 key predictors were identified from 27 candidate variables: Band 11, SLAVI, Band 12, WDRVI, NDVI, elevation, NDWI, GNDVI, band ratio (r3), and Band 9. The optimized RF model achieved R² = 0.34 and RMSE = 67.98 ± 19.79 t/ha on training data (Ntree = 500, Mtry = 3). However, test-set performance declined substantially (R² = 0.42, RMSE = 86.14 t/ha), indicating overfitting and reflecting limitations of spectral

title: GREENWASHING: WHY ENVIRONMENTAL CLAIMS NEED LEGAL REGULATION
abstract: Walk into a supermarket today and we can see that the entire establishment has turned green. Shampoos promise to be planet-friendly, clothes belong to consciousness collections, packaging is made of 100% sustainable materials, and companies announce their plans to become carbon neutral someday in the distant future. Green has turned out to be a very profitable color. But what happens when the color is greener than the product? This is where greenwashing comes in. To put it simply, greenwashing occurs when organizations make unsubstantiated or misleading claims about the environmental benefits of their services, products, or operations. There is an element of lying, but usually, it is a shade less egregious, as it could just be a combination of vague statements, selective information disclosure, appealing green imagery, or climate-friendly pledges that do not have a concrete plan behind them .The issue with greenwashing is that it does not just create bad advertising; it could deter consumers from choosing genuinely climate-conscious options and reward unsustainable companies for their misleading claims.

title: Crediting temporarily bound carbon reduces emissions and costs in integrated production of EU refineries
abstract: Abstract Oil refineries must transition to become climate-neutral, but their integrated production of fuels and chemicals makes this challenging. Carbon pricing systems can encourage cleaner production, but currently ignore carbon stored in plastic products. A promising approach is to credit this temporarily stored carbon, which would incentivize renewable materials. However, it remains unclear how such policies affect overall refinery operations. Here we show that crediting carbon stored in plastic products significantly reduces emissions, fossil fuel consumption, and production costs compared to current regulations. Using an optimisation model, minimising cost of integrated refinery production in Europe by 2050, we demonstrate that including this carbon credit leads to a more efficient system. Our findings provide guidance for policymakers designing carbon pricing mechanisms that can effectively accelerate the transition to sustainable refinery operations.

A sentiment analysis of public opposition to carbon capture and storage technology
abstract: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is recognized as an important technology for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and achieving climate targets, yet some segments of society express public opposition. Public opposition, even when expressed by minority groups, has at times influenced CCS project outcomes. Opposition extends beyond technical risk concerns, including emotional, symbolic, and territorial dimensions. This study examines how such opposition was constructed through protest materials, social media content, and press articles related to a specific CCS project. A mixed-methods design combined sentiment analysis using a natural language processing (NLP) model with qualitative content analysis. Because the corpus was deliberately sampled from oppositional channels, these sentiment scores characterize how opposition is expressed rather than the balance of public opinion at large. Within this corpus, opposition was articulated largely through negative sentiment (mean sentiment -0.44), particularly in materials from environmental NGOs and labor unions, with recurring concerns including seismic risk, proximity, institutional distrust, and perceived territorial injustice. title: Impacts of Exogenous Energy Shocks on the Carbon Neutrality Pathways of Guangdong Power System: A Coupled LEAP-NEMO Modeling Approach
abstract: In the context of global energy transition and climate change, exogenous energy shocks (such as energy price volatility, renewable energy uncertainty, and increasing power demand) pose growing challenges to power system carbon neutrality. However, existing studies mainly focus on optimizing emission-reduction pathways while neglecting system resilience under energy shocks. This study applies a coupled LEAP-NEMO model for Guangdong Province, integrating demand growth, generation evolution, dispatch optimization, system costs, and carbon constraints. Five scenarios (BAS, COM, COM_ES1, COM_ES2, and COM_ES3) are established to assess the impacts of exogenous energy shocks on carbon-neutral transition pathways. The results show that under COM scenario, Guangdong’s power system’s carbon emissions will peak by 2030 and reach net-zero by 2055. Different energy shocks produce substantially different effects on the carbon-neutral transition. Fossil fuel price shocks (COM_ES1) have limited impacts, with cumulative emissions changing by only 2.1% relative to COM. Renewable energy volatility (COM_ES2) reduces wind and solar generation and raises cumulative emissions by 73.7%, preventing carbon

title: Recalibrating the External-Cost Benefits of Road-to-Rail Freight Modal Shift: Evidence from South Korea
abstract: Effective modal shift policies require accurate valuation of the external costs associated with freight transport. However, South Korea’s logistics policy currently relies on valuation parameters that have not been systematically updated since 2013. This study recalibrates the unit benefits of shifting freight from roads to rails using a hybrid estimation framework that combines bottom-up emission estimation with a top-down allocation of aggregate external costs, grounded in national statistics harmonized to a 2022 base year (with some inputs drawn from the most recent earlier survey years and price-adjusted to 2022) and link-level national traffic data (KOTI View-T 3.0). We quantify the reductions in average external costs per ton/kilometer across five impact domains: air pollution, climate change, noise, traffic accidents, and congestion. The analysis yields a total unit benefit of KRW 151.81 per ton/kilometer, a figure approximately 3.7 times the inflation-adjusted benchmark currently in use.
