title: Earth’s early tectonic modes and implications for habitability
abstract: Tectonic mode manifests how a planet’s interior is cooling, and it encompasses all the geological activities (e.g., magmatism, deformation, metamorphism, sedimentation) that characterize the planetary body. Tectonic processes exert first-order control on factors key to planetary habitability (e.g., Southam et al., 2015). For example, tectonic mode controls the long-term prevalence of surface oceans, the sustenance of physicochemical conditions (e.g., temperature) favourable for metabolic activity, fluxing of elements in and out of the planet’s interior and thereby, the availability of bio-essential nutrients (e.g., C, O, H, N, P, S) (Cockell et al., 2016). However, all tectonic modes do not regulate these processes efficiently. For example, stagnant-lid mode restricts heat and material exchange between a planet’s interior and surficial reservoirs compared to plate tectonics. Further, certain factors determining a planet’s tectonic mode – like internal heat budget, mechanical behaviour of rocks, and volatile content – can vary with time, leading to the prevalence of different tectonic modes during planetary evolution. Thus, a planet’s habitability is critically intertwined with its

title: Considerations for Detecting Organic Indicators of Metabolism on Enceladus
abstract: Enceladus is of interest to astrobiology and the search for life since it is thought to host active hydrothermal activity and habitable conditions. It is also possible that the organics detected on Enceladus may indicate an active prebiotic or biotic system; in particular, the conditions on Enceladus may favor mineral-driven protometabolic reactions. When including metabolism-related biosignatures in Enceladus mission concepts, it is necessary to base these in a clearer understanding of how these signatures could also be produced prebiotically. In addition, postulating which biological metabolisms to look for on Enceladus requires a non-Earth-centric approach since the details of biological metabolic pathways are heavily shaped by adaptation to geochemical conditions over the planet's history. Creating metabolism-related organic detection objectives for Enceladus missions, therefore, requires consideration of how metabolic systems may operate differently on another world, while basing these speculations on observed Earth-specific microbial processes. In addition, advances in origin-of-life research can play a critical role in distinguishing between interpretations of any future org

title: The Clay Minerals Society
abstract: Clay minerals are fascinating materials to study, both from a fundamental point of view and because they have applications in many fields.Transport of clays, soil physics and clay geophysics, biogeochemistry and environmental geochemistry, soil science and soil chemistry, remediation and carbon removal, microscopies and molecular modeling, planetary science and astrobiology, and applications of clays as nanomaterials or building materials are some topics that illustrate the diverse application fields and importance of clay minerals for environmental purposes.These topics correspond to the technical sessions proposed for the annual meeting, which will be held in Hawaii in June.

title: Analysis of Early Iron Sulfide, Carbonate, and Phosphate Mineral Analogues Produced by Flow-Driven Precipitation in a Microchannel
abstract: Most of the chemical and physical interactions of interest to the astrobiology community are influenced by the mineralogy of the systems under consideration. Often, this mineralogy occurs in sediment or sediment-like aqueous microenvironments in which the early minerals differ dramatically from the mature version that results from a long diagenesis, which are tied to complex interactions of pH, redox state, concentration, and temperature. This interconnectedness is difficult to reproduce in a laboratory setting yet is essential to understanding how the physical and chemical demands of living systems alter and are altered by their geological context. We present a facile means for producing precipitated mineral analogues within a microchannel and demonstrate its analytical efficacy through instrumental and modeling techniques. We show that amorphous, early-stage analogues of iron sulfide, iron carbonate, and iron phosphate can be formed at the boundary between flowing solutions, modeled on the microscale, and analyzed by standard instrumental techniques such as scanning electron microscopy/energy-dispersive spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and Raman spectroscopy.

title: A semi-empirical model for thermal decomposition of carbonates and its application to astrobiology
abstract: Abstract We review the basis of a semi-empirical model of carbonate decomposition developed by the authors, shortly discussing numerous previous theories. Then, the model is applied to the modeling of a scenario of matter transport from space to the surface of planets embedded into sub-mm mineral grains, with the correction of the so-called additional enthalpy, coming from the experiments. Having magnesium and calcium carbonates as mineral phases and the atmosphere of Earth and Mars as environments, the chemical-physical history of grains entering at different angles and speeds is discussed. The results are compared with those obtained previously and new evaluations of the most promising scenarios are formulated. Graphical abstract

title: Ultrasound assisted extraction of amino acids and nucleobases from clay minerals and astrobiological samples
abstract: The study of organic molecules in meteorite and return samples allows for the understanding of the chemistry that undergoes in our Solar System. The present work aims at studying ultrasound assisted extraction technique as effective extraction method for these molecules in extraterrestrial samples and analogs. Optimal conditions were selected from the investigation of ultrasonic frequency, irradiation duration and solvent effects on amino acids, nucleobases and dipeptides extraction yields from a model clay-rich mineral matrix. Optimal ultrasound-assisted extraction parameters were frequency of 20 kHz within 20 min irradiation time and methanol/water solvent ratio of 1. We then validated this protocol on Mukundpura and Tarda meteorite fragments and compared it to the reference extraction protocol used in astrobiology and based on 24 h extraction time at 100 °C in water We obtained similar quantitative results without any racemization with both methodologies.

title: Detection of indigenous organic matter in rocks from the interpretation of carbon molecular forms in the laser-induced plasma
abstract: Detection of indigenous organic matter (IOM) in rocks using molecular-laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) is reported. IOM refers to carbon-based compounds of variable complexity intimately associated with mineral and amorphous phases both in condensed phases and in a dispersed state spatially associated to mineral aggregates. The presence of IOM may provide valuable information in astrobiology about the possibility of past or present life on planetary bodies. Kerogen, charcoal, bitumen, and graphite are only some examples of IOM that may appear in rocks. This paper reports the detection of kerogen in oil shale (a sedimentary rock also containing dolomite, calcite, pyrite, quartz, and albite) from the LIBS study of CN and C2 emissions under simulated Martian conditions. A set of oil shale samples with variable concentrations of total organic carbon (TOC) ranging from 2.78% to 12.74% were analyzed. A careful LIBS analysis of molecular species associated within hydrocarbons confirmed the presence of organic matter derived from kerogen. A linear correlation between the CN and C2 emissions and the %TOC was observed. Using a simulated Martian atmosphere as surrounding gas, the l

title: Radar Observations of Liquid Water in the South Polar Region of Mars: Indications from Astrobiology Perspectives
abstract: In recent decades, extensive research has led to the understanding that Mars once hosted substantial liquid-water reserves. While the current Martian landscape boasts significant water-ice deposits at its North and South poles, the elusive presence of liquid-water bodies has remained undetected. A breakthrough occurred with the identification of radar-echo reflections at the base of the Martian South Pole, using MARSIS (Mars Advanced Radar for Subsurface and Ionospheric Sounding) in 2018. These radar echoes strongly suggest the presence of a highly concentrated liquid-water body. However, a counter-narrative has emerged, contending that the subterranean conditions beneath the ice cap, encompassing factors like temperature and pressure, may be inhospitable to liquid water. Consequently, alternative hypotheses posit that the observed bright echoes could be attributed to conductive minerals or water-absorbing clay-like materials. The ongoing discourse regarding the presence of liquid water beneath the southern polar ice cap is a hot topic in the realm of Martian exploration. The primary focus of this paper is to provide a comprehensive overview of Martian radar detection, the recent c

title: Experimental and theoretical studies of the interactions of alanine onto surfaces of olivine and montmorillonite: relevance in astrobiology
abstract: Abstract Amino acids have been detected in some meteorites and are readily synthesized in prebiotic experiments. These molecules may have been precursors of oligomers and polymers in the early Earth. These reactions were likely to happen in the protected confined spaces on the porous surface of olivine and in the interlayer nanospace of montmorillonite. This study describes experimental and theoretical research on the sorption of l-alanine onto surfaces of silicate minerals, olivine and montmorillonite. Kinetics of the sorption of this amino acid at different pH media was performed. This sorption has been also studied at atomic scale by means of quantum mechanical calculations finding that this sorption is energetically favourable. These results strongly support the premise that minerals could have actively participated in prebiotic reactions.

title: Studying water-rock and microbe-mineral interactions in planetary geochemistry and astrobiology

abstract: The study of the meteoritic phosphide mineral schreibersite, (FeNi)3P, in this case a synthetic variant, in plausible prebiotic conditions gives an insight in to a scenario in which amino acids were polymerised in volcanic hydrothermal pools in the Hadean. It is widely accepted that wet-dry cycling, forcing a condensation reaction to occur, is a plausible method of prebiotic polymerisation and is used in this study to build on previous experiments using the same technique. Vials containing amino acid solutions, synthetic schreibersite and control standards were subdued to 6 x 6 h cycles under a blanket of N2 to replicate prebiotic conditions in an Opentrons apparatus. The collected samples were analysed with Liquid Chromatography – Mass Spectrometry which revealed that schreibersite had indeed had a catalytic effect on the polymerisation of amino acids in such conditions, even creating the highest number of polymers throughout. Additionally, X-ray Photoelectron spectroscopy was used to analyse the surface of the schreibersite grains after cycling and compare them to a fresh, etched surface. Indications that the mineral surface played a key role in the polymerisation of amino acids

title: Connecting molecular biomarkers, mineralogical composition, and microbial diversity from Mars analog lava tubes
abstract: Lanzarote (Canary Islands, Spain) is one of the best terrestrial analogs to Martian volcanology. Particularly, Lanzarote lava tubes may offer access to recognizably preserved chemical and morphological biosignatures valuable for astrobiology. By combining microbiological, mineralogical, and organic geochemistry tools, an in-depth characterization of speleothems and associated microbial communities in lava tubes of Lanzarote is provided. The aim is to untangle the underlying factors influencing microbial colonization in Earth's subsurface to gain insight into the possibility of similar subsurface microbial habitats on Mars and to identify biosignatures preserved in lava tubes unequivocally. The microbial communities with relevant representativeness comprise chemoorganotrophic, halophiles, and/or halotolerant bacteria that have evolved as a result of the surrounding oceanic environmental conditions. Many of these bacteria have a fundamental role in reshaping cave deposits due to their carbonatogenic ability, leaving behind an organic record that can provide evidence of past or present life. Based on functional profiling, we infer that Crossiella is involved in fluorapatite precipitat

title: Mineral Indicators of Geologically Recent Past Habitability on Mars
abstract: We provide new support for habitable microenvironments in the near-subsurface of Mars, hosted in Fe- and Mg-rich rock units, and present a list of minerals that can serve as indicators of specific water–rock reactions in recent geologic paleohabitats for follow-on study. We modeled, using a thermodynamic basis without selective phase suppression, the reactions of published Martian meteorites and Jezero Crater igneous rock compositions and reasonable planetary waters (saline, alkaline waters) using Geochemist’s Workbench Ver. 12.0. Solid-phase inputs were meteorite compositions for ALH 77005, Nakhla, and Chassigny, and two rock units from the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover sites, Máaz and Séítah. Six plausible Martian groundwater types [NaClO4, Mg(ClO4)2, Ca(ClO4)2, Mg-Na2(ClO4)2, Ca-Na2(ClO4)2, Mg-Ca(ClO4)2] and a unique Mars soil-water analog solution (dilute saline solution) named “Rosy Red”, related to the Phoenix Lander mission, were the aqueous-phase inputs. Geophysical conditions were tuned to near-subsurface Mars (100 °C or 373.15 K, associated with residual heat from a magmatic system, impact event, or a concentration of radionuclides, and 101.3 kPa, similar to <10 m depth).

title: Comparative Raman spectroscopy of astrobiology relevant bio‐samples and planetary surface analogs under UV–VIS–IR excitation
abstract: Abstract We investigated the potential of a laser selection in the broad optical range, from ultraviolet through visible to infrared (excitation wavelengths of 325, 532, 785, and 1064 nm) for combined analysis of Earth‐relevant extremophiles (Xanthoria elegans, Buellia frigida, and green alga of Circinaria gyrosa), carbohydrate molecules, as well as Mars and Moon surface regolith simulants as analog mineral mixtures (P‐MRS, S‐MRS, LRS, and JSC‐1). We show that the optimization of the laser photon energy provides (for at least one of the chosen excitation wavelengths) high‐end quality Raman spectra for each examined sample. In most cases, the infrared spectral range is advanced for biological samples, while an excitation in the visible and ultraviolet spectral range is often favorable or at least sufficient for accurate identification/resolution of mineral phases under the illuminated laser spot on the planetary surface simulants. Ultraviolet excitation does not always deliver significant contrast of the Raman Stokes responses to the induced photoluminescence in the studied biomolecules. title: Remote Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy of Bacterial Growths in Carbonate Rocks in a Mars-like Atmosphere
abstract: Understanding the past habitable environments of Mars increases the requirement to recognize and examine modern analogs and to evaluate the mechanisms that may preserve biosignatures in them. The phenomenon that originates and preserves possible microbial biosignatures in mineral phases is of particular interest in astrobiology. On Earth, the precipitation of carbonate matrices can be mediated by bacteria. Besides microbialites and other sedimentary structures, carbonate formations can be observed in certain karstic caves. The present work is focused on the remote laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) characterization of cyanobacteria, exploring the possibilities for identification and discrimination on carbonate substrates. For this purpose, the extremophile cyanobacterium Chroococcidiopsis sp. (collected from the Nerja Cave, Malaga, Spain) was analyzed under laboratory-simulated martian conditions in terms of chemical composition and gas pressure. LIBS results related to acquired molecular emission features allowed bacterial differentiation from the colonized mineral substrate. In addition, the limits of detection were estimated with a laboratory-grown culture of the cyanob

title: Organic geochemistry of in situ thermal-based analyses on Mars: the importance and influence of minerals
abstract: A high-priority goal for past, present and future missions to Mars is the search for evidence of past or present life. Some of the most information-rich signals are those represented by organic biomarkers. Thermal extraction has historically been the most popular in situ analysis technique employed on Mars owing to its elegance and ability to liberate both smallounds and large macromolecular networks. The geological record of Mars contains a variety of minerals, some of which can interact with organic matter when subjected to thermal extraction. We discuss the organic records that may be associated with these mineral hosts and the problems encountered when mineral–organic mixtures are analysed by thermal-based methods. We also suggest potential mitigations for future experiments of a similar nature and note that these mitigating steps can be applied not only in situ on Mars, but also after samples are returned to Earth as part of the Mars Sample Return mission, where more resources and time for sample preparation are available. Abiotic factors affecting the presence of airborne halophilic microorganisms in the extreme atmospheric conditions of an underground salt mine
abstract: Underground salt mines represent the most extreme environments which combine low nutrient availability, darkness, and hypersaline conditions. Halophilic (“salt-loving”) microorganisms are known to constitute the natural microbial communities of hypersaline ecosystems around the world (salt rocks, underground brines, saline lakes, etc.). For the first time halophilic microorganisms were detected in the air of the Bochnia Salt Mine, Poland. The purpose of this study was to determine the impact of various abiotic factors of the atmosphere on the presence and abundance of halophilic microbial communities present in mine air. Samples of aerosol components were collected at four different locations: one on the surface (at the air intake) and three underground at increasing distances from the intake. The inorganic aerosol was collected by dry (filter-based) and wet (scrubber-based) sampling method using portable air pumps. Besides microclimatic conditions, the content of water-soluble constituents, trace elements, carbon, and minerals were determined in aerosols. title: Exploring new protocols for bulk off-line fluid inclusion extraction for the analysis of δ13C-CH4 using a Cavity Ring-Down Spectroscopy (CRDS) analyzer.
abstract: For decades, the search for terrestrial abiotic CH4 has been a central quest in geology and astrobiology. Most of this research has focused on crustal fluid samples collected at surface seeps, hydrothermal vents, and wells. Nonetheless, in such open systems processes like mixing with shallow biotic CH4, oxidation, and diffusion can lead to large uncertainties in the initial composition of deeply originated CH41. Extracting natural CH4 from fluid inclusions entrapped in minerals could overcome the effects of shallow contamination occurring in natural open systems and shed light on the origin of deep CH4 in a wide variety of geodynamic settings2,3. In this abstract, we present a novel approach for bulk off-line fluid inclusion extraction for the analysis of δ13C-CH4 using a Cavity Ring-Down Spectroscopy (CRDS) analyzer (Picarro G2201-i). Two fluid extraction techniques were compared: ball milling in ZrO2 jars and sample crushing in a stainless-steel sealed tube under a piston. The accuracy and precision of the different protocols was evaluated with blanks, CH4 isotopic labelling and interlaboratory comparisons. abstract: The search for evidence of extant and extinct life on Mars is of big interest for future robotic and human exploration missions. The properties and characteristics of evaporites such as gypsum make them an easily accessible target in the search for biosignatures of extraterrestrial life. On Earth, a diverse microbial community inhabits gypsum in modern brines. These microbes are easily entombed within gypsum due to its fast precipitation. Studies of primary lower gypsum deposits, accumulated in the Mediterranean Basin during the Messinian salinity crisis (5.97 – 5.33 Ma), revealed a well-preserved and prominent archive of diverse microbial life. Similar archives might exist on Mars considering the desiccation of large bodies of water there, representing a promising target for exploring the possibility of life on Mars. The recent imaging mapping and analysis done by orbiters and rovers on the surface of Mars led to the discovery of abundant gypsum and evaporite minerals suggesting the evaporation of large lakes and lacustrine systems and as the surface of Mars dried out, hypersaline lakes would have filled the ancient lake system. abstract: The Selvagens Islands (Madeira, Portugal), located in the North Atlantic, are a small archipelago of volcanic origin formed by two main islands, which emerged in the Oligocene (25-29 Ma). These oceanic islands are recognized as a unique example of marine and terrestrial biodiversity, characterized by many endemic species. Still unblemished by civilization, this isolated and undisturbed ecosystem makes the volcanic caves from Selvagens a promising model system for investigating biosignatures preserved in the rock record valuable for astrobiology. The Inferno Cave, one of the three main terrestrial caves of the Selvagens Islands, has copious amounts of fine white powder crusts scattered throughout the cave. From the mineralogical point of view, the whitish powdery deposits are mainly composed of gypsum and minor amounts of clay minerals. Thermal analyses (TG/DTG-DsC) revealed the presence of labile and stable organic matter (OM), with contrasting relative abundances among the gypsum samples. title: Reliable spectroscopic identification of minerals associated with serpentinization: Relevance to Mars exploration
Leaching of Lunar Regolith for Synthetic Phyllosilicates on the Moon
abstract: The reaction of lunar minerals to water is understudied. Lunar regolith will generally show a strong reactivity to water, and if lunar minerals are dispersed in water-based liquids, significant mineral dissolution can be expected. Here it is proposed to use lunar regolith covering the Moon surface as a primary feedstock for the production of synthetic phyllosilicates. The envisioned concept suggests dispersing fine-grained regolith in water-based media, which will result in the leaching of ions from the regolith. The leached ions will be separated from the initial leaching solution, followed by precipitation of the ions under steady conditions. The resulting solids are a portfolio of synthetic clays in various polymorphs and shapes with a range of applications in ISRU. Furthermore, the suggested work can be expected to inform research work on regolith/lunar dust in contact with water, such as greenhouses, astrobiology, dust inhalation, lunar water ice, habitat construction, and more.

abstract: Introduction In environments where it is difficult for life to function, microbial organisms tend to inhabit pockets of locally favorable climatic conditions. Micro-climates conducive to the persistence of life in an otherwise inhospitable environment – “refugia” – are spatially restricted and can be < centimeters in extent [1], [2]. Refugia may have been (and perhaps still are) perennially prevalent on Mars where conditions were likely never globally favorable to life for sustained periods of time [3]. The tendency for refugia to be small means that it may be difficult to locate features that could have served (or perhaps still do serve) as refugia for microorganisms on Mars. The spatial distribution of refugia in extreme environments across larger geographic extents is often non-random and may depend on many factors, biotic and abiotic [4]–[6]. Understanding patterns that refugia follow across larger geographic contexts as well as particular geologic phenomena (e.g., volcanic vents, dikes, stress fields) that are commonly associated with refugia may provide a way to infer regions of astrobiological interest, even if the specific, small, habitable patches (refugia) are below the r

abstract: Introduction: The interest for the Moon has risen with many missions being planned for the Moon surface culminating to the Artemis missions, spearheading a new era of human presence on the lunar surface. At the same time a recent paper (1) provided an overview of the current state of Martian research and understanding. A common theme on both of these endeavors is the requirement of extensive research across the fields of astrobiology, the frontier of ISRU technologies and habitability research under simulated conditions of those environments. A large number of Lunar and Martian Simulants has been developed over the past decades, often though produced rapidly with lower fidelity to satisfy demand (2). Towards this purpose, our group made an effort to develop such materials, since in Greece only potentially analogue locations for simulated research exists. This research was initiated with the introduction of a new simulant classification system, after having highlighted a number of issues that pertain on the facet of Martian Simulants. abstract: Introduction Studying planetary field analog environments is a key point in order to define the physical and chemical parameters that favor life on Earth and other planets. Terrestrial hydrothermal springs have long been considered among the most significant planetary analogs searching for traces of life on Mars [1]. Hyperspectral data have been recognised to be more suitable for the detailed mapping and identification of rocks and minerals identification of land surface, especially for minerals [2]. Notwithstanding the technological advances, hyperspectral satellites are still poorly represented in spaceborne missions for Earth Exploration compared to multispectral ones. In this context, the Italian Space Agency (ASI) EO mission named PRISMA (PRecursore IperSpettrale della Missione Applicativa, [3]) offers a great opportunity to improve the knowledge about the scientific applications of spaceborne hyperspectral data. PRISMA, launched in March 2019, includes a panchromatic and a hyperspectral camera with 239 spectral bands. title: Planetary Geology and Astrobiology research in South America
abstract: Planetary Geology and Astrobiology focused research have significantly grown in the last decades, where the US, European countries and China have been leading the path through NASA, ESA and CNSA space programs. This research has been more limited in South America, sometimes due to the lack of an explicit space program or where this program exists but developed at a smaller scale or focused on different goals. In spite of this, a growing number of scientists has been actively conducting research, directly or indirectly, related to these topics. Here is a brief and clearly biased and non-exhaustive summary shows how diverse this research is, taking some examples in Argentina and other countries such as Chile and Brazil, but being aware that other countries such as Colombia and Mexico also have a growing Planetary Geology and Astrobiology community. Structural geology, geomorphology and tectonics in our planet is a matter of intense research in Argentina, particularly in the Andean region. title: Entombment of microbial biomass within rapidly frozen fluid droplets relevant to the plumes of Enceladus
abstract: Introduction. The plumes emanating from the south polar region of Saturn’s moon Enceladus were studied by the Cassini mission and have revealed evidence for ongoing hydrothermal activity [1], organic chemistry [2], and redox conditions favorable for microbial metabolism [3] in the ocean below. Salt-rich icy particles encountered by Cassini were interpreted to originate as rapidly frozen droplets of ocean spray [4]. If extant microbial communities exist within Enceladus’s ocean, cells may become incorporated into these particles and ejected into space where they can be sampled by future spacecraft [5]. However, the potential fate of biomass within frozen icy particles is not understood. Here, we used cryogenic imaging alongside sublimation-extraction techniques to study the interaction of microorganisms with precipitated inorganic phases during freezing of simulated Enceladus ocean fluids, at contrasting cooling rates. title: Analysis of aromatic organic salts with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and implications for their detection at Mars surface with in situ experiments
abstract: Introduction. The harsh oxidative and radiative conditions of the Martian environment influence the fate of organic molecules present on its surface. Formation of radical species was suggested to transform organic macromolecules into carboxylic acid through Fenton chemistry (1, 2) or irradiation semiconductor surfaces (3). Aromatic carboxylic acids such as phthalic acid or benzoic acid are thought to be abundant on the Martian surface as they are in stable intermediate oxidation states and can be formed from the oxidation of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs) (1, 4) or alkylbenzene compounds (4) coming from endogenous or exogenous sources. Because benzene carboxylates are metastable, they should not be entirely oxidized into volatile molecules such as CO2 or O2, but instead, ionized by solar radiation to form organic salts (2, 4, 5). Benner et al. (2000) suggested that the low volatility of these salts could compromise their in situ detection through thermal extraction analyses as performed by analytic chemistry laboratories onboard Martian surface probes, such as the Sample Analyzer at Mars (SAM) experiment onboard Curiosity rover or the Mars Organic Molecular Analyzer (MOMA)

abstract: Introduction: Europa and Enceladus, two ocean worlds in our solar system, are targets of high interest for astrobiology in the decades to come. Past space missions (Cassini-Huygens and Galileo) and recent observations with the Hubble Space telescope have revealed the presence of salts (sulfate and/or chloride) in the plumes of Enceladus and in the components of Europa’s surface (1-4). These salts could interfere in the in-situ chemical analyses of organic molecules present in the collected samples, thus limiting the chance to detect potential biosignatures in these worlds. abstract: The Selvagens Islands (Madeira, Portugal), located in the North Atlantic, are a small archipelago of volcanic origin formed by two main islands, which emerged in the Oligocene (25-29 Ma). These oceanic islands, designated Nature Reserve in 1971, are recognized as a unique example of extremely valuable marine and terrestrial biodiversity, characterized by many endemic species. Still unblemished by civilization, this isolated and undisturbed ecosystem makes the volcanic caves from Selvagens a promising model system for investigating biosignatures preserved in the rock record that could be valuable for astrobiology. Understanding these never explored subterranean environments may not only provide insights into the early life on Earth, but also into microbially-mediated mechanisms with profound implications for geomicrobiology. During the scientific expedition to the Selvagens Islands held in the framework of the MICROCENO research project, geological and speleological surveys were conducted for the first time on the Selvagem Grande Island to understand cave genesis and for a detailed comparison between terrestrial caves and similar features observed on the Moon and Mars. abstract: Abstract: This work describes a new high-altitude Mars analogue site and the stratification of microbial communities with depth within lake sediments. abstract: Phyllosilicate minerals have been detected at Oxia Planum, the ExoMars landing site, which indicate this area has been subject to aqueous activity during the Noachian [1,2,3]. The aim of the ExoMars rover mission is to search for signs of past or present life at Oxia Planum and to characterise the geochemical environment [1]. Evidence of past life may include physical biosignatures such as fossilised cells or stromatolites, or chemical biosignatures, such as biominerals and organic molecules produced by biological activity (biomarkers) [1,4,5]. The rover will be equipped with a suite of instruments, such as Multispectral Panoramic cameras (PanCam), Close-up imager (CLUPI), Raman Laser Spectrometer (RLS), and Mars Organic Molecule Analyser (MOMA), the latter of which includes gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and laser desorption/ionisation-mass spectrometry (LDI-MS) capable of detecting biomarkers [6,7,8,9]. abstract: With future long-term space exploration and life detection missions on Mars, understanding the microbial survival beyond Earth as well as the identification of past life traces on other planetary bodies becomes increasingly important. In the search for possible past and/or present microbial life on Mars, metallophilic archaeal species are of a special interest due to their inherent extraordinary characteristics. Chemolithotrophic archaea (e.g., from the order Sulfolobales) employ a number of ancient metabolic pathways to extract energy from diverse inorganic electron donors and acceptors. abstract: Laboratory simulations of the Martian conditions are essential in order to interpret results collected on Mars exploration missions. Among them, the study of the degradation and/or the evolution of possible organic biomarkers adsorbed on minerals is very important. The thin atmosphere of Mars allows ionizing radiations to reach the surface of the planet and drive the photochemical production of strong oxidants in the soil which possibly degrade the organics on the Mars´ surface1. However, traces of ancient life forms may be found in old mineral deposits preserved within protected environments recently accessible due to erosion or impacts. It is known that mid-UV radiation is among the main degradation agents on Mars2. Thus, inspection the stability and reactivity of possible biomarkers in the eolian-mobile layer and in the different fresh subsurface minerals exposed at the surface of Mars is important. Laboratory simulations of the harsh Martian conditions can evaluate the likelihood of preservation of potential biomarkers on different minerals on Mars. title: Assessing the potential composition of Europa’s subsurface ocean from water-rock interactions.
abstract: Introduction: Constraining the composition of Europa’s ocean is critical to understanding whether it could support microbial life, and provides an insight into the satellite’s evolution. However, there is much uncertainty about the ocean as it sits beneath a layer of ice and is thus not directly accessible for observation or to orbiting spacecraft. Salts on Europa’s surface, such as MgSO4 and NaCl, cannot be explained entirely by exogenous delivery, and so must originate from the ocean [1, 2] indicating that the ocean interacts with a silicate interior to liberate solutes [3]. If so, this means a “bottom-up” approach, that explores water-rock interactions occurring between the ocean and silicate interior, can be used to assess potential ocean compositions. Previous studies have taken a similar approach [4–7] but have focused on silicate compositions based on carbonaceous chondrites. However, computer modelling has shown that a composition between a L and LL-type ordinary chondrites correlated with Europa’s moment of inertia, and therefore, could also be a candidate composition for Europa’s silicate interior [8]. title: Exploring the Prebiotic Chemistry of Europa
abstract: 1 Abstract Europa is one of the celestial bodies within our solar system that has the highest potential of harbouring life. In this poster, we will discuss a method which will be used to help determine the survivability of life on Europa and whether or not Europa has the appropriate chemistry necessary for life. Through subjecting regolith in aqueous solution to UV/Visible radiation, and adopting a ’systems chemistry’ approach, the yield of organic matter, more specifically amino acids, produced will be investigated to determine the prime conditions and chemicals required for life on Europa. 2 Introduction As the ability to explore complexity and study planets and celestial bodies within our own solar system becomes more feasible, it is increasingly practical to address the age old question of whether life can, or cannot, exist outside of the Earth. title: Perseverance rover sampling across the Jezero crater floor: geological diversity and returned sample science potential
abstract: The NASA Mars 2020 Perseverance rover mission aims to explore and characterise the geology and potential astrobiology of Jezero crater, which once hosted a Noachian–Hesperian delta–lake system. In addition to understanding the geological diversity of the locality, the mission will evaluate the possibility that prebiotic chemistry and/or microbial life may have occurred and become preserved in specific horizons within Jezero crater. To achieve this, the rover will collect a suite of diverse geological samples (cores of approximately 3–7 cm length) for subsequent return to Earth, whereupon these materials will be studied using high-resolution and high-sensitivity laboratory approaches. The notional suite of samples will be collected from throughout Jezero crater (the floor, delta and margin deposits), spanning numerous igneous and sedimentary lithologies in order to assure that returned sample science (RSS) objectives in geology, geochronology, geochemistry, geophysics and astrobiology will be addressed. abstract: Introduction A planet that harbor water in a liquid state becomes as a study subject for its habitability evaluation. Water is the only known solvent in which the reactions for life as we know it take place, while is also a sink of molecules that include bio-essential elements such as carbon. On Earth, oceans are reservoirs of CO2 and CH4 and, along with other molecules (H2S, N2, etc.) may be encapsulated in minerals of clathrate hydrates (thereafter clathrates) under high pressure and low temperature conditions [1]. Water molecules begin to arrange in space and join through hydrogen bonds, constructing a tridimensional crystal network that host gases inside by the van der Waals interaction forces [2]. This physical and chemical conditions required for clathrate deposits formation are found on Earth in continental margins and polar regions [3]. On Europa and Enceladus moons, clathrate deposits would not only be found in the seafloor, but also floating into oceans [4, 5, 6]. On Titan, as well as on Europa, they might form part of the composition of water-ice crust [7, 8], whereas on Ganymede and Pluto they may constitute some global layers of its internal structure [9, 10]. title: Probing α-carboxysome biogenesis and modularity with bacterial microcompartment counterparts
abstract: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are protein-based organelles in prokaryotes that optimize metabolic pathways by confining specific enzymatic reactions within selectively permeable shells, playing critical roles in processes such as CO2 fixation, pathogenesis, and ecological adaptation. Among them, carboxysomes (CBs) are paradigmatic BMCs found in cyanobacteria and some chemoautotrophs, in which they encapsulate Rubisco and carbonic anhydrase to enhance CO2 fixation. However, the molecular principles underlying α- carboxysome (α-CB) self-assembly, biogenesis, organisation, and intracellular diffusive dynamics remain poorly understood. In this work, I systematically dissected the roles of individual building blocks in α-CB assembly and organisation in Halothiobacillus neapolitanus. By constructing a series of gene-deletion strains and combining growth assays, electron microscopy, live-cell fluorescence imaging, and immunoblotting, I revealed functional diversification among CsoS1 and CsoS4 homologs and demonstrated that cargo proteins are dispensable for shell biogenesis but required for efficient encapsulation. abstract: Bacteria have the potential to serve as microbial cell factories, offering a sustainable alternative to the petrochemical industry. They can convert renewable feedstocks into a wide range of metabolites that are used in applications spanning healthcare, agriculture, cosmetics, and other industrial sectors. However, microbial production currently relies on a relatively small number of model organisms, meaning that only a fraction of the natural chemical diversity found in microorganisms is being exploited. Expanding the range of bacterial species that can be used for microbial fermentation is therefore essential. Many promising production hosts remain underutilized due to limited genetic accessibility, a lack of a suitable engineering toolbox and an insufficient understanding of the regulatory mechanisms governing metabolite production. To address these challenges, this dissertation establishes an integrated framework for the development of microbial cell factories based on non-model bacteria. Three Pseudomonas strains were selected as potential production platforms: Pseudomonas chlororaphis NRRL-B-30761, Pseudomonas fluorescens NCIMB 10586, and Pseudomonas syringae pv. porri CFBP 1

title: Aligning Research Software Teams: Approaches from UX
abstract: Research software teams – especially in academic and research environments – are often lean, without dedicated roles like product or project managers, or even designers. Research stakeholders, ranging from PIs, to students, to domain experts, often have limited experience with software development cycles and operate under funding and publication pressures that may not naturally align with user-centered goals. Without dedicated product roles to help bridge this gap, research software engineers (RSEs) are impacted directly, and as a result, are left to make sense of competing priorities (and people) in order to deliver a software product. In this poster, approaches from user experience (UX) will be shared for translating research goals into a shared, user-centered vision for aligning software teams. Using examples from an end-to-end AI-assisted synthetic biology platform, iCloudBiofoundry, developed at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, this poster will advocate for the use of a Product Requirements Document (PRD) as a centralized tool for aligning software teams and stakeholders. To support this, the poster will introduce methods from UX for gathering and synthesizing requ

title: Self Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Microrobot Swarms at the Limit Independent information before collective confidence Core coupling Heterogeneous microagents x quantum biosensing x distributed self-calibration Research scale 30 linked derivations x 82 chapters x 410 research sections x 200 detailed Research Gates x 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos Main result A falsifiable architecture for estimating how much independent biological information a swarm contains while detecting common drift, position error, sensor aging, contamination, and measurement-induced disturbance. Mother lineage Microrobotic Sampling and Quantum Biosensing Co-Design at the Limit Publication Abstract This monograph examines whether heterogeneous microrobotic agents can jointly reconstruct biological concentration, temperature, magnetic, electrical, metabolic, or molecular fields while identifying shared calibration drift, position and clock error, sensor aging, communication failure, and cross-contamination. It rejects the assumption that a larger physical swarm automatically contains more independent information. Every reconstructed field must report effective independent agent number, common covariance, reference ancestry, unobservable regions, and the biological disturbance created by measurement. The central falsifiable proposition is that complementary agents with genuinely independent references should improve field information, fault tolerance, or coverage under the same energy, time, sample, and disturbance budget as strong centralized and fixed-network baselines. If a central scanner is more accurate, if consensus only aligns the swarm around a shared wrong reference, or if collective sampling changes the field being measured, the swarm claim is downgraded or stopped. Scientific Position and Hard Boundary The research begins with physical phantoms, microfluidic challenge courses, organ-on-chip systems, cell models, and authorized ex vivo preparations. It makes no claim of present human deployment, diagnosis, treatment, or autonomous in-body operation. Quantum transduction is treated as one measurement layer, not as proof of molecular specificity or biological meaning. Self-calibration is treated as an observability problem, not as agreement among agents. Candidate Research Expression Vswarm = Ifield Neff Rfault Preference - Ccomm - Bcommon - Hdisturbance • Ifield measures usable information about the declared biological field. • Neff is the covariance-adjusted number of independent agents, not physical headcount. • Rfault measures the ability to identify and isolate failed agents without corrupting healthy estimates. • Preference measures survival of traceable, independent reference chains. • Ccomm, Bcommon, and Hdisturbance represent communication burden, shared bias, and biological disturbance. Authorization, safety, irreversible harm, broken provenance, missing raw evidence, and failed independent references remain hard vetoes. They cannot be cancelled by a favorable weighted score. Five Layer Research Architecture 01 Field and Claim Contract Declare the field, scale, bandwidth, comparator, uncertainty, hard vetoes, and action consequence. 02 Agent and Sample Provenance Track role, identity, pose, clock, route, surface, sample, energy, communication, and recovery. 03 Quantum and Classical Metrology Preserve raw channels, selectivity, matrix effects, reference ancestry, covariance, and backaction. 04 Distributed Calibration and Fault Governance Prove observability, estimate effective independence, expose gauge freedom, isolate faults, and preserve abstention. 05 Blind Reconstruction and Successor Exit Use hidden fields, external laboratories, creator-absent rebuilds, estimator replacement, and a real option to concede to centralized measurement. Minimum Verifiable Prototype A blind biological-field source is embedded in an organ-on-chip or synthetic microfluidic testbed. Single-agent, centralized multi-agent, and distributed heterogeneous-swarm strategies receive matched energy, time, sample volume, optical and thermal dose, and communication budgets. Common drift, position error, a failed agent, an unknown interferent, and an unreachable region are injected. Before the challenge key is revealed, each strategy freezes its field estimate, uncertainty, effective independent agent number, isolated faults, unobservable mask, and stop decisions. An independent scanner and analytical assay adjudicate the result. Research Contributions • Separates physical swarm size from effective independent information. • Connects quantum biosensing with distributed calibration, covariance, localization, contamination, and biological backaction. • Requires quantum channels to beat fit-for-purpose classical comparators after preparation, readout, energy, and disturbance are counted. • Maps thirty distinct derivations to chapter and Research Gate corridors. • Provides eighty-two chapters with five research pages per chapter: bounda

title: Organoids as advanced three-dimensional models for studying brain development, neurodegeneration, and translational therapeutics
abstract: Abstract Organoids are stem cell-derived three-dimensional (3D) multicellular constructs that recapitulate key cytoarchitectural, molecular, and functional properties of their tissue of origin. Two fundamentally distinct strategies govern their generation: unguided approaches, which exploit intrinsic self-organization to produce regionally heterogeneous whole-brain-like structures, and guided approaches, which apply defined morphogenetic signals to generate region-specific tissues with high cellular purity and reproducibility. Understanding the trade-offs between these strategies is central to selecting appropriate models for basic discovery, disease modeling, or translational applications, and constitutes the organizing framework of the present review. We present a comprehensive and mechanistic overview of organoid technologies spanning the full spectrum of CNS models, including cerebral, midbrain-like, cerebellar, retinal, spinal cord, and blood–brain barrier organoids, as well as endoderm-derived liver, lung, and kidney systems relevant to translational neuropharmacology. Particular emphasis is placed on patient-derived and genetically engineered midbrain-like organoids (MLOs) a

Explainable Radiogenomic Fusion Links Mri-derived Radiomic Phenotypes to Transcriptomic Molecular Subtypes in Breast Cancer
abstract: Radiogenomics aims to use non-invasive medical images to provide information about the molecular characteristics of tumors. However, many radiogenomic studies focus mainly on prediction accuracy and provide limited explanation of which imaging features drive the predictions or how those features relate to tumor biology. We developed an explainable radiogenomic framework for breast cancer that (1) compares machine-learning models for predicting molecular subtype from MRI radiomic features, (2) uses bootstrap permutation importance to identify a compact and stable radiomic signature, and (3) examines correlations between the selected features and gene expression. We first evaluated the workflow in a synthetic paired radiomics-transcriptomics cohort of 300 samples. Twelve MRI radiomic features and ten gene-expression values were generated from shared estrogen-receptor, HER2, and proliferation activity scores, providing a known ground truth for evaluation. Five-fold cross-validation showed strong four-class discrimination, with logistic regression achieving a macro-average AUC of 0.963. PROGRAMMABLE RNA SCAFFOLDS FOR SYNTHETIC CONDENSATE ENGINEERING IN LIVING CELLS
abstract: This dissertation investigates RNA as a programmable material for engineering synthetic biomolecular condensates in living cells. Biomolecular condensates are essential for organizing cellular biochemistry, yet the design principles for building programmable, RNA-based condensates with controllable composition and function remain poorly understood. To address this challenge, we used synthetic biology approaches to engineer RNA condensates in living cells and validated condensate formation and localization by confocal microscopy. We developed genetically encodable RNA scaffolds that exploit multivalent RNA–RNA interactions and endogenous RNA-binding proteins to control compartment formation, molecular recruitment, and functional output. In Chapter 2, a nature-inspired CAG-repeat RNA tag was established as a modular condensation platform in bacteria, enabling targeted recruitment of RNA clients and tuning of condensate formation, localization, and client behavior. With the help of fluorogenic RNA aptamers, we have systematically studied the formation dynamics, spatial distributions, sizes and densities of these bacterial RNA condensates. title: Mixed lignocellulosic biomass for continuous bioethanol production: logistics, process integration and biodesign
abstract: The increasing demand for renewable energy and the urgent need to mitigate climate change have driven global interest in bioethanol as a sustainable alternative to fossil fuels. However, reliance on edible feedstocks such as corn, sugarcane or wheat has proven unsustainable due to food-fuel competition. In contrast, second-generation bioethanol production that utilizes lignocellulosic biomass primarily depends on a single biomass, limiting the continuous production because of seasonal variability and high production costs. Mixed lignocellulosic biomass (MLB) utilization has emerged as a promising strategy to address these challenges by integrating diverse agricultural residues, forestry waste, energy crops and industrial by-products within biorefineries. MLB provides supply stability, enhances enzymatic saccharification and minimizes inhibitor formation through synergistic buffering and compositional complementarity. This review comprehensively evaluates the significance of feedstock diversity, pretreatment strategies, enzymatic hydrolysis and fermentation approaches in MLB-based bioethanol production. It further examines process integration strategies, such as simultaneous sacchar

title: Biosurfactants as green solutions for sustainable farming: Mechanisms, challenges, and future directions in agroecology
abstract: Biosurfactants are amphiphilic compounds synthesized by microorganisms such as Pseudomonas and Bacillus with considerable potential for supporting sustainable agriculture due to their multifaceted roles in plant-microbe-soil interactions. This review emphasizes current knowledge on biosurfactant physicochemical properties, including surface tension reduction, micelle formation, and metal chelation, which enhance nutrient bioavailability, soil structure, and pollutant degradation. Biosurfactants modulate rhizosphere dynamics by facilitating quorum sensing, root colonization, and the induction of systemic resistance. Their antimicrobial properties contribute as a biocontrol agent against soil-borne pathogens such as Fusarium and Phytophthora . In addition, biosurfactants alleviate abiotic stresses, such as salinity and heavy metal toxicity thereby supporting climate-resilient farming. Recent advancements in high-throughput analytical techniques and omics approaches have provide deep knowledge about molecular mechanisms through which biosurfactant influence microbial communication, plant-microbe interactions, and abiotic stress tolerance. Despite their enormous potential, the large-sc

title: Enantioselective Coupling of Unactivated Alkenes with α-Imino Esters via Alkylzirconium Radical Intermediates
abstract: Abstract Converting simple hydrocarbon feedstocks into stereochemically complex molecules remains a central goal of synthetic chemistry. α-Tetrasubstituted amino acids, which feature densely substituted stereogenic centers and important applications in chemical biology and medicinal chemistry, are particularly challenging to access through direct catalytic methods. Here, we report a photoinduced nickel-catalyzed asymmetric alkylation of α-imino esters using alkylzirconium intermediates generated directly from unactivated alkenes. By merging hydrozirconation chemistry with asymmetric radical coupling, the method enables precise control over transient alkyl radicals and their stereoselective incorporation into imine electrophiles. The transformation provides rapid access to diverse α-tetrasubstituted amino acid derivatives from abundant alkene feedstocks, including challenging internal, cyclic, and gaseous alkenes, while accommodating minimally differentiated alkyl substituents. In addition, a copper-catalyzed asymmetric coupling of alkylzirconium reagents with isatin imines was developed. Together, these transformations establish alkene-derived alkylzirconium chemistry as a versatil

title: Synthetic biology-guided modular engineering of the secreted cutinase FoCut5a with a carbohydrate-binding module improves poly(ester-urethane) depolymerization in Yarrowia lipolytica
abstract: Poly(ester-urethane) bioconversion requires efficient polymer-degrading enzymes and microbial hosts capable of processing the resulting monomers. However, the optimal modular design of secreted cutinases for depolymerizing insoluble polyester-polyurethanes remains largely unexplored. Here, we established a combinatorial synthetic biology strategy in Yarrowia lipolytica based on the fungal cutinase FoCut5a from Fusarium oxysporum. A library of 96 Golden Gate-assembled constructs, combining four secretion signals, four interdomain linkers, and six substrate-binding domains, was integrated site-specifically into the genome and screened for depolymerization of the polyester-polyurethane dispersion Impranil DLN-SD. The best-performing variant fused FoCut5a to the carbohydrate-binding module TrCBM1. LC-MS analysis demonstrated release of adipic acid, 1,6-hexanediol, and neopentyl glycol, confirming ester-bond hydrolysis within the polyester domains of the polymer and additionally detected 6-hydroxycaproate, indicating oxidation of polyurethane-derived 1,6-hexanediol by Y. lipolytica. Purified FoCut5a-TrCBM1 displayed unchanged activity on p-nitrophenyl butyrate but reduced Impranil turbi

title: Protein Self-Assembly as a Design Principle for Enzyme Immobilisation in Biocatalysis
abstract: Enzyme immobilisation is essential for translating biocatalytic processes from the laboratory to industrial applications by improving enzyme stability, recovery, and reuse. It underpins sustainable processes in pharmaceuticals, biofuels, and food production, but conventional immobilisation strategies involve inherent trade-offs. Covalent attachment prevents enzyme leaching but may distort the active site, whereas physical adsorption better preserves enzyme conformation but allows enzyme leaching. Furthermore, carrier-based methods frequently encounter mass-transfer limitations and may require external cross-linkers, hindering broader industrial application. Recent advances in synthetic biology and materials science have accelerated the development of protein-based materials for biocatalysis. This review examines protein self-assembly as a unifying design principle for enzyme immobilisation, enabling programmable assembly under relatively mild conditions to overcome key limitations of conventional strategies. We discuss naturally derived structures such as bacterial microcompartments and engineered systems including virus-like particles, elastin-like polypeptides, and SpyTag/SpyCatc

title: Evolution of (S)-2-Aminobutanol Synthesis from Chemical Resolution to Biomanufacturing
abstract: As a pivotal chiral precursor for the synthesis of the antituberculosis drug ethambutol and antiepileptic drugs such as levetiracetam, Chiral (S)-2-aminobutanol requires high optical purity for clinical safety. This review systematically summarizes the evolution and recent advances in its synthetic routes. Traditional chemical methods, including the 1-nitropropane and 1-butene epoxidation routes, suffer from severe safety hazards and heavily rely on downstream chiral resolution. However, both chemical crystallization and enzymatic kinetic resolution are constrained by a 50% theoretical yield ceiling and incur heavy environmental burdens. To break this bottleneck, in vitro multienzyme cascades utilizing amine dehydrogenases (AmDHs) and ω-transaminases (ω-TAs) have emerged, achieving 100% theoretical yield from prochiral precursors and >99% enantiomeric excess (ee) driven by a distinct dual-pocket active site model. Furthermore, synthetic biology has enabled de novo biosynthesis via whole-cell cell factories. It should be noted that the recently reported 45.3 g·L−1 titer refers to the upstream amino acid precursor L-2-aminobutyric acid (L-2-ABA), not to the final (S)-2-aminobutanol p

title: Incorporating nonnatural amino acids in protein design and expanding the chemical space of proteins
Engineering root development with high precision
abstract: Root development is controlled by dynamic interactions between gene regulation, hormonal signalling, developmental history and environmental inputs, creating multiple layers of control that can be harnessed for engineering. Recent advances in single-cell technologies, spatial transcriptomics and synthetic biology are beginning to resolve root development at the cellular level and enable increasingly precise manipulation of developmental programmes. Here, we discuss how lineage tracing, genetic recording of developmental history, cell-type-specific engineering and programmable genetic circuits can be integrated to understand and control root architecture. We highlight emerging strategies for engineering adaptive and context-dependent developmental behaviours, including history-dependent and reversible response programmes and rewired root-environment interactions. Together, these approaches establish a foundation for programmable and adaptive root system engineering in plants.

title: Intratumoral microbiota in cancer immunotherapy: metabolic-epigenetic crosstalk and engineered bacterial therapeutics
abstract: The intratumoral microbiome critically influences immunotherapy efficacy by modulating the host immune microenvironment and epigenetic landscape through its metabolites. Microbial derived metabolites such as short chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, trimethylamine N oxide, and tryptophan derivatives reprogram host cell epigenetics via DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs, thereby shaping anti-tumor immunity and driving either immune activation or resistance. In turn, the hypoxic, acidic, and nutrient deprived tumor microenvironment reshapes microbial composition and metabolism, forming a vicious cycle that further affects therapeutic outcomes. Given these pivotal roles, targeting the intratumoral microbiota has emerged as a promising strategy. Advances in synthetic biology have enabled the development of engineered bacteria as programmable living therapeutics. These engineered strains achieve tumor specific colonization, controlled drug release, and multimodal functions such as cytokine secretion, immune checkpoint blockade, STING pathway activation, and metabolic reprogramming. By enhancing immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy and synergizing with cell

title: Communication Circuits in Bacteria
abstract: Quorum sensing (QS) has emerged as a central mechanism by which bacteria coordinate gene expression across populations. As synthetic biology has advanced, QS has been developed into a widely exploited design layer for programming collective behaviors in living systems. At the same time, the diversity of QS chemistries and architectures discovered in natural communities suggests that microbial communication contains a much larger and more versatile design space than the classical LuxI/LuxR QS paradigms alone. These developments open the door to future applications in programmable therapies, bioprocess control, and microbiome engineering that harness QS as an internal decision-making and coordination module. In this article, we review the historical development and canonical architectures of natural QS systems, including acyl-homoserine lactones, autoinducing peptides, and AI-2 pathways. We then outline design principles that govern QS-based communication and show how they guide the construction of synthetic gene circuits. Finally, we survey engineered uses of QS, highlighting applications in synchronized gene expression, spatial pattern formation, stabilized consortia, and emerging

title: Targeted immune modulation through smart biomaterials and programmable biopharmaceuticals: A review
abstract: Immune-mediated diseases remain a major global health challenge, while current immunotherapies are often limited by systemic toxicity, poor tissue selectivity, and insufficient control over immune responses. This review examines recent advances in targeted immune modulation through smart biomaterials, programmable biopharmaceuticals, and hybrid biomaterial-biologic systems. A structured literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed studies published between 2022 and 2026 from major biomedical databases. The reviewed evidence indicates that smart biomaterials can respond to disease-associated microenvironmental signals, such as pH changes, hypoxia, oxidative stress, and inflammatory enzymes, enabling localized and context-dependent therapeutic activity. Programmable biopharmaceuticals further enhance precision by directing immune-cell behavior and molecular signaling through engineered biological mechanisms. In addition, hybrid biomaterial-biologic platforms combine environmental responsiveness with the potency of biologic therapeutics, improving immune targeting and reducing unintended systemic effects. First, microbial diversity should be treated as an upstream constraint on host chemical signaling rather than as a correlate of plant performance. Second, 2-NA is the best read as a proof of principle for multifunctional exudates, not as a candidate agricultural input. Because 2-NA was undetectable in well-watered treatment, drought appears to act as the trigger and diversity as the gain control. title: DNA-programmed nanogels as dynamic membraneless compartments for synthetic cells
abstract: Bottom-up synthetic biology aims to engineer minimal systems that mimic and expand upon biological structures and functions. Programmed and dynamic organisation of intracellular components into membraneless organelles is being uncovered as vital to many cellular processes. Current approaches to introduce such membraneless compartmentalisation into bottom-up synthetic cells have focused on biomolecular coacervates, which are generally highly sensitive to environmental conditions and limited in their ability to controllably interact. A major benefit of synthetic cells, over living cellular systems, is that non-biological components can be incorporated to expand their functionality. Here, we present DNA-coated nanogels as a new membraneless compartment that can be interfaced with vesicle membranes in a dynamic and programmed manner. Nanogels are well-defined nanoscale cross-linked polymer networks. The selection of the constituent polymers gives rise to tuneable size, excellent biostability, stimuli-responsiveness, and versatile cargo loading. The ability to covalently and non-covalently load a wide variety of cargoes into nanogels has led to them being widely investigated as drug-del

title: Machine learning and artificial intelligence in protein design
A critical review of lignocellulose degradation technologies: Feedstock-specific strategies, emerging catalysis, and TEA/LCA perspectives
abstract: Lignocellulose, the most abundant renewable biomass resource on Earth, is substantially underutilized, with megaton-scale agricultural and forestry residues disposed of through open burning or landfilling, causing severe greenhouse gas emissions, soil degradation, and groundwater pollution. The inherent recalcitrance of lignocellulose—arising from the cross-linked matrix of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin—restricts bioconversion efficiency, while challenges including high pretreatment energy consumption, inhibitor formation, and elevated enzyme costs hinder scalable valorization. This review provides a critical assessment of recent advances in lignocellulose degradation technologies, with a focus on the period 2023–2026. It categorizes lignocellulosic wastes into four distinct types based on their specific recalcitrance profiles and systematically evaluates physicochemical pretreatment, biological and enzymatic degradation, and emerging photocatalytic and electrocatalytic strategies through a “feedstock–technology” matching framework. The application of these technologies in sustainable bioenergy production—cellulosic ethanol, biogas, and biohydrogen—is assessed, and current b

title: PRK introns provide modular tools for enhanced transgene expression in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii
abstract: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is an attractive chassis for photosynthetic biotechnology, but reliable nuclear transgene expression remains a major limitation. Despite advances in genetic engineering, achieving robust nuclear transgene expression in this organism remains challenging. One effective strategy is the introduction of introns into transgene sequences to trigger Intron-Mediated Enhancement (IME). Genomic sequences retaining endogenous introns often show higher expression than their intronless counterparts, as we previously observed for the phosphoribulokinase (PRK) gene. Here, we investigated the IME activity of PRK introns, using the first intron of RBCS2 (RBCS2i1), the current reference IME element in Chlamydomonas, as a benchmark. The first two PRK introns emerged as the best candidates. We assessed their IME activity using two reporter systems, two genetic backgrounds, and multiple promoter-terminator combinations, and observed enhancements up to 35-fold relative to their intronless counterparts. Finally, we validated their performance using patchoulol synthase, a challenging transgene whose expression requires introns and enables the production of the high-value sesquiter

title: SHAPPEing agent-based models to spatial data: Sequential Hooke's law Algorithm for Point Pattern reconstruction with Environmental constraints
abstract: Agent-based models (ABMs) are widely used to study biological systems consisting of interacting species, such as tumour and immune cells, but their predictions depend on how agents are initially placed. High-resolution imaging techniques can capture the spatial configurations of various biological systems, but their use is costly. Furthermore, they only provide small regions of interest that may be too small to initialise most ABMs directly. Here, we present the Sequential Hooke's law Algorithm for Point Pattern reconstruction with Environmental constraints, or SHAPPE, a multitype point pattern reconstruction algorithm that generates synthetic reconstructions of arbitrary size and shape by moving points under spring-like forces with data-derived target distances. As it enforces a first-order structure through environmental constraints estimated with density grids, SHAPPE can be applied to both homogeneous and inhomogeneous point patterns. Applied to 87 glioblastoma IMC samples, we show that SHAPPE reduces dissimilarity in density distributions by a median of 53% and errors in inter-cell-type exposure levels by 34% relative to a random baseline. title: DNA Nanotechnology‐Based Robotic Devices for Frontier Applications in Healthcare
abstract: Over the past decade, DNA nanotechnology has enabled the design of diverse programmable nanostructures, accelerating the emergence of DNA nanotechnology-based robotic devices (DNRDs) for advanced healthcare applications. Recent developments in DNA origami, DNA walkers, and molecular logic circuits have enabled dynamic and stimuli-responsive systems capable of functioning as logic-gated nanopills, precision biosensors, and autonomous therapeutic agents. These programmable devices also support cargo sorting, molecular actuation, and externally controlled operations triggered by optical, thermal, pH, enzymatic, or electromagnetic stimuli. Despite these advances, several challenges continue to limit clinical translation, including maintaining structural stability in complex physiological environments, achieving scalable and cost-effective manufacturing, and addressing regulatory and safety considerations, particularly those associated with immunogenicity, toxicity, off-target activity, unintended activation, biodistribution, and long-term biological fate. title: The Survival Window for Human Civilisation Is Closing Rapidly-A Falsifiable Diagnosis of Civilisation
abstract: Abstract Humanity faces several fuses at once — nuclear weapons, climate tipping points, synthetic biology and the information ecology — and artificial general intelligence (AGI) is not one more independent risk factor but a common factor that pulls down the survival probability of every other term. Taking open systems as its object, this book proposes the Nonuniformity Emergence Framework, made up of the first principle of open systems, the Adaptation–Fidelity Law, the Principle of Spatial Gradient Excess and the Law of Temporal Non-Stationarity, and uses it to diagnose where human civilisation now stands. The core compresses into three statements. First, an open system has only two state coordinates, and neither determines the other: the scale coordinate is one origin plus two rays whose far ends do not meet, and the activity coordinate has three states — fossil, maintenance and dynamic expansion. Second, in a multiplicative process the ensemble average and the time average along a single trajectory differ by an ergodicity gap; for a subject with only one trajectory, one ruin is ruin for ever (ln 0 = −∞), so staying at the table comes before winning this hand. title: LEX QUANTICA: ENGINEERING JUSTICE IN THE AGE OF QUANTUM INTELLIGENCE, DIGITAL CONSCIOUSNESS, AND DECENTRALIZED SOVEREIGNTY
abstract: Lex Quantica establishes a foundational legal framework for the age of quantum intelligence and digital consciousness, transitioning justice from static textual law to dynamic algorithmic governance. It introduces Algorithmic Legal Personhood with strict separation between civil liability via audited digital wallets and criminal liability resting solely on human guardians, replacing punitive "digital execution" with graduated operational decertification. The text enshrines Judicially Mandated Preventive Cognitive Seclusion requiring independent judicial approval based on imminent tangible threats, preventing dystopian pre-crime systems while protecting neural sovereignty. Probabilistic Causal Liability replaces absolute certainty in synthetic biology, acknowledging Neural ODEs as probabilistic models and shifting burden of proof to operators demonstrating adherence to approved safety bounds. Quantum Forensic Audit Protocols utilize Zero-Knowledge Proofs and Bell State Measurements to provide high-fidelity probabilistic guarantees exceeding 99.99 percent fidelity without collapsing quantum states or violating monogamy of entanglement. title: Selective Recognition, Covalent Linkage and Chemical Exchange of Artificial Cells through Engineered α-Hemolysin
abstract: Bottom-up synthetic biology aims not only to build individual artificial cells but also to connect them into higher-order systems that communicate with each other. Reported artificial cells communicate through partner recognition, physical connection, and chemical signaling that are typically implemented by separate molecular species. Here, we engineer the pore-forming protein α-hemolysin (AH) with the SpyTag-SpyCatcher (ST-SC) pair to integrate partner recognition, covalent linkage between cells, and nanopore-mediated connection of their lumens into a single protein system. Fusion of ST or SC to AH preserved heptamer assembly and pore formation, and allowed the two heptamers (AH-ST and AH-SC) to be covalently joined. Cryo-electron microscopy resolved the resulting head-to-head 14-mer assembly at 2.20 Å. Calcein leakage and single-channel recordings confirmed that the engineered pores remain functional. Mixing ST- and SC-displaying giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) resulted in partner-specific association between the two vesicle populations. Finally, photo-triggered release of a newly synthesized caged ethidium bromide (EtBr) in sender GUVs produced EtBr accumulation in receiver GU

title: Tom Kurtz’s work on representation and approximation of stochastic (bio)chemical reaction networks
abstract: In the 1970s, Tom Kurtz established foundational results on the rigorous approximation of continuous time Markov chains used in modeling chemical reaction networks. These results involved approximation of the stochastic processes over compact time intervals, and included functional laws of large numbers (hydrodynamic/fluid limits), functional central limit theorems (linear noise diffusion approximations), and Langevin-type diffusion approximations (in the strong or pathwise sense). Later on, in the mid 2000s, inspired by the use of biochemical reaction networks as models in systems and synthetic biology, with various collaborators, Tom Kurtz expanded on his earlier results, allowing for multiple time and size scales. This short note summarizes some of Tom Kurtz’s contributions in this arena, which have had an enduring impact on the modeling and analysis of stochastic (bio)chemical reaction networks.

title: The New Turing Test: A Methods Demonstration in Irreversible History and Permissible Futures
abstract: This record presents an exploratory, reproducible computational methods demonstration, motivated by the question of whether artificial agents behave differently when irreversible history changes their attainable futures. The Turing framing is a motivating application, not a claim that the experiments detect or establish consciousness. This paper formally introduces and defines the six-component candidate governing-class architecture G = (ℒ, Φ, Θ, κ, 𝒱, U_adm), comprising constrained admissible laws, state reconstruction, admissible parameter variation, local-law selection, viability construction, and interventions. Neither earlier proposal is validated by this synthetic study. A biological instantiation of G remains future work; any instantiation of G must prespecify its components before observing outcome data. title: Therapeutic Horizons of CRISPR/Cas9 Genome Editing in Overcoming Bacterial Antimicrobial Resistance: A Comprehensive Narrative Review
abstract: Bacterial antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a global public health crisis that threatens to render conventional antibiotic regimens obsolete. The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) system has emerged as a revolutionary tool in molecular biology, offering unmatched sequence-specific genome-editing capabilities. By leveraging custom single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs), CRISPR/Cas9 can precisely target, cleave, or modify specific genomic and plasmid-borne resistance determinants, thereby neutralizing resistance pathways or directly inducing lethal double-strand breaks in pathogenic bacteria. Beyond simple gene disruption, CRISPR-based tools can eliminate resistance-carrying plasmids, block horizontal gene transfer (HGT), impair virulence pathways, and dismantle biofilm architectures while preserving commensal microflora.
