Self-extending DNA recording with stochastic and programmed writing
abstract: Recording cellular histories requires new information to accumulate without erasing earlier records. Here we introduce Infinite Printer, a CRISPR recording architecture that couples self-extension to regeneration of a writable terminal context. A self-targeting prime-editing guide RNA (stpegRNA) directs repeat extension, while base editing generates diversity in situ without a separate insertion template for each character state. Earlier sequence remains upstream of the renewed terminus, linking substrate growth with record retention. Auxiliary pegRNAs specify payloads within a write–renew–write architecture. After three rounds of payload input, 4,436 distinct complete CCA-based records contained identities from all three pools. Longer AC/AT records retained shared upstream marks, and full-length sequence analysis resolved additional endpoint distinctions. Joint single-cell readout recovered 1,549 distinct records and 7,669 combinations across 12,302 transcriptome-linked cell labels from a single stpegRNA design. Spatial-transcriptomic readout recovered spacer records at 11,330 capture spots, linking record content to tissue coordinates and gene-expression profiles. Infinite Printe

title: Precision Plant Breeding: Integrating Genome Editing with Artificial Intelligence- A Review
abstract: Precision plant breeding seeks to link biological target discovery with the development and evaluation of useful alleles in crop improvement. Genome-editing platforms, including CRISPR–Cas nucleases, base editors, prime editors, multiplex editing and cis-regulatory editing, enable targeted genomic alterations; however, their successful use depends on appropriate target choice, editing performance and phenotypic validation. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers complementary approaches for integrating pangenomic, multi-omics, phenotypic and environmental data to prioritise genes and regulatory sequences, predict guide-RNA activity and off-target effects, and support selection across genetic backgrounds and environments. This review examines the potential of combining these methods within a design–build–test–learn framework that connects edit design with molecular verification, high-throughput phenotyping, genomic prediction and conventional breeding operations. Examples discussed include susceptibility-gene and promoter editing for disease resistance, regulatory interventions associated with stress responses, nutritional modification and the emerging application of AI-designed nucleas

title: Gene therapy for hereditary hearing loss: from molecular correction to clinical translation
abstract: The hearing aids and cochlear implants were extremely effective in restoring auditory function; however, none of these devices provides any cure to the underlying molecular disease. Recently there has been an unprecedented advancement in the multiple fields including genomic diagnostics, viral vector engineering, methods of delivering therapeutic cargo into the inner ear, and genome editing technologies leading to the emergence of gene therapy for HHL as a potential treatment option in the clinic. To date, adeno-associated viral (AAV)-mediated gene augmentation approach has demonstrated the most successful results for treatment of HHL and otoferlin (OTOF) related deafness was the first molecular disease for which a gene therapy has proven the possibility to restore auditory function in human patients. Preliminary AAV-OTOF trials significantly improved hearing and speech perception in children with congenital deafness. Later studies have provided additional data regarding the applicability of AAV-based gene therapy for older patients and gained some insights on safety, dose, delivery and durability of the treatment effect. CRISPR-Cas9 Editing of Grapevine Clade V-Related MLO Genes: Grapevine Powdery Mildew Resistance (Erysiphe necator) and Plant Development Effects
abstract: Clade V-MLOs are associated with powdery mildew susceptibility in several plants. In grapevine, four MLO genes (MLO3, MLO4, MLO13, and MLO17) belong to clade V and have been studied to determine their contribution to susceptibility to Erysiphe necator (Grape Powdery Mildew—GPM). Using somatic embryogenesis to generate knockout mutants in grapevine, we performed a series of multiplex gene-editing-mediated transformations to determine each clade V-related MLO’s contribution to GPM resistance. We characterized a hierarchy of contributions from the four MLOs to GPM, with MLO17 playing the largest role, followed by MLO3 and MLO13. In addition, MLO4 was a less essential modifier of GPM resistance: its loss-of-function, in combination with other MLOs, conferred a modest but consistent improvement in GPM resistance, and mlo mutants with a fraction of WT MLO4 allele chimerism lacked the mlo-associated developmental pleiotropic effects. Defects in flower development in most mlo4 mutant lines suggest a role for this gene in reproductive tissues. title: Assessing a natural gene drive for population control in house mice
abstract: House mice are a major invasive pest with significant impact on island ecosystems. Genetic biocontrol via gene editing offers promising new avenues for population control. An alternative idea dating back over half a century is to harness the unmodified, naturally occurring genetic element called t haplotype for population suppression. The t haplotype causes sterility in t/t homozygote males, while +/t heterozygote males transmit the t to most of their offspring via meiotic drive. We use population genetic modelling to systematically explore whether this approach can suppress invasive populations through the accumulation of t/t sterile males. We find that +/t fertile releases combined with the sustained release of t/t sterile males can achieve eradication, but require prolonged interventions, with eradication taking around 25 years under our baseline scenario. We then show that release effort and eradication times may be reduced substantially if releases are combined with trapping, culling, or the release of hyper-competitive ( Adonis ) males. title: CRISPR/Cas9-Mediated CD36 Gene Knockout: A Strategy to Investigate Cancer Progression and Therapeutic Potential
abstract: CD36 (Cluster of Differentiation 36) is a transmembrane glycoprotein that plays a crucial role in various cellular processes, and has been implicated in cancer progression, metastasis, chemoresistance, and radio-resistance. CD36 has recently gained attention as a potential therapeutic target in cancer treatment. CRISPR/Cas9 technology has revolutionized genome editing, enabling precise modifications of specific genes. This study aims to design a CRISPR-based toolkit for the effective knockout of the CD36 gene in human cancer cells. A total of 66 sgRNAs were designed using ATUM (Gene-GPSTM), Edit-R CRISPR Design Tool (Horizon), and CHOPCHOP (v.3), and three sgRNAs were selected based on the target location, on-target efficiency, and minimized off-target effects. The designed sgRNAs were synthesized and cloned into the pSpCas9(BB)-2A-Puro vector, and the recombinant plasmids were verified through colony PCR and sequencing. Donor templates were designed to incorporate an EcoRI restriction site and a 6xHis-tag at the double-stranded break. title: Breeding, genetics, and physiology of improving phosphorus use efficiency in food legumes
abstract: Phosphorus (P) is a crucial plant macronutrient, but the non-renewable nature of P sources for plant growth in soils globally limits crop productivity, causing great concern for future sustainable agriculture and global food security. Thus, improving plant phosphorus use efficiency (PUE) by increasing P-utilization and P-acquisition efficiencies is immediately needed in various crops, including legumes, for intensive cropping systems. This review explores how to harness genetic variability in PUE traits across grain legume gene pools using various conventional breeding and emerging breeding approaches. The role of phytohormones in root architecture development, importance of root exudates secretion, and microbe-assisted breeding represent important strategies for improving PUE, considering the non-renewable nature of P resources and its essential role in plant growth. The genetic makeup of PUE is intricate, orchestrated by quantitative traits and significantly affected by environmental factors. Biparental quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping has been employed to decipher the genetic basis of PUE traits. Progress in legume genomics, particularly high-throughput single nucleotide p

title: SUGP1 Deficiency Leads to Splicing Dysregulation and Reduced piRNA Abundance in Insects
abstract: SUGP1 (SURP and G-patch domain containing 1) participates in splice-site recognition through its interaction with SF3B1, and loss of this factor leads to aberrant splicing. While its role in pre-mRNA splicing is well-documented, its impact on small RNA pathways remains poorly understood. Here, we used CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SUGP1 editing in Bombyx mori BmE cell populations and RNAi to systemically knock down SUGP1 in Drosophila melanogaster. SUGP1 loss caused widespread splicing abnormalities in both species and reduced transposon-derived piRNA abundance as shown by small RNA-seq. Notably, the expression and splicing patterns of known piRNA pathway genes remained largely unchanged. Integrating silkworm transcriptomic data with the Flag-SUGP1 Co-IP/MS interactome revealed no direct association with the components of the piRNA biogenesis pathway, but identified a physical interaction with the Y-box protein (YBX), suggesting a potential link connecting splicing surveillance to RNA metabolism and proteostasis. title: In-vivo CRISPR/Base-Editing “One-Shot” Therapies Targeting PCSK9
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To assess and present the current state of gene editing for reduction of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) with emphasis on technology and ongoing trials for genetic editing of protein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9). RECENT FINDINGS: There are two ongoing clinical trials in humans to edit PCSK9 using CRISPR-Cas9 base editing technology packaged within lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Preliminary interim and preclinical data suggest that this strategy is effective for long-term reduction of PCSK9 and LDL-C following a single IV infusion. Monoclonal antibodies that neutralize circulating PCSK9 have demonstrated the utility of PCSK9 inhibition for reducing LDL-C and ASCVD. Although there is an increasing number of pharmacologic strategies for inhibiting PCSK9, gene editing is an attractive option due to its potential to permanently reduce circulating PCSK9 levels and by extension LDL-C and ASCVD. There are two ongoing clinical trials in humans investigating the safety and efficacy of gene editing for PCSK9 with encouraging preliminary results. title: Precision Medicine in Sickle Cell Disease: From Molecular Pathways to Curative Strategies
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a monogenic β-globin disorder characterized by hemoglobin S polymerization, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion, yet it exhibits remarkable clinical heterogeneity. Despite advances in supportive care and disease-modifying therapies, substantial variability in severity, treatment response, and long-term outcomes persists. Therefore, this review aims to examine the biological and clinical foundations of precision medicine in SCD, emphasizing genomic modifiers, molecular pathways, and phenotype-driven therapeutic strategies. Key pathogenic pathways including hemoglobin polymerization, vascular adhesion, and inflammatory and oxidative amplification have enabled the development of targeted agents such as hydroxyurea, voxelotor, crizanlizumab, and L-glutamine, each demonstrating domain-specific targets. Pharmacogenomic insights, particularly involving fetal hemoglobin regulatory loci (e.g. BCL11A and HBS1L-MYB), further elucidate variability in disease expression and therapeutic response. abstract: Abstract Background: CRISPR platforms could modify molecular causes of neurological disease and engineer cells used in neurosurgical treatment. Their clinical value depends on disease mechanism, editing modality, anatomical delivery and the capacity of surviving neural circuits to recover.Objective: To assess CRISPR therapeutics in neurology and neurosurgery, distinguish human evidence from preclinical findings, and identify requirements for clinical translation.Methods: A targeted narrative review of web-indexed PubMed records, primary publications, trial descriptions, regulatory guidance and sponsor reports was conducted through 11 October 2026. Evidence was assessed by study design, model, delivery, functional outcomes and source maturity. No meta-analysis or formal certainty grading was undertaken.Findings: Human evidence includes hepatic editing for hereditary transthyretin amyloid polyneuropathy and edited immune cells for high-grade glioma. title: Edited HSPCs rescue frataxin deficiency and inflammation-driven multisystemic pathology in Friedreich’s ataxia mice
abstract: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is a multisystemic neurodegenerative disorder caused by GAA repeat expansion in intron 1 of frataxin (FXN), resulting in FXN deficiency and mitochondrial dysfunction. Current therapies do not correct the underlying genetic defect. Here, we demonstrate that ex vivo CRISPR/Cas9 excision of the GAA expansion in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) provides durable, systemic therapy for FRDA. A single infusion of gene-edited Sca1+ HSPCs, mPPL-001, into myeloablative, humanized YG8JR mice resulted in long-term engraftment of donor-derived cells across hematopoietic and FRDA-affected tissues. mPPL-001 increased FXN expression and corrected multiple key pathogenic drivers of FRDA, including mitochondrial stress, microglial and macrophage activation, and inflammatory signaling. These coordinated effects improved motor functions, preserved cerebellar architecture, mitigated cardiac pathology, and promoted survival of insulin-producing β cells in the pancreatic islets of Langerhans. Collectively, these findings establish FXN-edited autologous HSPCs as a one-time, disease-modifying therapy for FRDA and support advancement toward a first-in-human trial.

title: Poison exon splicing in the human brain provides a new paradigm for understanding and targeting neurological disorders
abstract: Poison exons are highly conserved exons whose inclusion creates premature termination codons and triggers nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of the mature transcript. Despite their important role in post-transcriptional regulation, poison exons remain poorly annotated due to the lack of systematic transcriptome-wide approaches. A comparative analysis of 954 eukaryotic transcriptomes reveals that Homo Sapiens exhibits the highest enrichment of NMD-targeted isoforms. By systematically predicting and annotating splicing events that generate premature termination codons, we identify 9,814 poison exons in the human genome. Using RNA-seq datasets from GTEx and BrainSpan, we analyze poison exon splicing across tissues and developmental stages and identify 83 poison exons uniquely found in the human brain, 973 with brain-specific differential splicing, and 1,284 differentially spliced during brain development. By integrating ClinVar annotations with SpliceAI predictions, we identify 1,625 pathogenic variants associated with neurological disorders that are predicted to affect the splicing of 743 poison exons, and we functionally validate the impact of a subset of them using CRISPR prime-editing

title: A Multi-Kinase Inhibitor Screen Identifies mTOR Signaling as a Vulnerability in Advanced Prostate Cancer
abstract: Abstract The receptor tyrosine kinase AXL has context-dependent roles in prostate cancer (PCa). Although AXL signaling has been implicated in PCa progression, it can also promote disseminated tumor cell dormancy. Paradoxically, AXL expression has been reported to be lost in metastatic PCa. This raises two critical questions: Is AXL loss associated with aggressive disease, and does it create therapeutically exploitable vulnerabilities? In this study, we comprehensively analyzed AXL expression across pan-cancer and PCa cohorts and found that AXL downregulation was significantly associated with treatment resistance, aggressive PCa phenotypes, and shorter overall survival. To investigate the functional consequences of AXL loss, we used CRISPR-Cas9 based gene editing to generate isogenic AXL KO cells and characterized their proliferative and migratory properties. To identify therapeutically exploitable vulnerabilities associated with AXL loss, we screened these cells against a library of 1,814 kinase inhibitors using the isogenic cell lines. title: Cells heal themselves: gene-edited hematopoietic stem cells restore frataxin deficiency in multiple organs
abstract: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is a triplet repeat expansion disorder with multisystem, progressive symptoms caused by reduced frataxin protein levels and compromised mitochondrial function. Restoration of frataxin protein is a focus of clinical trials involving adeno-associated viral vectors, but substantial barriers exist because of the immune response they elicit. In this issue of the JCI, Sivakumar et al. harnessed CRISPR/Cas9 editing of endogenous hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) to excise the frataxin gene (FXN) repeat expansion ex vivo, followed by autologous transplantation. A single, systemic infusion of corrected HSPCs resulted in long-term engraftment and sustained multiorgan benefit in a humanized mouse model of FRDA. This improvement in brain, cardiac, and pancreatic symptoms, mediated by myeloid progeny of the engrafted stem cells, provides strong support for the potential effectiveness of this approach in humans and bypasses the need to correct the FXN deficiency in the affected tissue and cells directly.

title: PolyFab: an efficient in vitro pathway assembly tool for natural product synthesis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
abstract: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a widely used industrial chassis for the heterologous biosynthesis of natural products. However, achieving high-level expression of heterologous genes and developing efficient metabolic engineering strategies remain major challenges. Here, based on the polycistronic expression system and the Golden Gate assembly, we have developed an efficient in vitro synthetic pathway assembly method named PolyFab. PolyFab enables the seamless and efficient ligation of multiple transcriptional units (TU) in vitro. When combined with the CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system, these TUs can be integrated into the yeast genome seamlessly with high efficiency. By using PolyFab, we have accomplished the de novo synthesis of the important flavonoid compound apigenin in yeast and carried out overall metabolic engineering optimization of the yeast chassis. Eventually, through shake flask fermentation, the engineered strain produced 165.49 mg/L of apigenin. This work provides an effective tool for rapid pathway construction and multi-gene integration in yeast, facilitating the microbial production of complex natural products.

title: A Meta-Analysis of Animal Experiments on CRISPR-Cas9 Gene Editing for Hereditary Blood Disorders: Efficacy Assessment and Challenges in Hematopoietic System Reconstitution
abstract: Background: Hereditary blood disorders lack curative therapies. As an emerging therapeutic strategy, the efficacy and safety of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing technology in preclinical animal models require systematic integration and evaluation. This study, through a meta-analysis, aims to comprehensively evaluate the editing efficiency, therapeutic efficacy, and impact on hematopoietic system reconstitution of CRISPR-Cas9 in animal models, in order to clarify its potential for clinical application and the existing challenges. Methods: Following the PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched the PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, and Wanfang databases for animal studies on hereditary diseases involving CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing technology, up to September 2024. Data on gene editing efficiency, induced insertions and deletions (InDels), cellular markers (hCD45 + , percentage of CD235a + erythrocytes, and CD3 + immune cell levels), and lymphocyte subsets in the bone marrow and spleen (CD34 + , CD19 + , CD3 + ) were extracted. title: Bioethics in assisted reproduction and embryology
abstract: The use of assisted reproductive therapies, advances in embryo research, and developments in scientific fields such as gene editing and in vitro gametogenesis have attracted the attention of bioethicists for years. On one side, the 14-day rule has faced criticism from embryo researchers advocating for its extension. On the other side, the increasing number of cryopreserved embryos worldwide has raised practical and ethical concerns about their fate. While advancements in scientific research, especially gene editing and in-vitro gametogenesis (IVG), are not yet fully applicable, their potential future use appears to pose significant bioethical questions. In this review, we examine the evolving bioethics of embryo research, focusing on the 14-day rule, the challenges surrounding surplus cryopreserved embryos, and the future dilemmas posed by CRISPR-based gene editing, IVG, and preimplantation genetic testing for polygenic risk (PGT-P). We also highlight the critical role of multidisciplinary, patient-centered counseling in ART practice, to foster informed consent, realistic expectations, and psychosocial well-being. Finally, we underscore the need for anticipatory ethical frameworks

title: Physiological Manipulation of Plants for Crop Improvement Through Biotechnology
abstract: The increasing population, changing environment, decreasing agricultural land, and disturbances in the food chain are the major threats to food security. Crop production through conventional methods poses a challenge to meet the food demand of the growing population. Therefore, the inclusion of biotechnological approaches for manipulating the physiological function of plants can play an important role in meeting the food demand. A higher yield can be attained as a result of genetic alterations aimed at improving characteristics, including photosynthetic efficiency, nutrient utilization, and stress tolerance. Understanding the intricacies of photosynthesis is crucial for crop improvement through biotechnological methods. 228 Focusing on genes related to light absorption, carbon fixation, and sugar synthesis, plants with higher biomass and enhanced photosynthetic efficiency can be developed. Biotic and abiotic stress are also responsible for reducing the crop yield. The introduction of genes that have been identified to be associated with such stress resistance into the plant genome can protect the crop, thereby producing a higher yield. title: NANOTECHNOLOGY-ENABLED NON-VIRAL DELIVERY SYSTEMS FOR CRISPR/CAS9 GENE THERAPY: CURRENT PROGRESS AND TRANSLATIONAL CHALLENGES
abstract: CRISPR/Cas9 has become a versatile platform for programmable genome editing and has generated substantial interest as a therapeutic modality for inherited and acquired diseases. However, clinical translation depends not only on editing specificity but also on safe and efficient delivery of the Cas9 nuclease and guide RNA to the intended cells. Viral vectors can provide high transduction efficiency, but concerns related to immunogenicity, payload constraints, manufacturing complexity and, for some vectors, genomic integration have encouraged development of non-viral alternatives. This review examines nanotechnology-enabled non-viral delivery strategies for CRISPR/Cas9, with emphasis on plasmid DNA, messenger RNA and ribonucleoprotein cargo formats. Major delivery barriers – including extracellular degradation, protein-corona formation, limited tissue penetration, cellular uptake, endosomal entrapment, intracellular trafficking and nuclear access – are discussed together with strategies for overcoming them. title: Generation of Elite Ideal Rice Germplasm via CRISPR/Cas9‐Mediated Multiplex Targeted Gene Editing
abstract: Summary statement Gene editing of five key negative regulatory genes, GS3 , OsBADH2 , Xa13 , Bsr‐d1 and OsSULTR3;6 , generated an elite ideal‐type rice variety mk‐10 , which exhibits a longer grain shape, enhanced tolerance to heat and alkali stress, increased 2AP content, and simultaneous resistance to Xoo , rice blast and Xoc .

title: Epigenetic and Transcriptomic Regulations in Brain Disorders
abstract: Epigenetic and transcriptomic mechanisms are pivotal to the human brain’s complexity, adaptability, and function, regulating gene expression without altering the DNA sequence. These processes, involving DNA methylation, histone modifications, non-coding RNAs, alternative RNA splicing, and regulatory RNAs, enable the brain to respond to developmental cues, environmental factors, and neural activity, shaping neuronal identity, synaptic plasticity, and cognitive processes. Dysregulation of the epigenetic and transcriptomic mechanisms is associated with neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and Rett syndrome, psychiatric conditions like schizophrenia and major depressive disorder, and neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and Huntington’s. This chapter explores how epigenetic and transcriptoincludmic systems interact through feedback loops and system-level regulation to maintain neural resilience. Advanced tools, such as single-cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and CRISPR-based gene editing, allow precise mapping of gene expression across specific cell types and brain regions. title: RNA-Based Therapies for Lipoprotein(a) Reduction: Antisense Oligonucleotides, Small Interfering RNAs, and Emerging Platforms
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an independent, genetically determined, and causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and calcific aortic valve stenosis. Elevated Lp(a) affects approximately 20% of the global population and is not meaningfully modified by lifestyle intervention or existing lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy. This review summarizes the biology of Lp(a) as a therapeutic target, evaluates the efficacy of currently available lipid-lowering agents against this target, and describes the mechanistic principles, clinical evidence, and unresolved questions associated with RNA-based and emerging small-molecule and gene-editing approaches to Lp(a) reduction. RECENT FINDINGS: Four RNA-directed agents targeting hepatic apolipoprotein(a) [apo(a)] synthesis have entered phase 2/3 development. This includes pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO), and olpasiran, zerlasiran, and lepodisiran, which are N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). title: CRISPR/Cas genome editing strategies to enhance abiotic stress tolerance in sugar crops
abstract: Sugar crops including sugarcane, sugar beets, and sweet sorghum, are fundamental for global sucrose supply and crucial feedstocks for bioethanol production and industrial bioproducts. However, yield and sucrose accumulation are significantly influenced by abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity/alkalinity, heat, chilling/freezing, and heavy metal toxicity. The polygenic complexity of stress tolerance, particularly in sugarcane with its large, polyploid, and haplotype-diverse genome, presents significant challenges for conventional breeding, rendering it slow and imprecise. This review combines advances in genome-editing technologies, including CRISPR/Cas systems (Cas9 and Cas12a), along with transcriptional techniques (CRISPRa/i), base editors, and prime editors. These tools, combined with the progress in reference genomes, haplotype-resolved assemblies, and pangenomes, have facilitated precise gene discovery, genomic selection, and targeted editing. CRISPR-based approaches offer promising avenues for enhancing key stress-responsive pathways governing oxidative homeostasis, membrane integrity, osmotic regulation, hormone signaling, and ion-homeostasis in sugar crops. title: Advancing the Translational Pipeline: From In Vivo and In Vitro 2D Models to Next-Generation Cell Culture Models for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Modelling and Drug Discovery
abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is still a global health challenge, as there is no effective treatment due to the inadequacy of conventional experimental platforms for comprehending pathogenic mechanisms and developing therapy. Objectives: This review details the recent progress and clinical utility of next-generation iPSC-derived 3D in vitro systems integrated with microfluidics, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, multi-omics readouts, and AI-based machine learning, which are emerging as transformative platforms for recapitulating key ALS pathological hallmarks. Methods: A literature search was performed using PubMed and Web of Science, including only English-language publications. All the published papers collected covered the period from January 2015 to June 2026. Results: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cerebral organoids, assembloids, and organ-on-a-chip technologies are revolutionizing research into ALS by providing a way to model the complex spatial organization, cellular heterogeneity, and neural network dynamics of the human brain. title: Beyond Viruses: Transposons and CRISPR-Programmable Nonviral Systems for Genome Engineering
abstract: Human gene therapy has been transformed by repurposing mobile genetic elements as tools for efficient gene delivery and precise genome modification. Viruses, transposons, and retrotransposons mobilize genetic material through distinct mechanisms with distinct advantages for genome engineering platforms with therapeutic potential. This review describes the mechanisms, performance characteristics, and translational relevance of nonviral methods of gene transfer and genome engineering, with emphasis on engineered systems such as the Sleeping Beauty (SB) and piggyBac (PB) DNA transposons, R2 retrotransposon-based platforms, CRISPR-associated transposons (CASTs), and prime editing (PE). Clinical trials using both SB- and PB-engineered cells have shown feasibility by demonstrating sustained therapeutic effect through stable transgene integration, such as CD19-directed CAR-T cell therapy for hematological malignancies. These transposon-based vectors enable robust gene transfer for cell engineering, but are fairly promiscuous with respect to where in the genome they insert their genetic cargo. title: EU and US Consumers’ Willingness to Pay for Genome-edited Apples
abstract: New Plant Engineering Techniques (NPETs) refers to new biotechnology tools that allow alterations to a plant’s genome by adding, resequencing, or silencing some of its genes or combined with genes from a crossable plant (so-called cisgenesis). NPETs include genome editing (GenEd) tools, such as Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR), and transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALEN). These techniques lead to mutations in plants, which could have been obtained with conventional hybridization and genetic mutation techniques. For that reason, they may be perceived as more natural. These techniques might raise fewer concerns than transgenic techniques incorporating foreign genes into a plant leading to genetically modified organisms (GMOs). GMOs are as safe as conventional plant substitutes. Nevertheless, consumers in most countries have discounted if not rejected GMOs, especially in Europe. It is important to gauge the social acceptability of these NPETs and their market potential.

title: Reproductive containment of fish using a gene-on/off strategy derived from CRISPR/Cas9 system
abstract: Reproductive containment delays germplasm degradation and is a promising solution for potential ecological concerns associated with genetically modified fish, while also helping protect intellectual property rights related to fish varieties. However, current methods for fish fertility control, which typically involve interfering with germ cell survival or migration using molecular techniques, face a major challenge—modified traits are not often inheritable. Here, we developed a novel strategy to control fish fertility using an induced gene-editing system derived from CRISPR/Cas9. Targeting DANA as the gene-editing site, we established two transgenic zebrafish lines, one carrying a piwi : Cas9 cassette that expresses germ-cell specific Cas9, and the other expressing DANA -targeting guide RNA. In the germ cells of the two hybrid offspring, extensive DNA breaks were expected to occur in DANA , sufficient to disrupt genome structure and induce germ cell apoptosis. These effects were confirmed by Sanger sequencing, immunofluorescence, and TUNEL assays. Germ cells in all hybrid fry were reduced, with approximately 17% showing a complete absence of germ cells. title: A CRISPR-Cas13 system based diagnostic tool for arboviruses
abstract: The unpredictability of the emergence and re-emergence of arboviruses underscores the need for enhancing global preparedness in surveillance capacity for tracking and predicting the growth of arboviral epidemics and case-specific arboviral disease management. In particular, the development of a more advanced clinical diagnostic tool is important for low-resource countries with a higher chance of occurrence of new arboviral epidemics. Despite rapid improvements, the current diagnostic approaches still have limitations and are incapable of meeting the increasing demand for an ideal diagnostics for routine clinical diagnosis of arboviruses. Furthermore, the global incidence of common arboviruses like mosquito-borne dengue viruses (DENV) and Zika viruses (ZIKV) continues to increase dramatically over the years due to globalization, natural and demographic changes. The co-circulation of these arboviruses and different serotypes of the same arbovirus presenting similar clinical symptoms in the tropical regions of the world have further challenged the limits of current diagnostics. title: Uncovering early-stage vaccine candidates against Fasciola hepatica through integrative comparative proteomic analysis and proof-of-concept CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing
abstract: Fasciolosis, mainly caused by the liver fluke Fasciola hepatica , is a globally distributed parasitic disease that affects both livestock and humans, generating significant economic losses and public health concerns. Current control strategies rely mainly on anthelmintic treatments, but the increasing emergence of drug-resistant parasite populations highlights the urgent need for alternative approaches. Although numerous vaccine candidates have been investigated over the past decades, the development of an effective commercial vaccine has been hindered by inconsistent protection across host species and experimental conditions, one of the main limitations being the difficulty in selecting and validating suitable antigens. We implemented a bioinformatic prioritization pipeline by integrating stage-specific proteomic datasets (including ex vivo, in vivo, and secretomes) of early F. hepatica infection. Candidates were selected based on their consistent detection across all datasets and analysed their structural stability, predicted solubility, and antigenic potential. title: Gene Therapy: Routes of Inner Ear Delivery
abstract: Gene delivery and the various routes of administration used to deliver viral vectors constitute a rapidly evolving field, with recent success in restoring hearing in children with OTOF variants in ongoing clinical otoferlin trials. With the rise of gene therapy for major hereditary hearing disorders, both syndromic and nonsyndromic, there has been parallel progress in the development of new delivery methods. Advances in intratympanic injection of antibiotics and corticosteroids, along with nearly half a century of experience in cochlear implantation surgery, have enabled multiple local and systemic approaches to access the inner ear. Recent industry investment in gene therapy and delivery technologies has accelerated scientific progress, underscoring the need for continuous evaluation of the most suitable gene delivery strategies for different causes of hearing loss. Although most gene delivery in animal models has been performed via round window membrane injection, yielding promising results in cochlear hair cell transduction, potential drawbacks remain for clinical translation-particularly limited vector distribution, which may result in a basal-to-apical gradient. title: The RNA helicase DDX1 modulates intraerythrocytic development and gene expression in Plasmodium falciparum
abstract: Abstract Background RNA helicases participate in multiple aspects of RNA metabolism, but the functions of most helicases in malaria parasites remain poorly understood. PfDDX1 is a conserved DEAD-box RNA helicase whose role during the asexual blood-stage development of Plasmodium falciparum has not been defined. Methods Endogenous PfDDX1 fusion-protein lines were generated using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing. PfDDX1 expression and subcellular distribution were examined by Western blotting and immunofluorescence assays. A PfDDX1-HA-ddFKBP conditional knockdown line was used to assess parasite proliferation, intraerythrocytic developmental cycle (IDC) progression, merozoite production, and erythrocyte invasion. Comparative RNA sequencing was performed using morphologically stage-matched ring- and schizont-stage parasites. RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-seq) was used to identify PfDDX1-associated RNAs. Results PfDDX1 contains conserved helicase-associated domains and showed a predominantly nuclear or perinuclear distribution during asexual blood-stage development. title: The Role of SOD1 and Oxidative Stress in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: An Overview
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disorder that selectively affects motor neurons. The median survival time after diagnosis is 2 to 5 years. Oxidative stress (OS), driven mainly by reactive oxygen species (ROS), plays a central role in motor neuron (MN) degeneration. In this narrative review, we analyse the pathogenic role of SOD1 variants and their contribution to OS in ALS. SOD1 mutations alter the Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase enzyme, thereby promoting oxidative damage and triggering neuroinflammatory cascades via the MAPK, NF-κB and Nrf2/ARE signalling pathways. We also discuss emerging proteomic and machine-learning biomarkers, as well as the current therapeutic landscape. Riluzole and edaravone are approved treatments, while AMX0035 was approved in 2022 but withdrawn in 2024. Masitinib and EPI-589 remain investigational. In the realm of genetic therapies, the antisense oligonucleotide tofersen received accelerated FDA approval in 2023 for SOD1-ALS, primarily due to its ability to reduce plasma neurofilament light chain levels. title: A silent intergenic locus for efficient and versatile transgene expression in Plasmodium falciparum
abstract: Abstract Genetically modified Plasmodium falciparum parasites expressing transgenes such as fluorescent markers are crucial tools for malaria research. However, current reporter lines often rely on integrated transgene constructs that disrupt the coding sequence of a native gene, potentially affecting progression in the life cycle of the tool parasite line. We identified six candidate Silent Intergenic Loci (SILs): putatively editable intergenic regions without transcriptional activity, where gene insertions occurred in P. falciparum after its divergence from Plasmodium berghei and Plasmodium vivax . We characterised the largest candidate SIL on chromosome 12, SIL12, by integration of a constitutively expressed cytosolic mScarlet reporter. The resulting PfRed12 parasites progressed normally throughout the life cycle, from asexual blood-stage replication to mosquito stages and subsequent liver infection. Importantly, they infected both Anopheles stephensi and Anopheles coluzzii mosquitoes. abstract: Two-pore domain potassium (K2P) channels are important regulators of the resting membrane potential in various cell types. They are conserved across different phyla and are involved in a wide range of physiological processes and biological functions (Chapter 1). The K2P gene family is greatly diversified and expanded in nematodes, specifically in the model organism Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans). The C. elegans genome contains 47 different K2P-encoding genes, more than three times the number found in mammals (15).Biophysically, this large group of K2P channels in C. elegans are likely to contribute greatly to the maintenance of the negative resting membrane potential of cells. However, the biological significance of having such an expanded and diversified K2P gene family is unclear, given that only a few K2P channels have been functionally characterized, mostly in gain-of-function (GOF) mutations. In this PhD thesis, I investigated the possible physiological and biological functions in different aspects of several body wall muscle- or neuron-enriched K2P channels, in combination with loss-of-function (LOF) mutants and various behavioral assays. title: CRISPR/Cas9 System for High-Throughput Metabolic Engineering in Lactic Acid Bacteria
abstract: Abstract Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are generally recognized as safe, which makes them ideal hosts for producing food-related chemicals. Traditional metabolic engineering has mostly focused on editing one or a few genes, which often fail to meet the demands of industrial production. High-throughput metabolic engineering based on large-scale genome editing tools holds considerable promise for accelerating the construction of industrial strains. Nevertheless, achieving high-throughput metabolic engineering in Laboratories, which requires large-scale systematic modification of entire metabolic networks, remains a major challenge. This Review first summarizes the progress in the metabolic engineering of LAB. It then highlights the application of CRISPR/Cas9 for precise gene editing in the LAB. Next, we systematically review the large-scale genome editing tools in bacteria. Finally, we discuss future directions for developing large-scale genome editing tools in Laboratories. Through these efforts, we expect that LAB can be developed into efficient microbial cell factories for the sustainable production of food chemicals.

abstract: The generation of homozygous lines represents a critical step in vegetable crop breeding and germplasm improvement. Conventional self-pollination and purification methods are time-consuming and prone to severe inbreeding depression. In contrast, haploid breeding technology enables the rapid acquisition of completely homozygous doubled haploid (DH) lines within one to two generations via chromosome doubling, serving as a revolutionary pathway to substantially shorten breeding cycles and enhance breeding efficiency. In this review, the major evolutionary milestones of plant haploid induction technologies are systematically summarized, tracing their development from spontaneous occurrence to in vitro regulation and modern in vivo precision genetic manipulation. The primary technological pathways for constructing in vivo haploid inducer lines via gynogenesis, androgenesis, distant hybridization, and the recent targeted knockout or modification of key reproductive genes (such as CENH3, MTL/PLA1/NLD and DMP) using CRISPR/Cas9 and other gene-editing tools are emphatically discussed. Inherited Anemia: A Contemporary Clinical and Lab Review
abstract: Inherited anemias represent a diverse group of genetic disorders characterized by impaired red blood cell production, increased destruction, or abnormal hemoglobin synthesis. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the contemporary clinical landscape, diagnostic workflows, and therapeutic advancements for both major and rare inherited anemias. Major hemoglobinopathies, including thalassemia and sickle cell disease (SCD), continue to impose a significant global health burden, while rare conditions such as hereditary hemolytic anemias (HHAs), congenital dyserythropoietic anemias (CDAs), and Diamond–Blackfan anemia (DBA) present unique diagnostic challenges. Recent years have seen a paradigm shift in laboratory investigations, primarily driven by the integration of next-generation sequencing (NGS) and third-generation sequencing (TGS) into clinical practice. These technologies have revolutionized the identification of causative variants, particularly in complex or multiallelic cases that elude traditional biochemical assays. title: Loss of nono impairs cardiac morphogenesis and excitation–contraction coupling via the PI3K/Akt pathway in zebrafish
abstract: Pathogenic variants in NONO are clinically linked to congenital heart disease (CHD), but in vivo mechanisms and gene-targeted interventions remain poorly explored. Using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing and morpholino silencing, we established knockout (KO) and knockdown (KD) zebrafish models to study nono in cardiogenesis. Adult KO hearts displayed severe structural remodeling, characterized by ventricular distortion, disorganized sarcomeres, and myocardial fibrosis. High-speed optical mapping and calcium imaging revealed reduced conduction velocity, increased dispersion, and spatial heterogeneity in action potential and Ca 2+ transients, disrupting excitation–contraction coupling. In larvae, nono deficiency downregulated core transcription factors ( nkx2.5, gata4 ), suppressed the PI3K/Akt pathway, and triggered myocardial apoptosis. Exogenous delivery of nono mRNA (Rescue) restored PI3K/Akt signaling, mitigating embryonic cardiovascular defects and functional failure. title: The AF-2 domain of estrogen-related receptor interacts with PPRC1 to modulate larval epidermal marking in Bombyx mori
abstract: Estrogen-related receptors (ERRs) have no natural ligands, vertebrate ERRs rely on their activation function-2 (AF-2) structural domain to recruit coactivators for transcriptional regulation. While metabolic regulation in insects differs significantly from that in vertebrates, it remains unclear whether the regulatory function of insect ERR requires coactivators. Using silkworms as the research subject, this study aims to analyze the molecular mechanisms of ERR-regulated metabolism in insects and refine the metabolic regulatory network. This study applied CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technology to knock out the AF-2 domain of BmERR in the lepidopteran silkworms and examined its effects on functional role, associated interacting factors, and related physiological processes. title: Guard Cell Protein Kinases Regulate Rapid Stomatal Opening in Response to Elevated Temperatures and Water-Use Efficiency in Arabidopsis and Cereals.
abstract: Plants balance photosynthesis and water conservation by regulating stomatal apertures, yet how stomata respond to elevated temperature remains poorly understood. By developing a gas exchange technique that maintains constant leaf-to-air vapor pressure differences (VPDleaf), we discovered robust, reversible stomatal opening in response to warming. Genetic analyses in Arabidopsis and Brachypodium distachyon revealed that this warming-induced opening depends on guard cell CO2 sensing rather than blue light, abscisic acid (ABA), phytochrome B (phyB), or EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3) pathways. Mutants deficient in CO2 signaling components— including ht1, mpk12/mpk4-gc, and cbc1/cbc2—lost the stomatal warming response, indicating a conserved CO2-dependent mechanism across monocots and dicots. Warming rapidly enhanced photosynthesis, lowering intercellular CO2 and triggering stomatal opening, while further heat stress induced a photosynthesis-independent opening pathway, possibly involving brassinosteroid signaling. title: CRISPR-Cas9 in Cancer Therapy: Therapeutic Strategies, Delivery Systems, and Immuno-oncology Applications
abstract: Abstract: Cancer genomics has transformed the field of oncology, with cancer now considered a highly heterogeneous and genetically complex disease driven by a variety of somatic and germline alterations. This complexity, which includes mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, often undermines conventional therapies and leads to drug resistance and relapse, underscoring the critical need for precision medicine. CRISPR-Cas9 system is a revolutionary gene-editing technology that can overcome these challenges by allowing for precise, efficient, and programmable genome modification. Here, the study reviews the different applications of CRISPR-Cas9 in cancer research and therapy. It highlights its foundational role in creating advanced in vitro and in vivo cancer models, enabling the accurate reproduction of tumor biology and the performance of mechanistic studies. Also discussed is the utility of CRISPR-based functional genomic screens to identify novel therapeutic targets and resistance mechanisms. title: Transcriptomic profiling of human iPSC-derived Schwann-like cells reveals NF2-regulated gene regulatory networks
abstract: Abstract Schwann cells are vital to development and maintenance of the peripheral nervous system and their dysfunction has been implicated in a range of neurological and neoplastic disorders, including NF2 -related schwannomatosis ( NF2 -SWN). We have developed a novel human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) model for the study of Schwann cell differentiation in health and disease. We performed transcriptomic, immunofluorescence, and morphological analysis of hiPSC derived Schwann cell precursors (SPCs) and terminally differentiated Schwann cells (SCs) representing distinct stages of development. To further validate our findings, we performed integrated, cross-species analyses across multiple external datasets at bulk and single cell resolution. Our hiPSC model of Schwann cell development shared overlapping gene expression signatures with human amniotic mesenchymal stem cell (hAMSCs) derived SCs and in vivo mouse models, but also revealed unique features that may reflect species-specific aspects of Schwann cell biology. CRISPR/Cas12a-Based Aptasensor for Cas9 Protein Detection in Spiked Food Matrices
abstract: Residual gene editors are a concern associated with the widespread application of CRISPR/Cas9 technology. Here, we developed a CRISPR/Cas12a-based fluorescent aptasensor for the qualitative and quantitative detection of Cas9 protein. Secondary structure prediction and molecular docking were combined to identify potential binding sites of the Cas9-specific aptamer. A fluorescence aptasensor was constructed based on competitive binding: in the presence of Cas9, the aptamer binds to the target and releases complementary DNA (cDNA), which activates the trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a. Cas12a subsequently cleaves a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) reporter labeled with a fluorophore and a quencher, generating a fluorescence signal, expressed in relative fluorescence units (RFU), that increases with Cas9 concentration. The optimized conditions comprised a trans-cleavage reaction time of 20 min, a Cas12a:CRISPR RNA (crRNA) molar ratio of 1:1, a final aptamer concentration of 180 nM, and a combination of low- and high-salt buffers to balance molecular recognition and protein stability. The proposed assay enabled Cas9 protein detection in buffer and Cas9-spiked soybean milk and cereal matrices

India's indigenous CRISPR-based gene-editing therapy for sickle cell disease: innovation to equitable implementation
abstract: In November 2025, the Government of India launched BIRSA 101 (Bhagwan Birsa Munda), the country's first indigenous CRISPR-based gene-editing therapy for sickle cell disease (SCD), with the aim of a one-time curative approach.1 It was developed by CSIR-Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology (CSIR-IGIB), with technology transfer to the Serum Institute of India for future clinical development and large-scale manufacturing.2 This is an important milestone for a country with one of the highest burden of SCD.

title: Stem Cell Gene Editing: A Comprehensive Review of Innovations, Clinical Applications, and Ethical Horizons
abstract: ABSTRACT- The days since humanity has had mortality bought by old age and disease, discussion of extending life with inventions in biology and health sciences, have always had a major place in scientific and medical fields. Although a novel idea, in the past few decades, there has been an upsurge of Stem Cell therapies and Gene Editing talks in the developmental stages, and many have already been employed with success. Stem cells have shown promising aspects in cell regeneration and tissue repair, however, the generation of complete and complex internal organs and organ systems, outside the body is still in the works. Gene editing is another highly effective scientific resource which has shown the possibilities of modifying and altering the gene at the molecular level. The CRISPR- Cas systems, along with many others, are of significance due to their ability of targeted gene modification in the Genomic DNA of a variety of organisms, amongst which, it has proved especially useful in the disease therapy and treatment. Gene Editing and Stem Cell Technologies together have provided us with a much stronger chance of disease treatment and gene targeting, than we have ever had before, ther

title: Chromatin Modifications Orchestrate DNA Repair Pathway Choice: Epigenetics Strategies for Enhancing CRISPR –Cas9‐Mediated Knock‐In Efficiency
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated precise gene knock-in relies on homology-directed repair (HDR) at low frequencies in most mammalian cells, limiting precise gene editing in both research and therapeutic applications. Although multiple strategies have been developed to increase knock-in efficiency, their application can be restricted by technical complexity, limited applicability, or potential safety concerns. In this review, we propose a shift in focus from conventional strategies toward epigenetic methods to increase knock-in efficiency. It has been proved that histone modifications such as H3K36me3, H3K9me3, H4K20me2, and H2AK15ub are involved in DNA damage signallings and the recruitment of key HDR and non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) factors. We further discuss conceptual strategies for transient chromatin modulation to bias repair pathway choice and highlight associated technical challenges and safety considerations. Together, these findings and insights highlight the essential role of histone modification in shaping chromatin states and orchestrating DNA repair dynamics. Accordingly, epigenetic regulation emerges as a compelling strategy to facilitate high-fidelity gene knock-in, offeri

title: Application of the Transgenic Approach in the Plant System
abstract: Transgenic technology has emerged as one of the most powerful and innovative tools in modern agriculture, offering effective solutions to the growing challenges of population expansion, climate change, land degradation, and increasing biotic and abiotic stresses. The ability to introduce precise and beneficial genes from diverse organisms, including bacteria, fungi, animals, and other plants, into plant genomes has transformed crop development for improved productivity and resilience. Early breakthroughs, such as the use of Agrobacterium tumefaciens for gene transfer, laid the foundation for plant genetic engineering, further refined by advanced techniques such as gene gun delivery and CRISPR-mediated genome editing. These approaches enable the creation of crops that exhibit enhanced resistance to insects, pathogens, drought, salinity, extreme temperatures, and other environmental pressures.

title: Modern Techniques Used in Gene Cloning and Gene Editing to Raise Transgenic Plants
abstract: Modern agriculture targets the improvement of crop yield, nutritional value, and resistance against both biotic and abiotic factors. Genetic modifications are done through mutagenesis techniques. Traditional methods that involved physical or chemical agents lacked specificity and caused unintended mutations at random sites within the genome. But significant progress has been made in crop breeding with recent advancements in genome editing. The introduction of site-directed nucleases to edit genes has significantly reduced off-target effects and enabled precise gene editing. A few limitations that were observed in initial gene-editing tools like Zinc finger nucleases (ZFNs) and Transcription activatorlike effector nucleases (TALENs) were overcome in the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR/Cas) mechanism. The discovery of the CRISPR/Cas system proved to be a game-changer in the field of genome editing. As a result, it is extensively used in plant transformation to analyze gene function and improve desired characteristics. Significant advances have been made in understanding the CRISPR/Cas mechanism, leading to the development of variants that have furthe

title: Genome editing of the rutin-degrading enzyme gene FtRDE2 reduces seed bitterness in Tartary buckwheat
abstract: Tartary buckwheat (F. tataricum) is a climate-resilient pseudocereal, yet its global adoption is constrained by its bitter seeds. Here, we employed the CRISPR/Cas9 system to disrupt the rutin-degrading enzyme 2 gene (FtRDE2), which catalyses the hydrolysis of rutin to quercetin, a major contributor to bitterness. Two independent ftrde2 mutant lines showed no detectable rutinosidase activity: mutant seed extracts maintained stable rutin levels and lacked the rapid accumulation of quercetin observed in wild-type controls. Consistent with these biochemical changes, sensory evaluation showed that wild-type flour was consistently identified as more bitter than flour from either ftrde2 mutant line. These results provide direct genetic evidence that FtRDE2 is a major determinant of rutinosidase-dependent seed bitterness and demonstrate the potential of genome editing to reduce bitterness in Tartary buckwheat.

title: Towards AI-Integrated Digital Twin Frameworks for Nanocarrier-Mediated CRISPR Gene Editing: A Perspective
abstract: Non-viral nanocarrier delivery remains a major translational bottleneck for clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based genome editing because functional outcome emerges from coupled losses across biodistribution, cell uptake, intracellular trafficking, endosomal escape, access to the relevant cellular compartment, editing, and tolerability. This Perspective develops three complementary conceptual tools. The Delivery-Specificity-Toxicity (DST) framework treats formulation design as a constrained multi-objective problem. The Composite Nano-Bio Delivery Efficiency (CNBDE) framework represents functional delivery as a chain of conditional probabilities rather than a product of statistically independent barriers, with shared formulation and biological variables allowed to alter multiple stages simultaneously. We explicitly distinguish the chain-rule formulation from the simpler independence approximation and clarify that the novelty of CNBDE lies in CRISPR-specific mechanistic decomposition and its linkage to measurable state variables, not in multiplication itself. Heterogeneous literature values are reclassified by evidence maturity instead of being treat

title: Septins regulate cytokinesis and multicellular development in the closest living relatives of animals
abstract: ABSTRACT Septins are cytoskeletal proteins that regulate cytokinesis in fungi and animals, yet their functions in choanoflagellates — the closest living relatives of animals — have remained unknown. Salpingoeca rosetta, a choanoflagellate that switches between unicellular and multicellular forms, encodes four septins closely related to animal and fungal septins. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of S. rosetta septins revealed that a subset regulate cell size, with two mutants exhibiting an elevated frequency of oversized cells and one exhibiting smaller cells. Three of the four septins were required for proper rosette colony development, while two also regulated rosette structural integrity. Characterization of Sros_septA , which showed the strongest phenotype, revealed a role in cytokinesis: mutant cells exhibited late-stage cytokinesis failure, resulting in enlarged, multinucleated cells. Cytokinesis failure rate increased in uninduced Sros_septA mutant cells and was further elevated upon rosette induction, suggesting that the multicellular context places heightened demands on the septin cytoskeleton. Endogenously tagged Sros _SeptA dynamically redistributed from the basal pole in

title: Targeting the gene encoding human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 basic zip factor via CRISPR/Cas9 potentially affects ATL cell survival
abstract: Abstract Herein, we investigated the role of an essential transcription factor in the human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1) provirus, the HTLV-1 basic zip factor (HBZ), in HTLV-1 infections and adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL). We designed five synthetic guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting HBZ and introduced them into ATL and HTLV-1 infected cell lines using clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9). Of all sgRNAs, sgRNA 171 was the most efficient in introducing mutations at the target site as 70–80% of Cas9/sgRNA 171-transfected host cells contained mutations. Various types of mutations, including deletions, substitutions, insertion, and combinations, were detected in the Cas9/sgRNA 171-treated cells. Based on the predicted peptide sequence, most mutant clones were assumed to inactivate the HBZ mRNA. The mRNA levels of the transactivator from the X-gene region ( tax ) increased after HBZ editing by Cas9/sgRNA 171. No off-target effects were observed in the four human genome regions partially homologous to the sgRNA 171 target sequence. Furthermore, ST-1 cells transfected with Cas9/sgRNA 171 displayed significantly r

Regulatory Strategy, Project Management, and IND Readiness in the Early Development of Ex Vivo CRISPR-Edited Autologous Cell Therapy for Hemoglobinopathies: A Case Analysis for Pre-IND Meetings and the IND Application for FDA
abstract: This article examines early drug development through the lens of regulatory affairs and project management, with emphasis on readiness for Pre-IND meetings and the IND application for FDA. Sickle cell disease (SCD) and transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (TDT) are inherited blood disorders that have long needed durable, disease-modifying options. This article examines the category of ex vivo, CRISPR-edited autologous hematopoietic stem cell therapies, using exagamglogene autotemcel as an illustrative example, to show how a defensible target and therapy selection rationale can be built. The analysis covers the biology of fetal hemoglobin reactivation through the erythroid-specific enhancer of the BCL11A gene, the mechanistic logic of editing a patient's own stem cells, the pivotal clinical evidence, and the regulatory lifecycle, including the expansion of the approved population to children aged 2 years and older in July 2026. It closes with recommendations for strengthening a rationale document and safeguarding it against legal and copyright exposure. The article is scoped to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) biologics pathway; the underlying science is universal, but

title: Genome editing of susceptibility and resistance genes for engineering disease-resistant crops: Recent advances, challenges, and future prospects
Alzheimer’s disease target and drug discovery by leveraging multiomics and electronic health data
abstract: Despite prolific genomic data from individuals with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), translation into treatments has lagged. Here we applied Mendelian randomization to multiple AD genome-wide association studies and functional multiomics datasets to nominate druggable targets, identifying 19 targets for individuals of European ancestry and 7 for African ancestry. This included epoxide hydrolase 2 (EPHX2), for which we identified a protective missense variant (p.Arg287Gln). Experiments in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons and cerebral organoids from patients with AD validated the protective role of p.Arg287Gln via reduced levels of EPHX2 and phosphorylated tau (pTau-181). Pharmacological inhibition of EPHX2 improved cognitive performance in the 5xFAD mouse model of AD. Finally, by leveraging electronic health data from 111,680 patients with mild cognitive impairment, we identified 12 drugs associated with reduced AD incidence, including trazodone (targeting ADRA1A) and baclofen (targeting GABBR1). Thus, integrating multiomics data, functional validation and electronic health data identifies new approaches for treating AD. Hou et al. show a drug target compendium supported by hu

title: Targeting HPV16 E5 and E6 through gene-silencing approaches: mechanisms, preclinical evidence, and therapeutic perspectives
abstract: Cervical cancer, a significant global health challenge, is strongly associated with persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly HPV-16. The viral oncoproteins E5 and E6 are critical to HPV-mediated carcinogenesis, as they promote cell proliferation, immune evasion, apoptosis resistance, and genomic instability. E5 contributes to tumor progression by modulating growth factor signaling and promoting cell survival. E6, on the other hand, primarily drives malignant transformation by targeting the tumor suppressor p53 for degradation. Given their pivotal roles in cervical cancer, both oncoproteins are promising therapeutic targets. Recent advancements in gene-silencing technologies have provided novel opportunities for the selective inhibition of HPV oncogenes. Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and CRISPR/Cas-based genome-editing systems have demonstrated significant potential in suppressing E5 and E6 expression, restoring tumor suppressor functions, inducing apoptosis, and enhancing the sensitivity of cancer cells to conventional therapies. This narrative review summarizes the biological functions of HPV16-derived E5 and E6 in cervical carcinogenesis, and

title: What's New Is Old: “Cultural Lag” and Governance of Risk in the Life Sciences
abstract: As advancement in the life sciences quickens, management of risks remains reactive, creating problematic delays in risk mitigation and difficulties for development of a holistic risk governance strategy. A reactive posture for addressing risk undermines biosecurity and contributes to public distrust in science. This problem is not new. A temporal offset between scientific advancement and oversight of associated risks was described more than a century ago. In 1922, the American sociologist, William Ogburn, coined the term, "cultural lag." Cultural lag was premised on the interconnectedness of technology and society and referred to a period of maladjustment between the introduction of a new technology and societal responses to mitigate its downsides. We examine the consequences of cultural lag for risk governance in the life sciences by looking at three recently introduced technologies, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, the proposed creation of mirror life, and microbiome engineering. Our observations lead to three recommendations for addressing cultural lag. The first recommendation is structural, namely, consolidation of governmental oversight on emerging technologies; the second is goal-o

title: An integration-free CRISPR platform for genetic dissection of respiratory virus host dependencies in human nasal epithelium
abstract: Abstract Respiratory viruses, including coronaviruses, generally initiate infection in the upper respiratory tract, where mechanistic studies of host-virus interactions require models amenable to genetic manipulation. Human nasal air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures are realistic models of the nasal epithelium, but robust CRISPR/Cas9 engineering workflows for this primary cell system have been lacking. Here, we established an integration-free CRISPR/Cas9 workflow for genetic engineering of human nasal basal cells, which are subsequently differentiated into gene-edited ALI cultures. GFP-based sorting of RNP-transfected nasal basal cells substantially increases editing, achieving knockout efficiencies of 70–90% across gene targets (B2M, SLC35A1, ACE2, and TMPRSS2). Genetic disruption of ACE2 markedly reduces infection by SARS-CoV-2 and hCoV-NL63, confirming its important role for both viruses in the human nasal epithelium. TMPRSS2 knockout substantially reduces replication of both viruses, demonstrating SARS-CoV-2 depending on TMPRSS2 in the human nasal epithelium and providing genetic evidence in primary human cell cultures that hCoV-NL63 relies on TMPRSS2. title: CRISPR/Cas9-Based Co-editing of KUP9 and CIPK9 Genes in Rapeseed (Brassica napus) to Improve Drought Tolerance and Yield Traits
abstract: Drought stress restricts rapeseed yield. KUP9 is involved in potassium ion transport and osmotic regulation whereas CIPK9 mediates abscisic acid signaling and stomatal movement which form an interaction network through potassium homeostasis and signal transduction. A dual-gene tandem expression cassette vector based on CRISPR/Cas9 was designed, optimization of genetic transformation and screening strategies were performed, and we obtained plants co-edited for KUP9 and CIPK9 showing enhanced root potassium uptake, synergistically accumulating proline and soluble sugars, and preferential allocation of photosynthates into seeds; yield components showed a non-antagonistic relationship with drought-tolerance physiological indicators, and its yield loss under moderate drought was decreased by about 30%, and this co-editing strategy decouples the negative correlation between drought tolerance and yield.

title: BEST-03 | CRISPR-CAS9 CORRECTION IN SEVERE HEMOPHILIA A
abstract: Background and Aims. Haemophilia A (HA) is a rare X-linked recessive bleeding disorder caused by variants in the F8 gene, which encodes coagulation factor VIII (FVIII). HA is characterized by FVIII deficiency, leading to impaired hemostasis and spontaneous bleeding episodes. In patients with HA, increasing FVIII activity above 2–5% can significantly improve quality of life. The aim of the study is to correct the F8 variant and to restore FVIII expression in a male patient with severe hemophilia A through CRISPR–Cas9 base editing in liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs).Materials and Methods. Peripheral blood stem cells were isolated and reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) after transduction with a non-integrative Sendai virus system. The clones obtained were stabilized, and their pluripotency was characterized by specific markers such as Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and Nanog. Gene correction of HA-iPSCs was performed using CRISPR-Cas9 DNA base editing technology targeting the F8 variant NM_000132.4: c.6967C>T.
